question: What do the terms 'negative margins' and 'positive margins' mean in relation to breast cancer surgery?
source_excerpt: Your pathology results will say how close the cancer cells are to the edges of the area of tissue that was removed. This is called the surgical margin. It might be described as: • Negative or clear margins, meaning no cancer cells were seen at the outer edge of the tissue removed • Positive margins, meaning the cancer cells are very close to, or reach the edge of, the tissue
answer: After breast cancer surgery, the pathology report will indicate if the cancer was completely removed with a clear border or 'margin' of normal tissue around it. Negative or clear margins mean no cancer cells were seen at the outer edge of the tissue removed. This is the ideal outcome, as it suggests all the cancer was successfully removed. Positive margins mean the cancer cells extend very close to or reach the edge of the tissue that was removed. This indicates that some cancer cells may remain, and further surgery may be needed to remove any remaining cancer.

question: What do the terms 'superior', 'inferior', 'medial', 'lateral', 'superficial/anterior', and 'posterior/deep' refer to in a pathology report?
source_excerpt: Your pathology report will give the distance of the cancer from the margins around it. You might see the words: • Superior (top) • Inferior (bottom) • Medial (towards the middle) • Lateral (towards the edge) • Superficial/anterior (front) • Posterior/deep (back)
answer: These terms describe the location or direction of the surgical margins around the area of tissue removed during breast cancer surgery. Superior means the top margin, inferior means the bottom margin, medial means towards the middle of the body, lateral means towards the outer edge, superficial/anterior means the front or surface margin, and posterior/deep means the back or deeper margin. The pathology report will specify the distance of the cancer from each of these margins to indicate if they are clear or involved with cancer cells.

question: How do surgical margins affect further treatment options for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: If you have negative or clear margins, you are unlikely to need more surgery. If you have positive or close margins, you may need to have another operation to remove more tissue. This may involve more breast-conserving surgery, but sometimes it means having a mastectomy to make sure all the cancer has been removed. Your treatment team will discuss with you which treatments are most suitable for you.

This could involve more breast-conserving surgery, or in some cases a mastectomy may be recommended to completely remove the cancer. Your treatment team will discuss the most suitable options based on your specific margin status and other factors.

question: What is lymphovascular invasion and how does it affect breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: If breast cancer cells spread into these vessels, it's called lymphovascular invasion. This increases the chances of the breast cancer spreading to somewhere else in the body. The pathology results will say if there is any lymphovascular invasion in the tissue removed during surgery. Having lymphovascular invasion is different from having breast cancer in the lymph nodes (see page 17). If you have lymphovascular invasion, you may be offered treatments such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

These treatments can target any cancer cells that may have entered the bloodstream or lymphatic system. question: How do doctors check if breast cancer has spread to the lymph nodes?
source_excerpt: If you have invasive breast cancer, your treatment team will usually want to check if any of the lymph nodes (glands) under the arm contain cancer cells. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is often done if tests before your surgery show no evidence the lymph nodes contain cancer cells. The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node or nodes cancer cells are likely to spread to. If tests before your operation show your lymph nodes contain cancer cells, your surgeon is likely to recommend a lymph node clearance. This is when all the lymph nodes under the arm are removed.

This involves removing the first lymph node(s) that cancer would likely spread to first. question: What do the pathology results from lymph node surgery tell me?
section: Pathology results from lymph node surgery
source_excerpt: The pathology results will say how many lymph nodes were removed during surgery and how many contained breast cancer cells. For example, 2/10 means 2 out of the 10 lymph nodes removed had cancer cells inside them. There are a few ways the pathology report might describe what was found in your lymph nodes, including: • Negative lymph nodes, meaning the nodes tested do not contain cancer cells • Isolated tumour cells (ITCs), meaning the nodes contain very few cancer cells • Positive lymph nodes, meaning there are cancer cells in the nodes. Generally, the more positive lymph nodes there are, the more likely the cancer may have or could spread somewhere else in the body • Extracapsular or extranodal spread, meaning cancer cells were found in the tissue surrounding the lymph nodes • Micrometastasis, meaning there was only a very tiny area of breast cancer (0.2mm to 2mm) in the lymph nodes
answer: The pathology results from your lymph node surgery will provide important information about the extent of cancer spread to your lymph nodes. The report will indicate how many lymph nodes were removed during the surgery and how many of those nodes contained breast cancer cells. For example, if the report says '2/10', it means that 2 out of the 10 lymph nodes removed had cancer cells inside them. The results may also describe the lymph node status in different ways, such as negative (no cancer cells), isolated tumor cells (very few cancer cells), positive (cancer cells present), extracapsular/extranodal spread (cancer cells in surrounding tissue), or micrometastasis (a very small area of cancer in the nodes). Understanding the lymph node status helps guide further treatment decisions.

question: What is the purpose of chemotherapy for people with lymph node-positive breast cancer?

answer: For people with lymph node-positive breast cancer, chemotherapy is often recommended to help destroy any remaining cancer cells that may be present in the lymph nodes or elsewhere in the body. Chemotherapy aims to eliminate any undetected microscopic cancer cells and reduce the risk of the cancer returning or spreading further. It is an important part of the treatment plan for many patients with lymph node involvement. Your care team will discuss if chemotherapy is advisable for your specific situation.

question: What does it mean if a breast cancer is estrogen receptor positive (ER-positive)?
source_excerpt: Some breast cancers use the hormones oestrogen or progesterone in the body to help them to grow. These are known as oestrogen receptor positive (ER-positive) and progesterone receptor positive (PR-positive) breast cancers.
answer: If a breast cancer is estrogen receptor positive (ER-positive), it means that the cancer cells have receptors that allow them to use the hormone estrogen to help them grow. ER-positive breast cancers use the estrogen produced by the body to fuel their growth and spread. Understanding the ER status is important for determining the most effective treatment options, as hormone therapy drugs can be used to block estrogen from binding to these receptors and slow or stop the cancer's growth.

question: How is the hormone receptor status of a breast cancer determined?
source_excerpt: Invasive breast cancers are tested to see if they are ER-positive or PR-positive using tissue from a biopsy or after surgery.
answer: The hormone receptor status of a breast cancer is determined through testing of the tumor tissue sample obtained from a biopsy or surgery. The invasive breast cancer cells are tested to see if they have receptors for the hormones estrogen (ER) and progesterone (PR). This testing looks at the amount or proportion of cancer cells that have these hormone receptors present on their surface. If a significant number of cells have estrogen or progesterone receptors, the cancer is classified as ER-positive or PR-positive.

question: What do the scores for hormone receptor status indicate?
source_excerpt: Pathology results often give a score to show: • The amount of hormone receptors on the cancer cells • The proportion of cancer cells with receptors You'll usually see the Quick or Allred score (between 0 and 8) or the H score (between 0 and 300). For both of these, the higher the scores, the more ER-positive or PR-positive the breast cancer is. The percentage of cells with hormone receptors is often given from 0% to 100%. A score of more than 1% is considered hormone receptor positive.
answer: The pathology report will provide scores that indicate the level of hormone receptor positivity for the breast cancer. Common scoring systems include the Quick or Allred score (ranging from 0 to 8) and the H score (ranging from 0 to 300). In general, a score or percentage above 1% is considered hormone receptor positive. The higher the score or percentage, the more hormone-driven the cancer growth is likely to be.

question: What is the purpose of hormone therapy in breast cancer treatment?
section: How hormone receptors affect treatment options
source_excerpt: Hormone therapies block or stop the effect of oestrogen on breast cancer cells. Different hormone therapy drugs do this in different ways. You will only be prescribed hormone therapy if your breast cancer is ER-positive.
answer: Hormone therapy is a type of treatment used for breast cancers that are estrogen receptor positive (ER-positive). The goal of hormone therapy is to block or stop the effects of estrogen on the breast cancer cells, as estrogen can stimulate the growth of ER-positive breast cancers. Different hormone therapy drugs work in different ways to achieve this, but they are only prescribed if your breast cancer tests positive for estrogen receptors. If your cancer is only progesterone receptor positive, the benefits of hormone therapy are less clear, and your doctor will discuss with you if it is an appropriate treatment option.

question: What does it mean if my breast cancer is HER2-positive?
source_excerpt: Some breast cancer cells have a higher-than-normal level of a protein called HER2 on their surface, which makes them grow more quickly. This is known as HER2-positive breast cancer. If your breast cancer is HER2-positive you will usually be advised to have chemotherapy and a targeted therapy such as trastuzumab or Phesgo, which is a combination of trastuzumab and pertuzumab (another type of targeted therapy). Targeted therapies block the growth and spread of cancer.
answer: HER2-positive breast cancer means that the cancer cells have higher than normal levels of a protein called HER2 on their surface. This causes the cancer cells to grow more quickly. All invasive breast cancers are tested for HER2 levels using tests like IHC, FISH, CISH or DDISH on a sample of the tumor tissue. A score of 3+ on the IHC test or a positive result on the other tests indicates HER2-positive breast cancer. If your cancer is HER2-positive, you will likely be recommended to receive chemotherapy along with a targeted therapy like trastuzumab or Phesgo that blocks the effects of the HER2 protein.

question: What treatment options are available for HER2-low breast cancers?
section: How HER2 levels affect treatment options
source_excerpt: There is also evidence that HER2-low breast cancer may benefit from HER2 targeted therapy. The drug trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu) can be used to treat HER2-low breast cancers in some instances. However, this is not currently available throughout the UK.
answer: For breast cancers that test as HER2-low, which means they have a borderline or low level of HER2 protein, there is some evidence that targeted therapy against HER2 may be beneficial. Specifically, the drug trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu) can be used to treat HER2-low breast cancers in certain cases. However, this treatment is not currently available throughout the UK, so availability may be limited. question: What are genomic assays and how do they help with breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Genomic assays (also called gene expression profiling or gene assays) are tests that look at groups of genes found in breast cancer cells. They help identify who is most likely to benefit from chemotherapy as well as hormone therapy, and how likely the cancer is to return (recurrence). Your team will use the tests, along with other information about the breast cancer, to help decide what treatment to recommend.

question: Who is eligible for genomic assays and when are they recommended?

Your treatment team will discuss having genomic assays with you if they think they would help with making decisions about your treatment.

question: What is the EndoPredict test and how does it help determine treatment for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: This test predicts how likely the cancer is to spread somewhere else in the body. It's suitable for some people who will be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years. The test gives a score, known as an EPclin Risk Score, that's reported as low or high risk. A low risk score means it's unlikely the breast cancer will spread to somewhere else in the body. Most people with a low risk score will not need chemotherapy. A high risk score means it's more likely the breast cancer will spread to somewhere else in the body. Chemotherapy is recommended for most people with a high risk score.

question: How does the Oncotype DX test help determine if chemotherapy is needed for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: This test predicts how likely the cancer is to spread to somewhere else in the body. It's suitable for some people who will be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years. The test gives a score, called a Recurrence Score, from 0 to 100. The higher the score, the more likely breast cancer is to come back and the more likely you are to benefit from having chemotherapy as well as hormone therapy. Chemotherapy is usually recommended if you have: • A score of 26 or above and you are over the age of 50 • A score of 16 or above and you are aged 50 or under

question: What is chemotherapy and how does it work for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy is a treatment that destroys cancer cells using anti-cancer drugs. Normal cells in the body divide and grow all the time in an ordered and controlled way. Cancer cells divide and grow in a disordered and uncontrolled way. Chemotherapy destroys cancer cells by affecting their ability to divide and grow. Different chemotherapy drugs work in different ways and affect cancer cells at different times in their growth. This is why a combination of drugs is often used and given in cycles. See page 8 for more information about chemotherapy cycles. Chemotherapy also affects other normal cells throughout the body, which causes side effects (see page 17).
answer: Chemotherapy is a treatment that uses anti-cancer drugs to destroy cancer cells. It works by affecting the ability of cancer cells to divide and grow in an uncontrolled way. Normal cells in the body divide and grow in an ordered, controlled manner, but cancer cells divide and grow in a disordered, uncontrolled way. Chemotherapy drugs target and destroy these rapidly dividing cancer cells. Different chemotherapy drugs work in different ways and affect cancer cells at different stages of their growth cycle. That's why a combination of drugs is often used and given in cycles to effectively target the cancer cells. While chemotherapy targets cancer cells, it can also affect some normal cells, which leads to side effects.

question: When is chemotherapy given for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt:
Primary breast cancer 
Before surgery 
You may have chemotherapy before surgery to slow the growth of 
fast-growing breast cancer. Or you may have it to shrink a larger 
breast cancer before surgery. This may mean breast-conserving 
surgery is an option, rather than a mastectomy. 
Chemotherapy given before surgery is called primary or 
neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
You may be more likely to have chemotherapy before surgery 
if you have inflammatory or triple negative breast cancer, or if 
your breast cancer is HER2-positive. 

After surgery
You may have chemotherapy after surgery for primary breast 
cancer to reduce the risk of the cancer coming back or 
spreading. This is called adjuvant chemotherapy. 
You may be given chemotherapy in combination with other 
treatments, such as targeted therapy. 

Secondary breast cancer
Chemotherapy can also be used to treat secondary breast 
cancer. Secondary breast cancer is breast cancer that has 
spread to another part of the body, such as the bones, lungs, 
liver or brain. 
Secondary breast cancer, also called metastatic breast cancer, 
can be treated but cannot be cured. 
Chemotherapy aims to slow down and control the growth of 
secondary breast cancer and relieve symptoms.
answer: Chemotherapy can be given at different stages of breast cancer treatment. Before surgery (called primary or neoadjuvant chemotherapy), it may be used to slow the growth of fast-growing cancers or shrink larger tumors, potentially allowing for breast-conserving surgery instead of a mastectomy. This is more common for aggressive types like inflammatory, triple negative, or HER2-positive breast cancers. After surgery (adjuvant chemotherapy), chemo aims to reduce the risk of the cancer returning or spreading. It's often combined with other treatments. For secondary or metastatic breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body, chemotherapy helps control the growth and relieve symptoms, although it cannot cure it at this stage.

question: What is the purpose of giving chemotherapy before breast cancer surgery?

source_excerpt:
You may have chemotherapy before surgery to slow the growth of

answer: Chemotherapy given before surgery, called primary or neoadjuvant chemotherapy, has a few key purposes. Firstly, it can help slow the growth of fast-growing, aggressive breast cancers. Secondly, it may shrink larger tumors, potentially allowing breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) instead of a full mastectomy. This pre-surgery chemo is more likely for certain breast cancer types like inflammatory, triple negative, or HER2-positive, which tend to be more aggressive. By shrinking the tumor first, neoadjuvant chemo gives some patients a better chance at less extensive surgery while still effectively treating the cancer.

question: What factors determine if chemotherapy will be recommended for primary breast cancer?

source_excerpt: If you have primary breast cancer, whether you're offered chemotherapy will depend on: • The size, stage and grade of your breast cancer • The oestrogen receptor status • The HER2 status • Whether you have an inherited altered gene that increases breast cancer risk, such as BRCA1
answer: Whether chemotherapy is recommended for primary breast cancer depends on several factors related to the specific characteristics of your cancer and your overall health. Your treatment team will also take into account your general health condition and any other medical issues you may have. The goal is to develop a personalized treatment plan that gives you the best possible outcome based on the unique features of your cancer and your individual circumstances.

question: What are genomic assays and how are they used in breast cancer treatment?

section: Genomic assays (also called gene expression profiling or gene assays)
source_excerpt: When the benefit of chemotherapy is less certain, your treatment team may suggest tests called genomic assays. These tests look at groups of genes found in breast cancer cells. They help identify who is most likely to benefit from chemotherapy and how likely the cancer is to come back (recurrence). The tests are carried out on breast tissue removed during surgery or during the original biopsy on your breast. The results are provided separately from your pathology report. Your treatment team will consider them alongside your other pathology results to help them decide what treatments to recommend. Genomic assays are not suitable for everyone. If any of these tests are suitable for you, your treatment team will discuss this with you.

section: Genomic assays (also called gene expression profiling or gene assays)
source_excerpt: Genomic assays you may be offered are: EndoPredict EndoPredict is a test that predicts how likely breast cancer is to spread to somewhere else in the body. It's suitable for some people who will be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years. Oncotype DX Oncotype DX is a test that predicts how likely breast cancer is to spread to somewhere else in the body. It's suitable for some people who will be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years. The test gives a score between 0 and 100. People who score above a certain number are more likely to be offered chemotherapy.
answer: Two specific genomic assays that may be offered for breast cancer treatment are EndoPredict and Oncotype DX. EndoPredict is a test that predicts how likely breast cancer is to spread to somewhere else in the body. It is suitable for some people who will be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years. Oncotype DX is another test that predicts how likely breast cancer is to spread to other parts of the body. It is also suitable for some people who will be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years. The Oncotype DX test gives a score between 0 and 100, and people who score above a certain number are more likely to be offered chemotherapy.

question: How can I get help in deciding whether to have chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Your treatment team may ask you if you want to have chemotherapy. This is a personal decision and you'll need to weigh up the likely benefits against potential side effects. You can talk this through with your treatment team or breast care nurse. They can answer your questions and support you with your decision. You can also speak to our specialist nurses on 0808 800 6000 or at breastcancernow.org
answer: Deciding whether to undergo chemotherapy is a very personal decision that requires careful consideration of the potential benefits and side effects. Your treatment team, including your doctors and breast care nurse, are available to discuss this decision with you in detail. They can provide information, answer your questions, and support you through this process. Additionally, you can speak to the specialist nurses at Breast Cancer Now by calling their helpline at 0808 800 6000 or visiting their website for further guidance.

question: What should I expect before starting chemotherapy treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Before starting your treatment, a member of your treatment team will discuss how and when you'll have chemotherapy and how side effects can be managed. answer: Before starting chemotherapy, your treatment team will discuss the details of your treatment plan, including how and when you'll receive chemotherapy, and how potential side effects can be managed. You'll undergo various tests and assessments, such as blood tests, height and weight measurements, and tests to check your heart function like an ECG, echocardiogram, or MUGA scan. Additionally, you'll be provided with a 24-hour contact number or information on who to reach out to if you feel unwell at any time during your treatment, even overnight or on weekends. You'll also be asked to sign a consent form after discussing the benefits and risks of the chemotherapy treatment.

question: How long does chemotherapy treatment typically last for breast cancer patients?

source_excerpt: How long you have chemotherapy will depend on your individual situation. Your treatment team will discuss this with you.

question: What should breast cancer patients be aware of before starting chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Things to consider before chemotherapy • Chemotherapy can cause hair loss (see page 21) • Chemotherapy may affect your fertility (see page 33). If you're concerned about this, it's important to discuss it with your treatment team before you begin treatment
answer: Before starting chemotherapy, it's important for breast cancer patients to be aware of and consider a few potential side effects and impacts. Chemotherapy can cause hair loss, which is a common side effect. Additionally, chemotherapy may affect fertility, so if you are concerned about this, it's crucial to discuss it with your treatment team before beginning treatment. Your healthcare providers will explain all the potential side effects and considerations to you thoroughly before you start chemotherapy.

question: What medications are given before chemotherapy for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You'll usually be given anti-sickness (also called anti-emetic) drugs before each chemotherapy treatment. The drugs you're given will depend on the type of chemotherapy you're having, but will often include a steroid drug called dexamethasone as well as the anti-sickness medication.
answer: Before each chemotherapy treatment for breast cancer, you will typically be given anti-sickness (also called anti-emetic) medications. The specific anti-nausea drugs you receive will depend on the type of chemotherapy you are having, but will often include a steroid drug called dexamethasone as well as other anti-sickness medications. These pre-chemotherapy medications help prevent and manage nausea and vomiting, which are common side effects of chemotherapy. Your healthcare team will explain the anti-sickness regimen you'll receive before your treatments.

question: How is intravenous chemotherapy administered?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: The most common way of giving chemotherapy involves inserting a small needle and a plastic tube called a cannula into a vein. It's usually inserted in the back of your hand or lower arm. The needle is removed and the cannula is left in place. The chemotherapy drugs are slowly injected into the vein. If a large volume of fluid is used it will be given as an infusion (drip) through the cannula over a fixed period of time.
answer: Intravenous chemotherapy is typically given through a small plastic tube called a cannula that is inserted into a vein, usually in the back of your hand or lower arm. The chemotherapy drugs are slowly injected through the cannula, either directly or as an infusion (drip) over a set period of time. This allows the medication to enter your bloodstream for treatment.

question: Where do patients typically receive intravenous chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You'll normally have your treatment at hospital as an outpatient or day case. This means you'll be able to go home the same day. You may be at the hospital for a short time only. However, because of tests, waiting times and how long it takes to prepare and give the chemotherapy drugs, you may be there for most of the day. In some areas of the country, chemotherapy may be given in a mobile treatment centre or in your home.
answer: Most patients receive intravenous chemotherapy as an outpatient or day case at the hospital. This means you'll be able to go home the same day after your treatment. However, you may need to be at the hospital for most of the day due to tests, waiting times, and the preparation and administration of the chemotherapy drugs. Some areas offer chemotherapy in mobile treatment centers or at home as well.

question: What is a chemotherapy cycle and how long does it typically last?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You'll normally have chemotherapy as a series of treatments with a break between each treatment. This allows your body time to recover from any short-term side effects. The treatment and period of time before the next one starts is called a cycle. Cycles usually last between 1 and 6 weeks.
answer: Chemotherapy is usually given as a series of treatments called cycles, with breaks in between to allow your body to recover from any short-term side effects. A cycle consists of the chemotherapy treatment itself followed by a rest period before the next treatment starts. Cycles typically last between 1 and 6 weeks.

question: Why might a patient's chemotherapy treatment be delayed?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If the number of blood cells in your body is too low, your treatment may need to be delayed (see pages 17 to 19 for an explanation of how chemotherapy affects the number of blood cells).
answer: Your chemotherapy treatment may need to be delayed if your blood test results show that the number of blood cells in your body is too low. This is because chemotherapy can affect your blood cell counts, so your healthcare team will monitor your levels closely. If your counts are low, they may postpone your next cycle until the levels recover to avoid potential complications.

question: What is lymphoedema and how does it relate to breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Lymphoedema is swelling caused by a build-up of fluid in the body's tissues. It usually affects the arm, but it may also affect the hand and fingers. Lymphoedema can also affect the breast, chest, and occasionally the shoulder or the area on the back behind the armpit. Some people develop lymphoedema after surgery or radiotherapy to the lymph nodes under the arm and the surrounding area.
answer: Lymphoedema is swelling caused by a buildup of fluid in the body's tissues. It can occur after breast cancer surgery or radiotherapy to the lymph nodes under the arm and surrounding area. Lymphoedema most commonly affects the arm on the same side as the surgery, but it can also impact the hand, fingers, breast, chest, shoulder, or back near the armpit. While there is no consistent evidence that having injections or IV treatments in the 'at risk' arm increases lymphoedema risk, many treatment teams give chemotherapy through a vein in the opposite arm as a precaution. If you develop lymphoedema, your chemotherapy will be administered in the arm opposite your surgery to avoid further swelling.

question: How is chemotherapy administered if I have lymphoedema?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you have lymphoedema, the cannula will be placed in the arm on the opposite side to where you had surgery. If you have lymphoedema on both sides, your treatment team will talk to you about how your chemotherapy will be given.
answer: If you have developed lymphoedema after breast cancer surgery, your chemotherapy will be given through an intravenous (IV) line in the arm on the opposite side from where you had surgery. This helps prevent further swelling or complications in the affected arm. If you have lymphoedema in both arms, your treatment team will discuss the best approach for administering your chemotherapy safely and comfortably. They may use a central venous access device like a skin-tunneled catheter inserted into a vein in your chest. This allows chemotherapy to be given without using the arms and reduces lymphoedema risk.

question: What is a skin-tunneled catheter and how is it used for chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: A skin-tunnelled catheter (Hickman or Groshong line) is a fine silicone tube that's inserted into a vein through a small cut in the chest. It's also called a Hickman or Groshong line. The catheter is usually put in under a local anaesthetic, but a general anaesthetic (medicine to make you sleep) can be used if necessary. Your chemotherapy nurse will explain how to take care of your catheter. It can stay in place for several months. Your treatment team can also take blood samples from it. The catheter will be removed using a local anaesthetic.
answer: A skin-tunneled catheter, also called a Hickman or Groshong line, is a type of central venous access device that can be used to administer chemotherapy. It is a fine silicone tube that is inserted into a vein through a small cut in the chest, usually under local anesthesia. The catheter stays in place for several months throughout your chemotherapy treatment. Your chemotherapy nurse will show you how to care for the catheter properly. It allows your treatment team to give you chemotherapy and take blood samples without repeatedly accessing veins in your arms, which can help prevent lymphoedema. When your treatment is complete, the catheter is removed using local anesthesia.

question: What is a PICC line and how is it used for chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: A PICC is inserted into a vein in your arm, at or above the bend in your elbow, and into the large vein leading to your heart. It is usually put in under a local anaesthetic. The PICC line will be covered by a clear dressing. You'll be given instructions on how to look after it and change the dressing. It can stay in place throughout your treatment. Your treatment team can also take blood samples from it.

The PICC line can stay in place throughout your chemotherapy treatment, allowing your healthcare team to administer the chemotherapy drugs directly through the line as well as take blood samples from it. This can make the process of receiving chemotherapy and having blood drawn more comfortable and convenient.

question: What is an implanted port and how is it used for chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: An implanted port is a small disc connected to a thin tube (catheter). It's put under the skin, usually in your chest or arm. The other end of the tube goes into a large vein just above your heart. The port is hidden but can be felt under the skin. It's usually put in using a local anaesthetic. You may be given medication to help you relax. Chemotherapy drugs are given directly into the port. The area over the port may be numbed with an anaesthetic cream before a special needle is pushed into the port to give the chemotherapy. Your treatment team can also take blood samples from it. The implanted port can stay in place throughout your treatment.
answer: An implanted port is a small disc connected to a thin tube (catheter) that is surgically placed under the skin, usually in your chest or arm area. question: How is an implanted port removed after chemotherapy treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: The port can be removed under a local or general anaesthetic. When it needs to be removed, a small cut is made over the site of the port. The port is removed and the catheter is taken out of the vein. The wound is stitched and covered with a dressing. You'll be given instructions on caring for your dressing and what to do if you feel sore or bruised after the port is removed.
answer: After you have completed your chemotherapy treatment, the implanted port can be removed. This is typically done as an outpatient procedure under local or general anesthesia. A small incision is made over the site where the port is located, and the port itself is removed from under the skin. The catheter tube that was inserted into the vein is also carefully pulled out. The incision site is then stitched closed and covered with a dressing. You will be provided with instructions on how to care for the dressing and what to expect in terms of any soreness or bruising after the port removal procedure.

question: What is electrochemotherapy and how does it work for treating breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Electrochemotherapy, sometimes called ECT, is a treatment for secondary breast cancer that has spread to the skin (skin metastases). It combines a low dose of a chemotherapy drug with electrical impulses. The electrical impulses are given using an electrode directly to the areas being treated. This allows the chemotherapy to work in the treatment areas only, with little or no effect in other areas.
answer: Electrochemotherapy, also known as ECT, is a treatment option for secondary breast cancer that has spread to the skin (skin metastases). It combines a low dose of chemotherapy medication with electrical impulses. The electrical impulses are delivered directly to the treatment areas using an electrode. This allows the chemotherapy to be effective in those specific areas being treated, while having little or no effect on other parts of the body. If electrochemotherapy is a suitable option for your case, your treatment team can refer you to the nearest hospital that offers this therapy.

question: What are some common side effects of chemotherapy for breast cancer?

source_excerpt: Chemotherapy can temporarily affect the number of blood cells in the body. Blood is made up of red cells, white cells and platelets. You'll have regular blood tests. Your treatment team may change the dose of a drug to suit you and help manage its side effects.

It's important to communicate any side effects you experience to your care team, even if they're not listed, so they can help control or manage them effectively.

question: What should I do if I develop signs of an infection during chemotherapy?

source_excerpt: Your treatment team may give you guidelines to follow for reporting signs of an infection. question: How can I reduce my risk of infection during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
section: Tips to help reduce the risk of infection
source_excerpt: Tips to help reduce the risk of infection You can help reduce the risk of infection by: • Regularly washing and drying your hands thoroughly • Cleaning any cuts and grazes and covering them with a dressing or plaster • Avoiding people who are unwell or may be infectious • Eating as healthily as possible, and following any advice about food and drink given to you by your treatment team • Drinking plenty of fluids • Storing and cooking food correctly
answer: There are several steps you can take to help reduce your risk of infection while undergoing chemotherapy treatment:  1. Practice good hand hygiene by regularly washing and thoroughly drying your hands. 2. Keep any cuts or grazes clean, and cover them with a dressing or bandage. 3. Avoid close contact with people who are sick or may have an infectious illness. 4. Eat a healthy, balanced diet and follow any specific dietary guidelines provided by your treatment team. 5. Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids. 6. Properly store and cook food to prevent foodborne illnesses.  By taking these precautions, you can help minimize your chances of developing an infection when your white blood cell count is low due to chemotherapy.

question: What is the risk of blood clots for breast cancer patients receiving chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: People with breast cancer have a higher risk of blood clots. Having chemotherapy also increases the risk of blood clots such as a DVT (deep vein thrombosis). If you have a DVT, there's a risk part of the blood clot could break away and travel to the lung. This is known as a pulmonary embolism (PE). Blood clots can be life-threatening and should be treated quickly. Contact your treatment team or go to your local A&E department straight away if you have any of the following symptoms: • Pain in your arm or leg • Redness/discolouration of the skin of the arm or leg • Heat and swelling of the arm or leg • Swelling, redness or tenderness where a central line is inserted to give chemotherapy, for example in the arm, chest area or up into the neck • Shortness of breath that comes on suddenly • Pain or tightness in the chest • Unexplained cough or coughing up blood
answer: Breast cancer patients have a higher risk of developing blood clots, and this risk is further increased by chemotherapy treatment. Blood clots, such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), can be life-threatening and require immediate medical attention. It's crucial to be aware of the symptoms, which may include pain, redness, swelling, or discoloration in the arm or leg, shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your treatment team or go to the emergency department right away. Your healthcare team will closely monitor you and provide guidance to help prevent and manage any potential blood clot complications during your chemotherapy journey.

question: What can be done to manage nausea and vomiting during chemotherapy for breast cancer?

The anti-nausea medication can help manage these unpleasant symptoms, allowing you to better tolerate your chemotherapy treatment. Don't hesitate to discuss any concerns or difficulties with your healthcare team, as they can adjust the medication or provide additional support to help you through this challenging time.

question: Will I lose my hair during chemotherapy for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy can cause hair loss. It's completely natural to find this upsetting. How likely you are to lose your hair depends on the type and amount of chemotherapy drugs you're given. Not all chemotherapy will make you lose your hair. Some drugs don't cause any hair loss and some cause hair thinning. But others can make your hair fall out completely. You may begin to lose your hair about 2 weeks after the first treatment, but it can happen earlier. Hair loss is usually gradual, although it can sometimes happen quickly, possibly over a couple of days. As well as the hair on your head, you may lose your eyebrows, eyelashes, the hair in your nose, and other body hair. You may lose your body hair more slowly than the hair on your head.
answer: Yes, hair loss or thinning is a common side effect of chemotherapy for breast cancer. It's important to note that not only the hair on your head may be affected, but you may also experience loss of eyebrows, eyelashes, nasal hair, and other body hair. Body hair may thin out more slowly compared to the hair on your head. Losing your hair can be an emotionally challenging experience, and it's completely natural to feel upset about it. Your healthcare team can provide support and guidance to help you cope with this side effect.

question: What are some tips for managing fatigue during breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt:
• Keep a fatigue diary – recording your fatigue level each day, as well as any activities you do and treatment you're having, can help identify the causes of fatigue and show changes in energy levels. This can help you plan your day to get the most out of times when you have more energy
• Try to be active – there's strong evidence that exercise reduces fatigue. Aim to do regular, short amounts of activity or light exercise, such as walking or yoga. A local walking group can be a good way to get regular exercise and meet people
• Allow time to rest between daily activities but try to limit naps to less than 30 minutes so you sleep at night
• Try relaxation techniques – these can help you relax and regain energy. There are many good relaxation apps, audio downloads and CDs that can help, such as the Calm and Sleepio apps
• Try complementary therapies – these include massage, acupuncture and mindfulness and can help improve fatigue for some people. Speak to your treatment team before trying complementary therapies
• Drink plenty of fluids – being dehydrated can make you more tired
• Try to eat healthily – make the most of the times when your appetite is good, choosing a balance of healthy foods. You can find out more about diet during treatment in our Diet and breast cancer booklet
• Seek emotional support – individual counselling or a support group may help reduce fatigue. You could try talking to others who have gone through a similar experience. Find out more by visiting breastcancernow.org/information-support/support-you
• Accept offers of help from others where possible
answer: Fatigue is a common side effect of breast cancer treatment, but there are several strategies that can help you manage it. Keeping a fatigue diary to track your energy levels and identify patterns can help you plan your day accordingly. Regular light exercise like walking or yoga has been shown to reduce fatigue. It's also important to allow time for rest between activities, but limit naps to under 30 minutes so you can sleep well at night. Relaxation techniques like meditation apps, massage, or acupuncture may help you regain energy. Staying hydrated, eating a balanced diet when you can, and seeking emotional support through counseling or support groups can also combat fatigue. Don't hesitate to accept help from others when possible. Managing fatigue takes some effort, but these tips can help you feel more energized during your treatment journey.

question: What are some potential mouth problems that can occur during chemotherapy treatment for breast cancer?

question: What steps can be taken to help prevent or manage mouth problems during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: There's some evidence that keeping your mouth cold with ice, iced water or ice lollies while having some types of chemotherapy can reduce the risk of a sore mouth and ulcers. Other tips to reduce dental problems: • Clean your teeth or dentures after each meal • Use a soft toothbrush • Use a mouthwash (often provided by the hospital) • Take regular sips of water to keep your mouth moist • Use artificial saliva sprays to help with dry mouth • Chew sugar-free gum to encourage saliva to be produced • Add sauces or gravies to your food to keep your mouth moist and make swallowing easier • Avoid foods that can cause irritation such as citrus fruits and spicy, hard or salty foods • Use a lip balm • Avoid alcohol (also be aware of alcohol in mouthwash) • Avoid very hot or cold drinks and foods • Try to stop or limit smoking as this can cause irritation
answer: There are several tips that can help reduce dental problems and manage mouth issues during chemotherapy:  - Keep your mouth cold with ice, iced water, or ice lollies during chemotherapy infusions, as this may reduce sore mouth and ulcers. - Clean your teeth or dentures after each meal using a soft toothbrush. - Use a mouthwash provided by the hospital. - Take regular sips of water to keep your mouth moist. - Use artificial saliva sprays for dry mouth. - Chew sugar-free gum to stimulate saliva production. - Add sauces or gravies to food to keep your mouth moist and aid swallowing. - Avoid irritating foods like citrus fruits, spicy foods, hard foods, and salty foods. - Use a lip balm. - Avoid alcohol and be aware of alcohol in some mouthwashes. - Avoid very hot or cold drinks and foods. - Try to stop or limit smoking to prevent further irritation.

question: What steps can be taken to help prevent or manage mouth problems during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: There's some evidence that keeping your mouth cold with ice, iced water or ice lollies while having some types of chemotherapy can reduce the risk of a sore mouth and ulcers. Other tips to reduce dental problems: • Clean your teeth or dentures after each meal • Use a soft toothbrush • Use a mouthwash (often provided by the hospital) • Take regular sips of water to keep your mouth moist • Use artificial saliva sprays to help with dry mouth • Chew sugar-free gum to encourage saliva to be produced • Add sauces or gravies to your food to keep your mouth moist and make swallowing easier • Avoid foods that can cause irritation such as citrus fruits and spicy, hard or salty foods • Use a lip balm • Avoid alcohol (also be aware of alcohol in mouthwash) • Avoid very hot or cold drinks and foods • Try to stop or limit smoking as this can cause irritation

question: What should you do about dental care before and during chemotherapy treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: See your dentist for a check-up before chemotherapy begins. Avoid dental treatment during chemotherapy if possible. If you do need to have dental work during treatment, talk with your treatment team about the best time to have this. If you're having difficulty registering with a dentist, let your treatment team know. If you have any mouth problems, let your chemotherapy nurse or treatment team know as soon as possible.
answer: It's recommended to see your dentist for a check-up before starting chemotherapy treatment. During chemotherapy, it's best to avoid dental treatment if possible. If you do need dental work while undergoing chemotherapy, discuss the best timing with your treatment team. Let your chemotherapy nurse or oncology team know if you have any difficulty registering with a dentist or if you experience any mouth problems during treatment so they can provide guidance and support.

question: What should I do if I experience taste changes during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You may notice taste changes while having chemotherapy. Some foods may taste different, for example more salty, bitter or metallic. You may no longer like certain foods you used to enjoy. If this is the case, speak to your treatment team. They may be able to suggest ways of managing this. Your taste should return to normal once your treatment has finished.
answer: It's common to experience taste changes while undergoing chemotherapy treatment. Some foods may taste different, like more salty, bitter, or metallic. You may also find that you no longer enjoy certain foods that you used to like. If this happens, don't hesitate to speak to your treatment team. They can suggest ways to help manage these taste changes. The good news is that your normal sense of taste should return once your chemotherapy treatment is completed. In the meantime, your care team can provide guidance on dealing with changes to your taste and appetite.

question: What should I do if I experience pain or discomfort at the injection site during chemotherapy?

They can assess the situation and take appropriate steps to address your discomfort and ensure your safety.

question: How can chemotherapy affect my skin, and what should I do about it?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy drugs can make your skin dry or more sensitive. They can also cause rashes. Tell your treatment team as soon as possible if you develop a rash. Some chemotherapy drugs can cause a skin reaction called hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia). It usually affects the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, but you may also have symptoms in other areas such as the skin on your knees or elbows. Hand-foot syndrome can sometimes make it harder to carry out daily activities. It can also have an impact on quality of life. Your treatment team may prescribe gels or creams to apply to the affected areas. Ask your treatment team if they recommend any particular creams for your skin before using anything on it yourself.
answer: Chemotherapy drugs can cause various skin reactions and sensitivities. Your skin may become dry or more sensitive, and you may develop rashes. If you notice a rash or any skin changes, it's important to inform your treatment team as soon as possible so they can assess and address the issue.  Some chemotherapy drugs can also cause a specific skin reaction called hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia). This condition typically affects the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, but you may also experience symptoms in other areas like the knees or elbows. Hand-foot syndrome can make it more difficult to carry out daily activities and can impact your quality of life.  If you develop hand-foot syndrome, your treatment team may prescribe gels or creams to apply to the affected areas to help manage the condition. Before using any creams or lotions on your skin during chemotherapy, it's best to consult with your care team first and follow their recommendations to ensure they are safe and appropriate for your situation.

question: What changes can chemotherapy cause to my fingernails and toenails?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy may cause changes to the appearance of your fingernails and toenails. This can be a change in the nail colour or texture, such as ridges forming. Nails can become more brittle and cracked. Occasionally, the nail may lift off the nail bed and fall out, but it will grow back. As you're more at risk of infection while having chemotherapy, it's important to report any signs of infection to your treatment team. Signs of infection include redness or discolouration, heat, swelling or pain in or under your fingernails and toenails.
answer: Chemotherapy can cause several changes to your fingernails and toenails. You may notice a change in the color or texture of your nails, such as the formation of ridges. Your nails may also become more brittle and cracked. In some cases, the nail may even lift off the nail bed and fall out, but don't worry, it will grow back. Since chemotherapy can increase your risk of infection, it's crucial to report any signs of infection to your treatment team immediately. These signs include redness, discoloration, heat, swelling, or pain in or under your fingernails and toenails.

question: How can I take care of my skin during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
section: Tips for looking after your skin
source_excerpt:
The following tips may help you care for your skin:
• Eating a healthy diet
• Drinking plenty of water
• Taking care in the sun by covering your skin and wearing a hat
• Wearing high protection sunscreen
• Staying out of the sun during the hottest part of the day (11am to 3pm)
• Avoiding very hot showers or baths
• Avoiding scented soap
• Applying body lotion to help keep the skin moist (but choose unperfumed lotions without colour to minimise the risk of a reaction)
answer: During chemotherapy, it's important to take good care of your skin. Here are some tips that may help:  - Eat a healthy diet to nourish your skin from the inside. - Drink plenty of water to keep your skin hydrated. - Take care in the sun by covering your skin and wearing a hat. Use high protection sunscreen and avoid the sun during the hottest part of the day (11am to 3pm). - Avoid very hot showers or baths, as they can dry out your skin. - Use unscented, unperfumed soaps and body lotions to minimize the risk of skin reactions. - Apply body lotion regularly to keep your skin moisturized.  Following these simple tips can help protect and nourish your skin during your chemotherapy treatment.

question: What tips are there for caring for my hands and nails during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
section: Tips for caring for your hands and nails
source_excerpt:
Tips for caring for your hands and nails 
• Use hand cream to help moisturise your hands, feet and nails
• Use gloves for household chores to protect your nails
• If your toenails are affected, avoid tight-fitting shoes
• Don't wear false nails during chemotherapy as these can lead to infection or mask the signs of it 
• Avoid nail varnish as it tends to dry the nails out more, or you could try a water-based version as this is less harsh
• Keep nails short
answer: Here are some helpful tips for caring for your hands and nails during chemotherapy:  - Use hand cream to help moisturize your hands, feet, and nails. - Wear gloves when doing household chores to protect your nails. - If your toenails are affected, avoid wearing tight-fitting shoes. - Don't wear false nails during chemotherapy, as they can lead to infection or mask signs of infection. - Avoid nail polish, as it tends to dry out the nails further. You could try a water-based version, which is less harsh. - Keep your nails trimmed short.  Following these tips can help keep your hands and nails healthy and minimize any issues during your chemotherapy treatment.

question: What is peripheral neuropathy and what causes it during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
section: Numbness and tingling in your hands or feet
source_excerpt: Peripheral nerves send messages between the brain and the spinal cord (the central nervous system) and the rest of the body. Peripheral neuropathy happens when these nerves are damaged. It's most common in the hands and feet.
answer: Peripheral neuropathy is a condition where the nerves that carry signals between the brain/spinal cord and the rest of the body become damaged. During chemotherapy treatment for breast cancer, some of the drugs used can affect these nerves, leading to peripheral neuropathy. The nerves in the hands and feet are most commonly affected. This can cause symptoms like pain, numbness, tingling, altered sensations, and muscle weakness in the hands and feet. It's important to let your treatment team know if you experience any of these symptoms so they can help manage them appropriately.

question: How long do symptoms of peripheral neuropathy typically last after chemotherapy?

If any neuropathy symptoms do not improve as expected, it's important to discuss this with your treatment team, as they may be able to provide medication or other interventions to help relieve ongoing symptoms.

question: How can chemotherapy affect the digestive system and what can be done to manage those side effects?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy can affect your digestive system in different ways. Some people become constipated while others have diarrhoea. Contact your treatment team if you have diarrhoea 3 or more times than usual in 24 hours. Drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration. Some chemotherapy drugs can make indigestion more likely. Indigestion is discomfort or pain in your upper tummy. Some may also cause heartburn, which is a burning feeling in your lower chest. Let your treatment team know if you have any of these side effects. They can prescribe medication to help and give you information about diet. They may also refer you to a dietitian if necessary.
answer: Chemotherapy can impact your digestive system in various ways. Some people may experience constipation, while others have diarrhea. If you have diarrhea 3 or more times than usual in a 24-hour period, be sure to contact your treatment team right away. Drinking plenty of fluids is important to avoid dehydration. Certain chemo drugs can also increase the likelihood of indigestion, which is discomfort or pain in the upper abdomen, as well as heartburn, a burning sensation in the lower chest. Don't hesitate to inform your care providers about any digestive issues you experience. They can prescribe medications to help relieve the symptoms and provide guidance on dietary adjustments. If needed, they may also refer you to a dietitian for additional support in managing these side effects.

question: Can chemotherapy cause menopausal symptoms and how are they managed?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You may experience menopausal symptoms as a result of chemotherapy. You may have already been through the menopause, but having breast cancer treatment can cause you to have symptoms again. If you have not yet reached the menopause, your periods may stop or become irregular during chemotherapy. Whether your periods return after treatment will depend on your age and the type of chemotherapy you have had.
answer: Yes, chemotherapy can cause you to experience menopausal symptoms. Even if you have already gone through menopause, breast cancer treatment may trigger these symptoms again. If you have not yet reached menopause, your periods may stop or become irregular during chemotherapy. Whether your periods return after treatment ends depends on your age and the type of chemotherapy you received. Menopausal symptoms like hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and mood changes can be managed with hormone replacement therapy (HRT) or other medications. Your treatment team can provide guidance on managing these symptoms and may refer you to a menopause specialist if needed. Don't hesitate to discuss any menopausal issues you experience.

question: Can chemotherapy for breast cancer affect a woman's fertility or ability to become pregnant?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy causes changes in the ovaries, which can affect your ability to become pregnant (your fertility). Whether your fertility is affected depends on the type and dose of drugs used, your age and your current fertility status. Some people stop having periods (amenorrhoea) during chemotherapy, but this may be temporary. Your periods are less likely to return after finishing chemotherapy if you're aged 40 or above. Some studies have shown that using hormone therapy drugs to suppress the ovaries may protect them during chemotherapy.
answer: Yes, chemotherapy can potentially affect a woman's fertility and ability to become pregnant. The chemotherapy drugs can cause changes in the ovaries that impact fertility. Whether fertility is affected depends on factors like the specific drugs used, the dosage, the woman's age, and her current fertility status. Some women may temporarily stop having periods (amenorrhea) during chemotherapy, but their periods may return after treatment ends. However, for women aged 40 or older, it is less likely that periods will return after completing chemotherapy, suggesting a higher risk of permanent infertility. Your treatment team can discuss options like using hormone therapy drugs to temporarily suppress ovarian function during chemo in an attempt to preserve fertility, though this method is not guaranteed.

question: If a woman stops having periods during chemotherapy, does that mean she can no longer get pregnant?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Even if you stop having periods and experience menopausal symptoms, you may still be fertile and could become pregnant. Your treatment team will usually recommend barrier methods of contraception.
answer: No, even if you stop having periods and experience menopausal symptoms during chemotherapy, it does not necessarily mean you can no longer get pregnant. The chemotherapy drugs can cause temporary amenorrhea (lack of periods), but you may still be fertile and able to become pregnant. Your treatment team will usually recommend using barrier methods of contraception, such as condoms, during and after chemotherapy, even if you are not having periods. This is because there is still a risk of pregnancy as long as you have not gone through permanent menopause. It's important to discuss contraception options with your care team to prevent an unintended pregnancy while undergoing breast cancer treatment.

question: If I was diagnosed with advanced or secondary breast cancer before starting a family, what should I know about fertility?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you were diagnosed with locally advanced or secondary breast cancer before you started or completed a family, you may be concerned about your  fertility. question: Is it safe to take vitamin and supplement pills during chemotherapy?

question: Can I get vaccinated while undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc17 Chemotherapy For Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You should not have any live vaccines while you're having chemotherapy. Live vaccines include: • Mumps • Measles • Rubella (German measles) • Polio • BCG (tuberculosis) • Yellow fever Live vaccines contain a small amount of live virus or bacteria. If you have a weakened immune system, which you may do during chemotherapy, they could be harmful. It's usually safe to have these vaccinations 6 months after your treatment finishes. Talk to your GP or treatment team before having any vaccinations.
answer: You should not receive any live vaccines while undergoing chemotherapy treatment, as these could potentially be harmful if your immune system is weakened. Live vaccines contain a small amount of live virus or bacteria, which your body may not be able to handle well during chemotherapy. Examples of live vaccines include mumps, measles, rubella, polio, BCG (for tuberculosis), and yellow fever. It is usually safe to receive these vaccinations 6 months after your chemotherapy treatment is completed. However, the flu vaccine is acceptable, as it does not contain any live viruses. Consult your treatment team or GP before getting any vaccinations during or shortly after chemotherapy.

question: What is tamoxifen and how does it work?
section: What is tamoxifen? / How does tamoxifen work?
source_excerpt: Tamoxifen is a drug used to treat breast cancer. It's a type of hormone therapy, also known as endocrine therapy. Some breast cancers use oestrogen in the body to help them grow. These are known as oestrogen receptor positive or ER-positive breast cancers. Tamoxifen blocks the effects of oestrogen on ER-positive breast cancers. This stops oestrogen from helping the breast cancer cells grow.
answer: Tamoxifen is a drug used to treat breast cancer. It is a type of hormone therapy, also known as endocrine therapy. Some breast cancers use the hormone estrogen in the body to help them grow. These are called estrogen receptor positive (ER-positive) breast cancers. Tamoxifen works by blocking the effects of estrogen on ER-positive breast cancers. This stops estrogen from helping the breast cancer cells grow and spread. By interfering with the way estrogen fuels the cancer's growth, tamoxifen can help control and treat ER-positive breast cancers.

question: Who might be prescribed tamoxifen as part of their breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: You'll only be prescribed tamoxifen if your breast cancer is ER-positive. Invasive breast cancers are tested to see if they're ER-positive using tissue from a biopsy or after surgery. If your breast cancer doesn't use oestrogen to help it grow, it is known as oestrogen receptor negative (ER-negative). You'll also have tests to see if a hormone called progesterone is helping your breast cancer grow. If it is, it's called progesterone receptor or PR-positive. The benefits of hormone therapy are less clear for people whose breast cancer is PR-positive but ER-negative. Very few breast cancers fall into this category. But your specialist will discuss with you whether hormone therapy is appropriate if this is the case. If your cancer is found to be hormone receptor negative, then tamoxifen will not be of any benefit to you.

question: When is tamoxifen typically prescribed for breast cancer treatment?

It's usually given after surgery to reduce the risk of breast cancer returning in the same breast or spreading somewhere else in the body. This is known as adjuvant therapy. If you're going to take tamoxifen as part of your treatment for primary breast cancer, your specialist will tell you when it's best for you to do this.

question: What is tamoxifen used for in breast cancer treatment?
section: Breast cancer that has come back or spread
source_excerpt: Occasionally, tamoxifen may be used as the first treatment for breast cancer. This may be when surgery is not appropriate or needs to be delayed. Tamoxifen can also be used to treat people with oestrogen positive breast cancer who have: • Local recurrence – breast cancer that has come back in the chest/breast area or in the skin near the original site or scar • Locally advanced breast cancer – breast cancer that has spread to the chest wall or skin of the breast, or the lymph nodes around the chest, neck and under the arm or breastbone, but has not spread to other parts of the body. It cannot be removed by surgery • Secondary (metastatic) breast cancer – breast cancer that has spread to another part of the body, such as the bones, lungs, liver or brain

Tamoxifen helps treat these types of breast cancers by blocking the effects of estrogen, which some breast cancers depend on to grow.

If you know you are lactose intolerant, discuss this with your treatment team or pharmacist.

question: How long will I need to take tamoxifen for my breast cancer treatment?
section: How long will I have to take tamoxifen for?
source_excerpt: If you're being treated for primary breast cancer, you will usually take tamoxifen for between 5 and 10 years. If you go through the menopause while taking tamoxifen, your treatment team may recommend you change from tamoxifen to a different hormone therapy known as an aromatase inhibitor (such as anastrozole, exemestane or letrozole). If you're taking tamoxifen for locally advanced breast cancer or secondary breast cancer, you'll usually continue to take it for as long as it's keeping the cancer under control.

question: How does tamoxifen affect bone health in postmenopausal and premenopausal women?
source_excerpt: If you are postmenopausal there is evidence that tamoxifen slows down bone loss, reducing the risk of your bones losing strength and being more likely to break (osteoporosis). However, tamoxifen may slightly increase the risk of osteoporosis for premenopausal women. This is unlikely to lead to osteoporosis unless treatment has been given to stop the ovaries from working as well.
answer: Tamoxifen can have different effects on bone health depending on whether a woman is postmenopausal or premenopausal. For postmenopausal women, there is evidence that tamoxifen actually slows down bone loss and reduces the risk of osteoporosis (weakening of the bones). However, for premenopausal women, tamoxifen may slightly increase the risk of osteoporosis, especially if treatment has been given to stop the ovaries from working properly. It's important for premenopausal women on tamoxifen to discuss bone health monitoring with their doctor.

question: Does tamoxifen increase the risk of blood clots?
source_excerpt: People with breast cancer have a higher risk of blood clots. Taking tamoxifen also increases the risk of blood clots such as a DVT (deep vein thrombosis). If you have a DVT, there's a risk part of the blood clot could break away and travel to the lung. This is known as a pulmonary embolism (PE). Blood clots can be life-threatening and should be treated quickly.
answer: Yes, taking tamoxifen can increase the risk of developing blood clots, such as a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). People with breast cancer already have a higher risk of blood clots, and tamoxifen further elevates this risk. If a DVT occurs, there is also a risk that part of the clot could break off and travel to the lungs, causing a potentially life-threatening pulmonary embolism (PE). Blood clots require prompt medical treatment, so it's crucial to be aware of the symptoms and seek care immediately if you experience any signs of a clot while taking tamoxifen.

question: What symptoms should I watch out for that could indicate a blood clot while taking tamoxifen?

question: Can I take other medications while on tamoxifen?
section: Can I take tamoxifen with other drugs?
source_excerpt: Always check with your treatment team or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines with tamoxifen. A few studies have suggested some drugs may interfere with the way tamoxifen works, making it less effective. These include: • Fluoxetine (Prozac) • Paroxetine (Seroxat) • Bupropion (Wellbutrin, Zyban, Voxra, Budeprion or Aplenzin) • Quinidine (Quinidine Gluconate or Quinidine Sulfate) • Cinacalcet (Sensipar) More recent research suggests this is unlikely, but you may be recommended not to use these drugs with tamoxifen. If this is the case, your treatment team may suggest an alternative. Check with your treatment team before stopping taking these drugs as stopping them suddenly may be harmful.
answer: It's important to check with your treatment team or pharmacist before taking any other medications along with tamoxifen. Some drugs like fluoxetine (Prozac), paroxetine (Seroxat), bupropion (Wellbutrin), quinidine, and cinacalcet may potentially interfere with how tamoxifen works, making it less effective. However, more recent research suggests this is unlikely, but your doctor may still recommend avoiding these drugs while on tamoxifen. If that's the case, they can suggest an alternative medication for you. It's crucial not to stop taking any prescribed drugs suddenly, as that could be harmful. Always consult your healthcare team before making any changes to your medication regimen.

question: What is zoledronic acid and what is it used for in breast cancer treatment?

By interfering with this process, zoledronic acid may reduce the risk of breast cancer cells spreading to the bones and other areas.

question: When is zoledronic acid prescribed for primary breast cancer?

It can be used regardless of whether the menopause happened naturally or because of breast cancer treatment. You may be offered zoledronic acid if you are post-menopausal and have had treatment for invasive breast cancer that has spread to the lymph nodes under the arm. Zoledronic acid may also be considered if your cancer has not spread to the lymph nodes but other factors increase the risk of it returning. Zoledronic acid is usually started within 3 months of final surgery. If you are having chemotherapy after surgery, you'll usually start taking zoledronic acid within 2 months of completing chemotherapy.

question: What are some less common side effects of zoledronic acid?

Diarrhoea  
This is usually mild. Your treatment team can prescribe  
anti-diarrhoea medication to help control this.
Contact your treatment team if you have 4 or more episodes of 
diarrhoea within a 24-hour period. 
Drink plenty of fluids to avoid getting dehydrated.
Low calcium levels in the blood  
Zoledronic acid can cause calcium levels in the blood to drop 
too low. This is called hypocalcaemia. You'll have regular blood 
tests to check your calcium levels.

team know if you experience any of these.
Your treatment team may recommend calcium and vitamin D 
supplements.

question: What is osteonecrosis of the jaw and how can I reduce my risk of developing it?

question: What is radiotherapy and how does it work for breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc26 Radiotherapy For Primary Breast Cancer Web Pdf
source_excerpt: Radiotherapy uses high-energy x-rays to destroy cancer cells. It's given to destroy any cancer cells that may have been left in the breast and surrounding area after surgery. You may hear this called adjuvant radiotherapy.
answer: Radiotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that uses high-energy X-rays to destroy cancer cells. For breast cancer, it is given after surgery to target and destroy any remaining cancer cells in the breast and surrounding area. This helps reduce the risk of the cancer coming back in the future. The radiation is carefully focused on the area where the tumor was removed to maximize its effectiveness while minimizing exposure to healthy tissue. Radiotherapy is an important adjuvant (additional) treatment given along with surgery to give you the best chance of cure.

question: Are there any situations where radiotherapy may not be recommended for breast cancer?

Your cancer care team will carefully evaluate your individual circumstances and discuss whether radiotherapy is an appropriate treatment option for you based on factors like your medical history and genetic profile.

question: What are the radiotherapy options after breast-conserving surgery?
source_display_name: Bcc26 Radiotherapy For Primary Breast Cancer Web Pdf
source_excerpt: If you had breast-conserving surgery (a wide local excision or lumpectomy) you will usually have radiotherapy to the remaining breast tissue on that side. Your specialist may consider giving radiotherapy to the area of the breast where the cancer was removed, rather than the whole breast area. This is known as partial breast radiotherapy. It may be considered if the risk of the cancer coming back is low and you're going to be taking hormone (endocrine) therapy for at least five years. People with a very low risk of the cancer coming back may not need radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery. Your specialist will discuss your risk and explain whether radiotherapy is needed.
answer: If you had breast-conserving surgery (such as a lumpectomy or wide local excision), there are a couple different approaches your doctor may recommend for radiotherapy:  1. Whole breast radiotherapy: This is the most common approach, where radiotherapy is delivered to the entire remaining breast tissue on the treated side. This helps target any potential lingering cancer cells throughout the breast area.  2. Partial breast radiotherapy: In some cases with a low risk of recurrence, your doctor may consider only treating the specific area of the breast where the tumor was removed, rather than the whole breast. This can be an option if you will also be taking hormone therapy for at least 5 years after surgery.  For those with an extremely low calculated risk, radiotherapy may not be needed at all after breast-conserving surgery. Your cancer care team will review your personal risk factors and pathology results to determine if radiotherapy is recommended, and if so, which approach is most appropriate.

question: What are some common side effects of radiotherapy and when do they occur?

source_excerpt: Like any treatment, radiotherapy can cause side effects. Everyone reacts differently to treatment and some people have more side effects than others. Some side effects are temporary, but some may be permanent and some may appear months or years after treatment finishes. Immediate side effects may also be called early or acute side effects. For example, skin that has blistered or is peeling will take longer to heal.

question: What should I do to care for my skin during radiotherapy?
