source_excerpt: It's important to look after your skin during treatment. This will help prevent infection, reduce pain and help keep the area being treated comfortable. You will be given skincare instructions by your radiotherapy team. The following tips may also help.
answer: It's very important to take good care of your skin during radiotherapy treatment to prevent infection, reduce pain, and keep the treated area comfortable. Your radiotherapy team will provide you with specific skincare instructions, but here are some general tips that may help:  Wash the treated area gently with warm water and pat it dry with a soft towel. Avoid using harsh soaps or products that contain sodium lauryl sulfate, as these can cause irritation. You can continue using a gentle, fragrance-free moisturizer, but don't apply it right before your treatment. Let your team know if your skin blisters or peels.  You can keep using your regular soap and deodorant unless your team advises otherwise. Avoid exposing the treated area to extreme temperatures like hot water bottles, heat pads, saunas, or ice packs. Also, protect the area from sun exposure during and after treatment by using a high SPF sunscreen, even under clothing.  If you experience any skin issues or have concerns, don't hesitate to discuss them with your radiotherapy team. They are there to support you and ensure your comfort throughout the treatment process.

question: What are some tips for managing fatigue during and after radiotherapy for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc26 Radiotherapy For Primary Breast Cancer Web Pdf
source_excerpt: Fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that doesn't go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally. It's a very common side effect of radiotherapy and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. If you have also had chemotherapy, you may already be experiencing fatigue by the time you start radiotherapy. Occasionally fatigue is a long-term effect. Fatigue can also be caused by conditions such as anaemia (too few red blood cells). It's important to let your treatment team know if you're affected by fatigue to rule out other conditions. Fatigue affects people in different ways and there are a number of ways of coping with and managing it – your treatment team can help you with this. Tips to help manage fatigue: • Keep a fatigue diary – recording your level of fatigue every day can help you identify causes and plan activities • Plan your days so you have a balance of activity and rest • Do small amounts of physical activity each day, even a short walk can help • Accept that you may have good days and bad days • Prepare for a special occasion by getting some rest beforehand • Try to eat well – if your appetite is poor, it may help to eat smaller amounts more often and drink plenty of fluids to keep hydrated. You could also ask to be referred to a dietitian for advice • Accept offers of help from other people to save your energy for things you enjoy
answer: Fatigue, or extreme tiredness and exhaustion that doesn't go away with rest or sleep, is a very common side effect of radiotherapy for breast cancer. It can affect you physically and emotionally, and may last for weeks or months after treatment. Here are some tips to help manage fatigue:  - Keep a fatigue diary to identify causes and plan activities around your energy levels. - Balance activity and rest throughout your day. Do small amounts of physical activity like short walks when you can. - Accept that you may have good days and bad days with fatigue levels. - Prepare for special occasions by resting beforehand. - Try to eat well and stay hydrated. Eat smaller meals more frequently if your appetite is poor, and ask to see a dietitian for advice. - Accept offers of help from others so you can save your energy for things you enjoy.  Fatigue can also sometimes be caused by other conditions like anemia, so let your treatment team know if you're struggling so they can check for any underlying issues. Managing fatigue takes patience, but there are ways to cope during this challenging time.

question: What are some potential late side effects of radiotherapy for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc26 Radiotherapy For Primary Breast Cancer Web Pdf
source_excerpt: Some side effects can develop months or years after radiotherapy treatment ends. However, these side effects are much less common. Hardening of the tissue (fibrosis) is rare but may happen several months or years after radiotherapy has finished. If the fibrosis is severe, the breast can become noticeably smaller and firmer. If you have a breast reconstruction using an implant, radiotherapy can cause the reconstructed breast to become firmer, change shape or become uncomfortable. You may hear this called capsular contracture. If you have a breast reconstruction using your own tissue (tissue flap), radiotherapy can cause the tissue of the reconstruction to change shape or shrink. Under the skin you may see tiny broken blood vessels. This is known as telangiectasia. Although it's not harmful to you, it's permanent and there's no treatment for it. It may affect you emotionally and the way you see your body.

For women who have had breast reconstruction, radiotherapy can sometimes lead to changes in the reconstructed breast over time. With implant-based reconstructions, the rebuilt breast may become firmer, change shape or feel uncomfortable - a condition called capsular contracture. With tissue flap reconstructions using the patient's own tissue, the reconstructed breast tissue could shrink or change shape after radiotherapy. While serious late effects are very rare overall, the benefits of radiotherapy in reducing breast cancer recurrence outweigh the small risk of these potential issues.

question: What are some potential side effects of radiotherapy for breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc26 Radiotherapy For Primary Breast Cancer Web Pdf
source_excerpt:
Changes to the lungs 
Sometimes after treatment to the breast or chest wall area, 
part of the lung behind the treatment area can become 
inflamed. This may cause a dry cough or shortness of breath. 
It usually heals by itself over time. More rarely, hardening of 
the upper lung tissue can occur which can cause similar side 
effects.

Heart problems
There is a small risk of heart problems in the future from 
radiotherapy given on the left side. The risk is very low as care 
is taken to reduce the dose of radiotherapy to the tissues of  
the heart. 

Risk of another cancer developing 
There is a small risk of developing another cancer in the future 
from having radiotherapy. This is very rare, and much less of 
a risk than your breast cancer returning if you do not have 
radiotherapy. Your specialist will discuss this risk with you. 

Other side effects 
Other side effects include:
• Weakening of the bones in the treated area – can lead to  
rib and collarbone fractures 
• Damage to the nerves in the arm on the treated side  
– may cause tingling, numbness, pain, weakness and possibly 
some loss of movement
• Long-term skin reactions (chronic radiation dermatitis)  
– see 'Skin reactions'
answer: Radiotherapy for breast cancer can sometimes cause side effects, though many are temporary and manageable. Some potential side effects include inflammation or hardening of the lung tissue behind the treated area, which may cause a dry cough or shortness of breath. There is also a very small risk of future heart problems if treated on the left side, though care is taken to minimize radiation to the heart. Rarely, radiotherapy can increase the risk of developing another cancer in the future, but this risk is much lower than the risk of the breast cancer returning without radiotherapy. Other possible side effects are weakening of bones in the treated area, nerve damage causing numbness/tingling in the arm, and long-term skin reactions. Your treatment team can discuss managing any side effects you experience and ways to minimize risks. The benefits of radiotherapy generally outweigh the small risks of side effects.

question: Should I take any supplements or medications during radiotherapy for breast cancer?

question: What is anastrozole and how does it work?
section: What is anastrozole? / How does anastrozole work?
source_excerpt: Anastrozole is a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through a natural menopause (when periods stop). It can also be used in premenopausal women having ovarian suppression (treatment to stop the ovaries working). Anastrozole works by reducing the amount of oestrogen made in the body. Some breast cancers use oestrogen in the body to help them to grow. These are known as oestrogen receptor positive or ER+ breast cancers. Anastrozole will only be prescribed if your breast cancer is ER+. Anastrozole belongs to a group of drugs called aromatase inhibitors. Aromatase inhibitors stop the aromatase enzyme from working. This means there's less oestrogen in the body to help breast cancer cells to grow.

question: What are the different uses of anastrozole for treating breast cancer?
section: Breast cancer that has come back or spread
source_excerpt:
Anastrozole can also be used to treat people who have: 
• Local recurrence  – breast cancer that has come back in the 
chest/breast area or in the skin near the original site or scar
• Locally advanced breast cancer  – breast cancer that has 
spread to the tissues and lymph nodes (glands) around the 
chest, neck and under the breastbone. Sometimes breast 
cancer is locally advanced when it is first diagnosed. This may 
also happen when breast cancer comes back after treatment 
and may be referred to as regional recurrence
• Secondary (metastatic) breast cancer  – breast cancer that 
has spread to other parts of the body
Anastrozole can be given alongside a targeted therapy drug.
answer: Anastrozole can be used to treat several different situations related to breast cancer. Additionally, anastrozole is used to treat secondary (metastatic) breast cancer, which is when the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. In these cases, anastrozole may be given along with a targeted therapy drug. The treatment team will discuss if anastrozole is an appropriate option based on your individual situation.

question: How long will I need to take anastrozole for different breast cancer situations?

source_excerpt:
The recommended length of time that anastrozole is taken for 
will depend on your individual situation. 
People being treated for primary breast cancer will usually take

Some people start taking anastrozole after a number of years of

If you're taking anastrozole to treat breast cancer that has 
come back or spread to another part of the body, you'll 
usually take it for as long as it's effective and any side 
effects can be managed. 
If you're taking anastrozole to reduce the risk of breast cancer 
developing because of your family history, you'll usually take it 
for five years.

question: What are some common menopausal symptoms caused by anastrozole?
source_excerpt: Hot flushes and night sweats are common side effects of anastrozole. A hot flush can range from a mild sensation of warming which just affects the face, to waves of heat throughout the body. Some women also experience a drenching sweat affecting the whole body. Many women get flushes at night, leading to disturbed sleep which can mean being forgetful, feeling irritable and having difficulty concentrating. Many women find their desire for sexual contact decreases. Vaginal dryness is often caused by reduced levels of oestrogen or blocking its action can cause vaginal changes, such as dryness or irritation.
answer: Anastrozole, a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer, can cause menopausal symptoms like hot flushes and night sweats. Hot flushes can range from a mild warming sensation in the face to intense waves of heat throughout the body, sometimes accompanied by drenching sweats. Many women experience night sweats that disrupt their sleep, leading to forgetfulness, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. Another common side effect is a decreased sex drive or low libido, which may improve over time. Vaginal dryness and irritation can also occur due to reduced estrogen levels. While these side effects can be challenging, there are treatments available to help manage them, such as vaginal moisturizers, lubricants, and strategies for coping with intimacy changes.

question: What is cancer-related fatigue and how can I manage it while taking anastrozole?
source_excerpt: Cancer-related fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that doesn't go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally. It's a very common side effect of anastrozole and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. Occasionally fatigue is a long-term effect. Fatigue can also be caused by conditions such as anaemia (too few red blood cells). It's important to let your GP or treatment team know if you're affected by fatigue to rule out other conditions. Fatigue affects people in different ways and there's a number of ways of coping with and managing it. You can find lots more information on our website breastcancernow.org/fatigue or by calling our Helpline on 0808 800 6000. Macmillan Cancer Support produces a booklet called Coping with fatigue.

It's important to let your GP or treatment team know if you're experiencing fatigue, as it can also be caused by other conditions like anemia that need to be ruled out. question: How does anastrozole affect bone health, and what can be done about it?
source_excerpt: Anastrozole reduces the amount of oestrogen in the body. A lack of oestrogen over time can cause osteoporosis. Your specialist will sometimes check the strength and thickness (density) of your bones with a scan before or shortly after you start taking anastrozole. If you have been given bisphosphonates (see below) as part of your treatment you will not need a scan. Your bone density may be checked after two to five years while you're taking anastrozole, depending on the results from the initial scan or whether your specialist has any concerns. To help keep your bones healthy you can increase your intake of calcium and vitamin D. Most people do this by taking a supplement. You may also want to eat more foods that are rich in calcium, such as milk, cheese, yoghurt and cereals. For vitamin D, you can increase the amount of oily fish, mushrooms and eggs you eat. Stopping smoking and doing regular weight-bearing exercise can also help keep your bones strong. If your bones are already beginning to show signs of thinning or if you already have osteoporosis, you may be given another drug to increase bone density and strength. This will usually be from a group of drugs called bisphosphonates. Some people will have been given bisphosphonates as part of their breast cancer treatment. If you're concerned about this, you may find it helpful to speak to your specialist.
answer: Anastrozole reduces the amount of estrogen in the body, and a lack of estrogen over time can lead to osteoporosis (thinning of the bones). To monitor this, your specialist may order a bone density scan before or shortly after starting anastrozole, and then periodically every 2-5 years while you're taking it. To help keep your bones healthy, you can increase your intake of calcium and vitamin D through supplements or eating calcium-rich foods like dairy, cereals, and vitamin D-rich foods like oily fish, mushrooms, and eggs. Stopping smoking and doing weight-bearing exercise can also help strengthen bones. If your bones are already showing signs of thinning or you have osteoporosis, your doctor may prescribe bisphosphonate drugs to increase bone density and strength.

question: What are some potential side effects of taking anastrozole for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt:
Changes to hair or facial hair
You may have some hair loss or thinning while taking 
anastrozole. A small number of women notice an increase in downy facial hair. 

Skin changes 
You may develop a skin rash while taking anastrozole. 
This usually goes away when your treatment finishes. Your pharmacist, GP or treatment team can tell you what products you can use on your skin to help.

Vaginal bleeding 
Vaginal bleeding can happen in the first few weeks after starting anastrozole. It most commonly occurs when changing from one hormone therapy to another. This may also be due to vaginal dryness (see page 9). 
If the bleeding continues for more than a few days, tell 
your specialist. 

Changes to the liver 
Anastrozole can occasionally cause changes to how the liver 
works. These changes are usually mild and unlikely to cause any symptoms. Once you finish your treatment your liver will usually go back to normal.
answer: While taking anastrozole, some common side effects you may experience include hair loss or thinning, an increase in facial hair growth, skin rashes, and vaginal bleeding, especially in the first few weeks after starting the medication or when switching from another hormone therapy. These side effects are generally manageable, and your healthcare team can provide guidance on how to address them. For example, they may recommend products to help with skin rashes or vaginal dryness. It's also possible for anastrozole to cause mild changes in liver function, but this typically resolves once treatment is completed. If you experience persistent dizziness or any concerning symptoms, be sure to inform your doctor right away. While side effects can be unpleasant, it's important to remember that they are a sign that the treatment is working and that your care team is there to support you through this journey.

question: What should I do if I experience symptoms of a blood clot while taking anastrozole?
source_excerpt:
Blood clots
People with breast cancer have a higher risk of blood 
clots such as a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Their risk is 
higher because of the cancer itself and some treatments 
for breast cancer. If the cancer has spread to other parts 
of the body (secondary breast cancer), this also increases 
the risk.
People with a DVT are at risk of developing a pulmonary 
embolism (PE). This is when part of the blood clot breaks 
away and travels to the lung. 
Blood clots can be harmful but are treatable so it's 
important to report symptoms as soon as possible.
If you experience any of the following symptoms contact 
your local A&E department, GP or treatment team  
straight away:
• Pain, redness/discolouration, heat and swelling of the 
arm or leg
• Swelling, redness or tenderness where a central line is 
inserted to give chemotherapy, for example in the arm, 
chest area or up into the neck
• Shortness of breath
• Pain or tightness in the chest
• Unexplained cough or coughing up blood
answer: People with breast cancer have an increased risk of developing blood clots, such as a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), due to the cancer itself and certain treatments. If you experience any symptoms that could indicate a blood clot while taking anastrozole, it's crucial that you seek medical attention immediately. Contact your local emergency department, GP, or treatment team right away if you notice pain, redness, discoloration, heat, or swelling in your arm or leg, swelling or tenderness around a chemotherapy line insertion site, shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, an unexplained cough, or coughing up blood. Blood clots can be serious but are treatable, so don't delay in reporting any concerning symptoms. Your healthcare team will be able to evaluate your condition and provide appropriate treatment to address any blood clotting issues.

question: What is goserelin and what is it used for?
source_excerpt: Goserelin is a type of hormone (endocrine) therapy. You may hear it called by its brand name Zoladex. It's used as part of treatment for breast cancer in women who have not yet been through the menopause (pre-menopausal women). It can also be used to try to preserve fertility during chemotherapy, as chemotherapy can cause damage to the ovaries (see page 5).
answer: Goserelin, also known by its brand name Zoladex, is a type of hormone therapy used in the treatment of breast cancer in pre-menopausal women. It works by interfering with the hormone signals from the brain that control the ovaries, effectively switching off the production of estrogen. This lowers estrogen levels in the body, which can stop estrogen receptor positive (ER-positive) breast cancer cells from growing. Goserelin is prescribed specifically for ER-positive breast cancers, unless it is being used to try to preserve fertility during chemotherapy treatment.

This is called ovarian suppression, but you may also hear it called ovarian function suppression (OFS) or ovarian ablation.

question: What are the common side effects of taking goserelin?
source_excerpt:
Common side effects
Menopausal symptoms
Menopausal symptoms are the most common side effect of goserelin. These include:
• Hot flushes
• Night sweats
• Vaginal dryness
• A decrease in sex drive (libido)
Although these symptoms may be quite intense in the beginning, they usually improve over time.
Other common side effects
Other common side effects include:
• Soreness at the injection site 
• Change in breast size
• Spots (acne)
• Joint pain and stiffness
• Hair and skin changes
• Headaches
• Blood pressure changes (this does not usually need treatment)
answer: Goserelin, like any medication, can cause side effects, and everyone may react differently. The most common side effects are menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and decreased sex drive. These symptoms can be quite intense initially but usually improve over time. Other common side effects include soreness at the injection site, changes in breast size, acne, joint pain and stiffness, hair and skin changes, headaches, and blood pressure changes (which typically don't require treatment). It's important to discuss any side effects you experience with your healthcare team so they can help you manage them effectively.

question: Do I need to use contraception while taking goserelin for breast cancer treatment?

By lowering hormone levels, goserelin can help make other treatments like chemotherapy or radiotherapy more effective.

question: When might I receive paclitaxel chemotherapy before surgery for breast cancer?
source_excerpt:
Before surgery 
You may have paclitaxel before surgery to shrink a larger 
breast cancer. This may mean breast-conserving surgery is an 
option rather than a mastectomy. Breast-conserving surgery is 
where the cancer is removed with a margin (border) of normal 
breast tissue around it, also known as wide local excision or 
lumpectomy. A mastectomy is where all the breast tissue is 
removed, usually including the nipple.
Or you might have it before surgery to slow down the growth 
of a fast-growing breast cancer and reduce the chance of it 
spreading to other parts of the body.
You may be more likely to have chemotherapy before surgery if 
you have a certain type of breast cancer, such as inflammatory 
breast cancer, HER2-positive breast cancer or triple negative 
breast cancer.
When you have chemotherapy before surgery, it's called primary 
or neo-adjuvant chemotherapy.
answer: You may receive paclitaxel chemotherapy before surgery for a few different reasons. Firstly, it can help shrink a larger breast cancer tumor, potentially allowing you to have breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) instead of a full mastectomy. Secondly, it may be given to slow down the growth of an aggressive, fast-growing breast cancer and reduce the risk of it spreading to other parts of the body. Certain types of breast cancer, such as inflammatory breast cancer, HER2-positive, or triple negative breast cancers, are more likely to be treated with chemotherapy before surgery. This pre-surgery chemotherapy is called primary or neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Breast cancer that has spread

chemotherapy drugs or targeted therapy, to treat breast cancer

Breast cancer that has spread 
You may have paclitaxel, either on its own or with other 
chemotherapy drugs or targeted therapy, to treat breast cancer 
that has:
• Spread to the chest wall or skin of the breast, or the 
lymph nodes around the chest, neck and under the 
breastbone (known as regional recurrence or locally 
advanced breast cancer)
• Spread to other parts of the body (secondary breast cancer)

question: What tests or procedures will I need before starting paclitaxel chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Before starting your treatment a member of the treatment team will discuss how and when you'll have chemotherapy and how side effects can be managed. You'll have blood tests and your height and weight will be measured. You may also have tests to check your heart function, such as: • An ECG (electrocardiogram), a simple test that checks your heart rhythm • An echocardiogram (an ultrasound scan of the heart) You should be given a 24-hour contact number or told who to contact if you feel unwell at any time during your treatment, including at night or at the weekends.
answer: Before starting your paclitaxel treatment, your healthcare team will discuss the details of your chemotherapy schedule and how to manage potential side effects. You will have some pre-treatment tests, including blood tests to check your overall health. Your height and weight will also be measured. Additionally, you may undergo tests to evaluate your heart function, such as an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check your heart rhythm or an echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart). These tests help ensure it is safe for you to proceed with paclitaxel chemotherapy. Your care team will provide you with a 24-hour contact number in case you experience any issues or feel unwell during your treatment, even at night or on weekends.

question: How is paclitaxel chemotherapy administered?
source_excerpt: Paclitaxel is given into a vein (intravenously). This will usually be through a cannula, a small tube that's inserted into a vein in the back of your hand or lower arm. You could also have paclitaxel through: • A skin-tunnelled catheter (Hickman line): a tube inserted into a vein in your chest • A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC): a tube inserted into a vein in your arm at or above the bend in your elbow • An implanted port: a small device with a tube that goes into a vein that's put under the skin, usually in your chest or arm You will have paclitaxel as an outpatient.
answer: Paclitaxel is given intravenously, which means it is administered directly into a vein. This is typically done through a small tube called a cannula that is inserted into a vein in the back of your hand or lower arm. In some cases, paclitaxel may be given through other intravenous access devices, such as a skin-tunneled catheter (Hickman line) inserted into a vein in your chest, a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) in your arm, or an implanted port under the skin, usually in your chest or arm area. Regardless of the specific intravenous access method used, paclitaxel is given as an outpatient procedure, meaning you will not need to be admitted to the hospital for treatment.

question: What are the different dosing schedules for paclitaxel chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Paclitaxel can be given once every 2 weeks, over 3 hours (known as accelerated or dose-dense chemotherapy). Or it may be given weekly in lower doses over 1 hour.
answer: There are two common dosing schedules for paclitaxel chemotherapy. One option is to receive paclitaxel once every 2 weeks, given over a 3-hour infusion period. This is known as an accelerated or dose-dense chemotherapy regimen. Alternatively, paclitaxel can be administered weekly in lower doses, with each infusion lasting approximately 1 hour. Your healthcare team will determine the most appropriate dosing schedule for your specific situation and treatment plan.

question: How often will I receive paclitaxel treatment for primary breast cancer?
source_excerpt: For primary breast cancer, you'll usually have paclitaxel either every week or every 2 weeks for between 9 and 12 weeks. Your treatment team will explain how often you will have your treatment and for how long.
answer: For primary breast cancer, you'll typically receive paclitaxel treatment either once a week or once every two weeks for a period of 9 to 12 weeks. Your treatment team will explain the specific schedule and duration of your treatment plan. The cycles are spaced out to give your body time to recover between treatments, as chemotherapy can reduce the number of blood cells. If your blood tests show that your blood cell levels have not returned to normal, there may be a longer gap between cycles.

question: What are some potential side effects of paclitaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: Like any treatment, paclitaxel can cause side effects. Everyone reacts differently to drugs and some people have more side effects than others. These side effects can usually be managed and those described here will not affect everyone. If you're concerned about any side effects, regardless of whether they're listed here, talk to your chemotherapy nurse or treatment team.

Some common side effects of paclitaxel include low blood cell counts, allergic reactions, and other chemotherapy-related side effects. However, these side effects can usually be managed with proper care and monitoring. If you experience any concerning side effects, whether listed or not, it's important to discuss them with your chemotherapy nurse or treatment team. They can provide guidance on managing the side effects and ensuring your overall well-being during treatment.

question: What happens if my blood cell counts are low before a paclitaxel treatment cycle?
source_excerpt: You might have a longer gap between cycles if your blood tests show that the number of blood cells has not returned to normal.
answer: If your blood tests show that your blood cell counts, particularly red blood cells and white blood cells, have not returned to normal levels before your next scheduled paclitaxel treatment cycle, your treatment team may decide to delay the cycle and give your body more time to recover. This is done to allow your blood cell levels to replenish, as chemotherapy can reduce these vital cells. By extending the gap between cycles, it gives your body the opportunity to rebuild its blood cell reserves, ensuring you are in a better condition to receive the next dose of treatment.

question: What are some common side effects of paclitaxel chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Paclitaxel can temporarily affect the number of blood cells in the body. Blood is made up of red cells, white cells and platelets. You'll have regular blood tests. If these show the number of blood cells is too low, your next cycle of treatment may be delayed or the dose of chemotherapy reduced.
answer: Paclitaxel chemotherapy can cause some common side effects related to its impact on your blood cells. It can temporarily lower the number of red blood cells (causing anemia and fatigue), white blood cells (increasing infection risk), and platelets. Your treatment team will monitor your blood counts with regular tests and may need to delay your next cycle or adjust the dose if your levels are too low. It's important to watch for signs of infection like fever, feeling unwell, sore throat, or chills and report them immediately. Your doctor may also prescribe growth factor injections to help boost your white blood cell production and reduce infection risk.

question: What should I do if I develop signs of an infection during paclitaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: Your treatment team may give you guidelines to follow for reporting signs of an infection, but generally you should contact your hospital immediately if you have any of the following: • A high temperature (over 37.5°C) or low temperature (under 36°C), or whatever your chemotherapy team has advised • Suddenly feeling unwell, even with a normal temperature • Symptoms of an infection, for example a sore throat, a cough, needing to pass urine often or feeling cold and shivery Before starting chemotherapy, your treatment team should give you a 24-hour contact number or tell you how to get emergency care.
answer: If you experience any potential signs of infection while receiving paclitaxel chemotherapy, it's crucial to contact your hospital immediately. Watch out for a high fever over 37.5°C (or low fever under 36°C if advised), feeling suddenly unwell even without fever, symptoms like sore throat, cough, frequent urination, or chills/shivering. Your treatment team should provide you with a 24-hour contact number or instructions on how to get emergency care right away. Acting quickly on infection is important, as you may need prompt treatment like antibiotics when your white blood cell counts are low. Don't hesitate to reach out, as your safety is the top priority.

question: How can growth factor injections help during paclitaxel chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Sometimes your doctor may recommend injections of drugs called growth factors. This helps the body produce more white blood cells to reduce your risk of infection.
answer: During paclitaxel chemotherapy, your doctor may recommend injections of drugs called growth factors. These medications help stimulate your body to produce more white blood cells, which can become depleted by the chemotherapy. Having higher levels of white blood cells reduces your risk of developing a potentially dangerous infection when your immune system is compromised. Growth factor injections are a preventative measure to boost your body's defenses and keep you safer while undergoing treatment.

question: What should I tell my treatment team if I experience anemia symptoms?

Your care providers need to be aware of any potential anemia signs so they can properly evaluate your red blood cell levels and determine if any adjustments to your treatment plan are needed. question: What are the potential side effects of paclitaxel treatment on blood clotting?

While these side effects can be concerning, your healthcare team is there to support you through the treatment process.

question: How does paclitaxel treatment affect hair loss?
source_excerpt: Paclitaxel causes hair loss. Most people will lose all their hair, including eyebrows, eyelashes and body hair. You may begin to lose your hair about 2 weeks after the first treatment, but it can happen earlier. Hair loss is usually gradual but it can happen very quickly, possibly over a couple of days. Hair loss should be temporary and in most cases your hair will begin to grow back a few weeks after your treatment has ended. Permanent hair loss means your hair has not completely grown back 6 months or more after completing treatment. There is currently not enough evidence to say how often this happens.
answer: Paclitaxel can cause significant hair loss, including loss of hair on the head, eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair. Most people will lose all their hair, although the extent and timing can vary. Hair loss typically begins around 2 weeks after the first treatment, but it can happen earlier. The hair loss is usually gradual, but it can also happen very quickly over just a couple of days. While this can be a distressing side effect, it is important to remember that hair loss from chemotherapy is temporary. Your hair should begin to grow back a few weeks after completing treatment. In some rare cases, permanent hair loss may occur if hair has not fully regrown 6 months after treatment ends. Your treatment team can provide guidance and support for managing hair loss during this journey.

question: What is scalp cooling and how can it help with hair loss during paclitaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: You can try scalp cooling to stop you losing some or all the hair on your head. This involves wearing a cold cap before, during and for 1 to 2 hours after your treatment with the chemotherapy drugs. It lowers the temperature of your scalp, which reduces blood flow to your hair follicles to stop the chemotherapy drugs from reaching them. How well the cold cap works depends on the drugs and doses used, and it does not work for everyone.
answer: Scalp cooling is a technique that can potentially help prevent or reduce hair loss during paclitaxel treatment. The cold cap lowers the temperature of the scalp, which reduces blood flow to the hair follicles and can stop the chemotherapy drugs from reaching and damaging them. However, the effectiveness of scalp cooling depends on the specific drugs and doses used, and it does not work for everyone. If you are concerned about hair loss and want to explore this option, it's best to discuss it with your treatment team. They can provide guidance on whether scalp cooling may be suitable for your particular situation and treatment plan.

question: What is taxane acute pain syndrome (TAPS) and how can it be managed?
source_excerpt: Your muscles or joints may ache or feel painful 2 or 3 days after you have your treatment. This usually wears off after a few days to a week but may last a bit longer. This is sometimes called taxane acute pain syndrome, or TAPS. It can be very painful and you may need to take pain relief or anti-inflammatory drugs like paracetamol or ibuprofen. It's a good idea to have some of these available before starting your treatment just in case you need them. Be aware that pain relief can mask the signs of infection such as a high temperature, so you need to look out for the other signs (see page 6).
answer: Taxane acute pain syndrome, or TAPS, refers to aching or painful muscles and joints that can occur 2-3 days after receiving paclitaxel treatment. This side effect is usually temporary, wearing off within a few days to a week, but it can sometimes last longer. TAPS can be quite painful, so it's recommended to have pain relief medication like paracetamol or ibuprofen on hand before starting treatment, in case you need it. These medications can help alleviate the muscle and joint pain associated with TAPS. However, be aware that pain relievers can mask signs of infection like fever, so watch out for other potential infection symptoms.

question: What should I do if I experience nausea or vomiting during chemotherapy treatment?
source_excerpt: You may feel sick (nausea) although this is usually mild, and most people will not actually be sick (vomit). You'll be given anti-sickness medication, as tablets or into a vein, before each cycle of chemotherapy. You'll also have some anti-sickness tablets to take home. If nausea and vomiting are affecting you, let your treatment team know. Contact your treatment team or the 24-hour helpline number if you have severe vomiting and cannot drink any fluids without vomiting, even if it happens at the weekend or during the night.
answer: It's common to experience nausea (feeling sick) during chemotherapy treatment, although vomiting is usually mild. You'll be given anti-sickness medication before each treatment cycle to help prevent and manage these side effects. Make sure to take the anti-sickness tablets you're prescribed to take home as well. If nausea and vomiting are still affecting you significantly, let your treatment team know so they can adjust the medication or provide additional support. Contact them immediately if you experience severe vomiting that prevents you from drinking any fluids, even on weekends or at night. Your care team is there to help manage side effects and ensure you can get through treatment as comfortably as possible.

question: What are some potential skin reactions I may experience from chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: You may develop a rash anywhere on your body or your skin might change colour. This could be red and itchy or you may feel flushed. Your doctor might prescribe medicine to help. If you have skin reactions, mention this to your treatment team so they can monitor the symptoms. Some people have a skin reaction called hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia). It usually affects the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, but you may also have symptoms in other areas like the skin on the knees or elbows. Hand-foot syndrome can make it harder to carry out daily activities and can affect your quality of life. Your treatment team may prescribe gels or creams to apply to the affected areas.
answer: Chemotherapy treatment can sometimes cause skin reactions or changes. You may develop a rash anywhere on your body, or your skin might change color, becoming red, itchy, or flushed. Another possible reaction is called hand-foot syndrome, which affects the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, but can also occur on areas like the knees or elbows. Hand-foot syndrome can make daily activities more difficult and impact your quality of life. If you experience any skin reactions, be sure to mention them to your treatment team so they can monitor the symptoms and potentially prescribe medication or creams to help manage the reaction. Your care providers want to be aware of any side effects you're experiencing.

question: What is docetaxel and how does it work?
source_excerpt: Docetaxel is a chemotherapy drug. Chemotherapy destroys cancer cells by affecting their ability to divide and grow. Chemotherapy also affects other cells throughout the body, which causes side effects. Docetaxel is the non-branded name of the drug, but you may hear it called by one of its brand names such as Taxotere.
answer: Docetaxel is a chemotherapy drug used to treat breast cancer. It works by destroying cancer cells and preventing them from dividing and growing. Chemotherapy drugs like docetaxel affect all rapidly dividing cells in the body, not just cancer cells, which is why side effects can occur. While docetaxel is the generic name, you may also hear it called by its brand name Taxotere.

question: Can docetaxel be given before surgery for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: You may have docetaxel before surgery to shrink a larger breast cancer. This may mean breast-conserving surgery is an option rather than a mastectomy. Breast-conserving surgery is where the cancer is removed with a margin (border) of normal breast tissue around it, also known as wide local excision or lumpectomy. A mastectomy is where all the breast tissue is removed, usually including the nipple.
answer: Yes, docetaxel can be given before surgery to treat breast cancer. It may be used to shrink a larger breast cancer tumor prior to surgery. By reducing the tumor size, docetaxel can potentially allow for breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) instead of a full mastectomy (removal of the entire breast). So docetaxel given before surgery can increase the chances of having less extensive breast surgery.

question: How is docetaxel administered to patients?
source_excerpt: Docetaxel is given into a vein (intravenously). This will usually be through a cannula, a small tube that's inserted into a vein in the back of your hand or lower arm. You could also have docetaxel through: • A skin-tunnelled catheter (Hickman line): a tube inserted into a vein in your chest • A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC): a tube inserted into a vein in your arm at or above the bend in your elbow • An implanted port: a small device with a tube that goes into a vein that's put under the skin, usually in your chest or arm You will have docetaxel as an outpatient.

The treatment is given as an outpatient, with each dose taking around 1 hour to administer.

question: How often is docetaxel treatment given and what is the schedule like?
source_excerpt: Docetaxel is normally given once every 3 weeks, over about 1 hour. This is called a cycle. The gap between each cycle of treatment gives your body time to recover. Treatment can reduce the amount of blood cells in your body. You might have a longer gap between cycles if your blood tests show that the number of blood cells has not returned to normal (see page 5).

This gap between cycles gives your body a chance to rebuild healthy blood cells before the next round of treatment.

question: What are some common side effects of docetaxel chemotherapy?

Effects on the blood 
Docetaxel can temporarily affect the number of blood cells in the body. Blood is made up of red cells, white cells and platelets.

It's important to communicate any side effects you experience, even if they're not listed, with your chemotherapy nurse or treatment team.

question: What should I do if I have signs of an infection during chemotherapy treatment?
source_excerpt: Your treatment team may give you guidelines to follow for reporting signs of an infection. But generally you should contact your hospital immediately if you have any of the following: • A high temperature (over 37.5°C) or low temperature (under 36°C), or whatever your treatment team has advised • Suddenly feeling unwell, even with a normal temperature • Symptoms of an infection, such as a sore throat, cough, needing to pass urine often or feeling cold or shivery Before starting chemotherapy you should be given a 24-hour contact number or told where to get emergency care by your treatment team.
answer: It's important to be vigilant for signs of infection while undergoing chemotherapy, as the treatment can lower your white blood cell count and increase your risk of infection. Your treatment team will provide guidelines on what to watch out for, but generally you should contact the hospital immediately if you experience a high fever (over 37.5°C) or low temperature (under 36°C), feel suddenly unwell even with a normal temperature, or have symptoms like a sore throat, cough, frequent urination, or chills. Don't hesitate to reach out, as prompt treatment for an infection is crucial. Your care team will have given you a 24-hour contact number or instructions on where to seek emergency care.

question: What can be done to help reduce the risk of infection during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Sometimes your treatment team may recommend injections of drugs called growth factors. This helps the body produce more white blood cells to reduce your risk of infection.
answer: One way your treatment team may help reduce your risk of infection during chemotherapy is by recommending injections of drugs called growth factors. These medications help stimulate your body to produce more white blood cells, which are important for fighting off infections. Having a low white blood cell count is a common side effect of chemotherapy, so boosting your levels with growth factor injections can provide some extra protection against infections while your immune system is compromised.

question: How can chemotherapy affect my risk of bruising or bleeding?
source_excerpt: Docetaxel can reduce the number of platelets, which help the blood to clot. You may bruise more easily, have nosebleeds or your gums may bleed when you brush your teeth. Tell your treatment team if you have any of these symptoms.
answer: Chemotherapy drugs like docetaxel can reduce the number of platelets in your blood. Platelets are the cells that help blood to clot properly. With lower platelet levels, you may notice that you bruise more easily than usual, have nosebleeds, or experience bleeding from your gums when brushing your teeth. While these side effects can be concerning, they are relatively common during chemotherapy treatment. Be sure to notify your care team right away if you experience any bruising, bleeding, or signs of low platelets so they can monitor you closely and provide any necessary treatment or precautions.

question: What is the likelihood of hair loss with docetaxel chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Docetaxel causes hair loss. Most people will lose all their hair, including eyebrows, eyelashes and body hair. You may begin to lose your hair about 2 weeks after the first treatment, but it can happen earlier. Hair loss is usually gradual, but it can happen very quickly, possibly over a couple of days. Hair loss should be temporary and in most cases your hair will begin to grow back a few weeks after your treatment has ended. There's some evidence that it might take a long time for hair to grow back in people treated with docetaxel, or that hair loss may be permanent.
answer: Docetaxel chemotherapy is known to cause hair loss in most patients. The hair loss is usually complete, affecting not just the hair on your head but also eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair. While the hair loss may start gradually around 2 weeks after the first treatment, it can sometimes happen very quickly over just a couple of days. The good news is that this hair loss is typically temporary, and your hair should start growing back a few weeks after completing the chemotherapy treatment. However, there is some evidence that hair regrowth may take longer with docetaxel, or in some cases the hair loss could potentially be permanent. If you have concerns about hair loss impacting your treatment decisions, it's best to discuss them with your cancer care team.

question: Is there a way to prevent or reduce hair loss during docetaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: You can try scalp cooling to stop you losing some or all the hair on your head. This involves wearing a cold cap before, during and for 1 to 2 hours after your treatment with the chemotherapy drugs. It lowers the temperature of your scalp, which reduces blood flow to your hair follicles to stop the chemotherapy drugs from reaching them. How well the cold cap works depends on the drugs and doses used, and it does not work for everyone.
answer: Yes, there is an option called scalp cooling that may help prevent or reduce hair loss on the head during docetaxel chemotherapy. The cold temperature lowers blood flow to the hair follicles on the scalp, which can stop the chemotherapy drugs from reaching and damaging them as much. However, scalp cooling does not always work for everyone, and its effectiveness depends on the specific chemotherapy drugs and doses used. While it may help reduce hair loss on the scalp, it does not prevent hair loss on other areas of the body like eyebrows and eyelashes. If preserving your hair is a priority, discuss the option of scalp cooling with your treatment team.

question: What is taxane acute pain syndrome and how can it be managed?
source_excerpt: Your muscles or joints may ache or become painful 2 or 3 days after you have your treatment. This usually wears off after a few days to a week but may last a bit longer. This is sometimes called taxane acute pain syndrome (TAPS). It can be very painful and you may need to take pain relief or anti-inflammatory drugs like paracetamol or ibuprofen. It's a good idea to have some of these available before starting your treatment just in case you need them. Be aware that pain relief can mask the signs of infection such as a high temperature, so you need to look out for the other signs (see page 6).
answer: Taxane acute pain syndrome (TAPS) is a potential side effect where your muscles or joints may ache or become painful 2-3 days after receiving docetaxel treatment. This pain can be quite severe but typically wears off within a few days to a week, though it may last longer for some. To manage TAPS, you can take over-the-counter pain relief or anti-inflammatory medications like paracetamol or ibuprofen. It's a good idea to have some of these medications on hand before starting treatment in case you need them for TAPS. However, be aware that pain relievers can mask signs of infection like fever, so watch out for other potential infection symptoms.

question: What should I do if I experience nausea and vomiting during my docetaxel chemotherapy treatment?
source_excerpt: You may feel sick (nausea) although this is usually mild, and most people will not actually be sick (vomit). You'll be given anti-sickness medication, as tablets or into a vein, before each cycle of chemotherapy. You'll also have some anti-sickness tablets to take home. If nausea and vomiting are affecting you, let your treatment team know. Contact your treatment team or the 24-hour helpline number if you have severe vomiting and cannot drink any fluids without vomiting, even if it happens at the weekend or during the night.
answer: If you experience nausea (feeling sick) or vomiting during your docetaxel chemotherapy treatment, it's important to let your treatment team know. You'll also receive anti-sickness tablets to take home with you. If the nausea and vomiting become severe, where you cannot keep any fluids down, contact your treatment team or the 24-hour helpline immediately, even if it's during the night or weekend. Your healthcare team is there to support you through these side effects and ensure you stay hydrated and comfortable.

question: What should I expect in terms of fluid retention during docetaxel chemotherapy?

You'll usually be given steroid drugs to prevent an allergic reaction to docetaxel (see page 13), which will also help reduce the chance of fluid building up.

If you notice swelling or shortness of breath, be sure to mention it to your treatment team so they can monitor your symptoms and provide any necessary support.

question: What is hand-foot syndrome and how can it be managed during docetaxel treatment?

question: How can I take care of my mouth during docetaxel chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Looking after your mouth, including your teeth and gums, is very important during treatment. You may be given a mouthwash to reduce soreness and prevent mouth ulcers developing. It's a good idea to use a small, soft toothbrush during this time. See your dentist for a check-up before chemotherapy begins. Avoid dental work during these treatments if possible. If you need dental work during treatment, speak to your treatment team about the best time to have this. For more information on coping with a sore mouth, see our Chemotherapy for breast cancer booklet.
answer: Maintaining good oral hygiene and taking care of your mouth, teeth, and gums is very important during docetaxel chemotherapy. Your treatment team may provide you with a special mouthwash to help reduce soreness and prevent mouth ulcers from developing. It's recommended to use a small, soft-bristled toothbrush during this time to be gentle on your mouth. Before starting chemotherapy, it's a good idea to visit your dentist for a check-up. Try to avoid any dental work during treatment if possible, but if you do need dental work, discuss the best timing with your treatment team. For more detailed information on coping with a sore mouth during chemotherapy, refer to the 'Chemotherapy for breast cancer' booklet.

question: What can I do if I experience taste changes while receiving docetaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: While you're having docetaxel, your sense of taste can change and some foods may taste different, for example more salty, bitter or metallic. You may no longer enjoy some of the foods you used to. If this is the case speak to your treatment team – they may be able to suggest ways of managing this. Your taste should return to normal once your treatment has finished.

The good news is that your normal taste should return once your treatment is completed. In the meantime, your care team can provide guidance on adjusting your diet to accommodate these temporary taste alterations.

question: How can I manage diarrhea or constipation during docetaxel treatment?

question: What is cancer-related fatigue and how can I manage it during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Cancer-related fatigue is extreme tiredness that does not go away with rest or sleep. It's a very common side effect of breast cancer treatment and may affect you physically and emotionally. If you think you have fatigue, tell your GP or treatment team. They can assess you and offer advice on how to manage your energy levels. You can find lots more information on our website or by calling our helpline on 0808 800 6000. Macmillan Cancer Support produces a booklet called Coping with fatigue.
answer: Cancer-related fatigue is a very common side effect experienced by many breast cancer patients undergoing treatment. It is an extreme form of tiredness that does not improve with rest or sleep. This fatigue can impact you both physically and emotionally. If you think you are experiencing cancer-related fatigue, it's important to let your doctor or treatment team know. They can properly assess your condition and provide advice on strategies to help manage your energy levels during this challenging time. There are resources available with more information, such as on the Breast Cancer Now website or helpline, as well as from organizations like Macmillan Cancer Support which offers a booklet called 'Coping with Fatigue.' Don't hesitate to reach out for support in dealing with this side effect.

question: What should I do if I experience pain, redness or swelling at the injection site during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: If docetaxel leaks out of the vein it is being given in (called extravasation), it can damage the surrounding tissue. Tell your chemotherapy nurse immediately if you have pain, stinging or a burning sensation around the cannula while the drug is being given.
answer: It's important to notify your chemotherapy nurse immediately if you experience any pain, stinging, burning sensation, redness, discoloration or swelling around the area where the IV cannula (small plastic tube) is inserted or along the vein during or after your treatment. This could be a sign that the chemotherapy drug is leaking out of the vein, which can damage the surrounding tissue. Your nurse needs to be aware so they can take appropriate action to prevent further issues and ensure your safety.

question: What should I do if I experience shortness of breath, cough, or breathing problems during docetaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: Contact your treatment team straight away if you have: • Shortness of breath • A cough, with or without a high temperature • Any new or worsening breathing problems, such as chest tightness or wheezing You may need a chest x-ray or CT scan to check if you have ILD. If docetaxel has caused inflammation to your lungs, you may need to stop treatment temporarily and have steroids to treat the inflammation. Early treatment of the inflammation can help to prevent long-term damage to the lungs.

If confirmed, you may need to temporarily stop treatment and take steroids to reduce the inflammation in your lungs. Early treatment is important to prevent long-term lung damage. question: What is the risk of blood clots with docetaxel treatment for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: People with breast cancer have a higher risk of blood clots. Having docetaxel also increases the risk of blood clots such as a DVT (deep vein thrombosis). If you have a DVT, there's a risk part of the blood clot could break away and travel to the lung. This is known as a pulmonary embolism (PE). Blood clots can be life-threatening and should be treated quickly.
answer: Docetaxel chemotherapy can increase the risk of developing blood clots in people with breast cancer, who already have a higher baseline risk. Blood clots like deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can be very serious, as part of the clot could potentially break off and travel to the lungs, causing a life-threatening pulmonary embolism. It's crucial to watch for symptoms like pain, redness, swelling or discoloration in the arms or legs, shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, or coughing up blood. If you experience any of these warning signs, seek immediate medical attention as blood clots require prompt treatment. Your care team can discuss strategies to reduce your clotting risk during docetaxel treatment.

question: What symptoms should prompt seeking emergency care for a potential blood clot during docetaxel treatment?
source_excerpt: Contact your treatment team or go to your local A&E department straight away if you have any of the following symptoms: • Pain, redness/discolouration of the skin, heat and swelling of the arm or leg • Swelling, redness or tenderness where a central line is inserted to give chemotherapy, for example in the arm, chest area or up into the neck • Shortness of breath • Pain or tightness in the chest • Unexplained cough or coughing up blood
answer: If you experience any of the following symptoms while receiving docetaxel chemotherapy, it's crucial to contact your treatment team or go to the emergency room immediately, as they could indicate a life-threatening blood clot: pain, redness, discoloration, heat or swelling in the arm or leg; swelling, redness or tenderness at the site of a central line used for chemotherapy; shortness of breath; chest pain or tightness; or an unexplained cough or coughing up blood. Blood clots require rapid medical intervention, so don't hesitate to get these symptoms evaluated right away. Your healthcare team can then take appropriate steps to diagnose and treat any clots before they become even more dangerous.

question: Can docetaxel chemotherapy affect my fertility or ability to have children?
source_excerpt: At the moment, we don't know whether docetaxel affects fertility. The effects will depend on any other chemotherapy drugs you're having at the same time, or have had in the past, and your age. Some women stop having periods (amenorrhoea) during chemotherapy, although this may be temporary. Your periods are less likely to come back after finishing chemotherapy if you're over 40.
answer: Docetaxel and other chemotherapy drugs can potentially affect fertility, but the impact depends on several factors like your age and any other treatments you've had. It's important to discuss any concerns about fertility with your healthcare team before starting treatment. Some women may experience temporary amenorrhea (stopping of periods) during chemotherapy. If you are over 40, your periods are less likely to return after completing chemotherapy. Your team can provide guidance on preserving fertility options if this is a concern for you.

question: Is it safe to have sex during docetaxel chemotherapy treatment?

Men should also continue to use contraception for 4 months after treatment ends.

For men, contraception should continue for 4 months after the end of treatment.

question: Can I get travel vaccinations while undergoing chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: You should not have any live vaccines while you're having chemotherapy. Live vaccines include: • Mumps • Measles • Rubella (German measles) • Polio • BCG (tuberculosis) • Yellow fever Live vaccines contain a small amount of live virus or bacteria. If you have a weakened immune system, which you may do during chemotherapy, they could be harmful. It's safe to have these vaccinations 6 months after your treatment finishes. Talk to your GP or treatment team before having any vaccinations. If anyone you have close contact with needs to have a live vaccine, speak to your treatment team or GP. They can advise what precautions you may need to take depending on the vaccination.
answer: It's generally not recommended to get live vaccines while undergoing chemotherapy, as your immune system may be weakened and the live viruses or bacteria in these vaccines could potentially be harmful. question: How is HER2 status determined for breast cancer patients?
section: How do I know if my breast cancer is HER2 positive or HER2 negative?
source_excerpt: All invasive breast cancers are tested for HER2 levels. This is done in a hospital laboratory on a sample of breast cancer tissue removed during a biopsy or surgery. The results are usually available within 1 to 3 weeks. There are various tests to measure HER2 levels. A test called IHC (immunohistochemistry) is usually done first. It involves a special staining process performed on a sample of breast cancer tissue. It's reported as a score ranging from 0 to 3: • 0 or 1+ means the breast cancer is HER2 negative • 2+ is borderline • 3+ means the breast cancer is HER2 positive Breast cancers with a borderline result (2+) should be retested using more specialised techniques. These tests give a result of HER2 positive, HER2 low or HER2 negative.
answer: All invasive breast cancers are tested for HER2 levels to determine if they are HER2 positive or HER2 negative. This testing is done in a hospital laboratory on a sample of the breast cancer tissue removed during a biopsy or surgery. The results are usually available within 1 to 3 weeks after the procedure.   There are different tests used to measure HER2 levels. The most common initial test is called immunohistochemistry (IHC), which involves a special staining process on the tissue sample. The IHC test results are reported as a score from 0 to 3+:  0 or 1+ means the breast cancer is HER2 negative 2+ is a borderline result  3+ means the breast cancer is HER2 positive  If the IHC test shows a borderline 2+ result, more specialized tests are done to confirm if the cancer is HER2 positive, HER2 low, or HER2 negative. Speak to your treatment team for more details on understanding your HER2 test results.

question: When is trastuzumab given for primary breast cancer?
source_excerpt: Trastuzumab can be used as a treatment for primary breast cancer (breast cancer that has not spread beyond the breast or the lymph nodes under the arm). Before surgery Sometimes, trastuzumab is given before surgery. This is known as neo-adjuvant or primary therapy. It may be used to slow down the growth of breast cancer to reduce the chance of it spreading to other parts of the body. Or it may help shrink a large breast cancer before surgery. Trastuzumab is given with chemotherapy, and usually with another drug called pertuzumab (Perjeta). After surgery Trastuzumab can be given after surgery to reduce the likelihood of the breast cancer returning or spreading to another part of the body. This is known as adjuvant treatment. Trastuzumab may be given with or after chemotherapy, and sometimes with pertuzumab.

After surgery, trastuzumab may be given with or after chemotherapy, and sometimes with pertuzumab, to reduce the risk of the cancer returning or spreading to other parts of the body. question: What are some common side effects of trastuzumab treatment?
source_excerpt:
Flu-like symptoms
Fever, chills and mild pain in some parts of the body can occur during or shortly after your treatment. These symptoms are more common the first time you have trastuzumab and do not usually last long. Taking pain relief can help.

Extreme tiredness
Fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that does not go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally.

It's a very common side effect of trastuzumab and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. Occasionally fatigue is a long-term effect.

This fatigue can last for weeks or months after treatment ends, and in some cases, it can be a long-term effect. It's important to let your treatment team know if you experience fatigue so they can rule out other conditions like anemia. They can also provide guidance on coping with and managing fatigue.

question: How can trastuzumab affect my blood cell counts, and what should I watch out for?
source_excerpt: Trastuzumab given with chemotherapy can temporarily affect the number of blood cells in the body. If you're having chemotherapy, you'll have regular blood tests to check your blood count. Blood is made up of red cells, white cells and platelets. If the number of blood cells is too low, your next cycle of treatment may be delayed or the dose reduced. Not having enough white blood cells can increase the risk of getting an infection. Your treatment team may give you guidelines to follow for reporting signs of an infection, but generally you should contact your hospital immediately if you experience any of the following: • A high temperature (over 37.5°C) or low temperature (under 36°C), or whatever your chemotherapy team has advised •  Suddenly feeling unwell, even with a normal temperature • Symptoms of an infection, for example a sore throat, a cough, a need to pass urine frequently or feeling cold or shivery You may need antibiotics. Having too few red blood cells is called anaemia. If you feel particularly tired, breathless or dizzy, let your treatment team know.
answer:
Trastuzumab, especially when given in combination with chemotherapy, can temporarily affect the number of blood cells in your body. This includes red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. If you're receiving chemotherapy along with trastuzumab, your treatment team will monitor your blood counts through regular blood tests. If your blood cell levels drop too low, your next treatment cycle may be delayed or the dose reduced to allow your body to recover.

Specifically, low white blood cell counts can increase your risk of infections. Be vigilant for signs like a high fever (over 37.5°C) or low fever (under 36°C), feeling suddenly unwell even with a normal temperature, or symptoms like a sore throat, cough, frequent urination, or chills. Contact your hospital immediately if you experience any of these, as you may need antibiotics or other interventions.

Low red blood cell counts (anemia) can cause fatigue, breathlessness, or dizziness. Let your treatment team know if you experience these symptoms so they can address the anemia appropriately.

question: What is exemestane and how does it work?
section: What is exemestane? / How does exemestane work?
source_excerpt: Exemestane is a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through a natural menopause (when periods stop). It can also be used in premenopausal women having ovarian suppression (treatment to stop the ovaries working). Exemestane works by reducing the amount of oestrogen made in the body. Some breast cancers use oestrogen in the body to help them to grow. These are known as oestrogen receptor positive or ER+ breast cancers. Exemestane will only be prescribed if your breast cancer is ER+. After the menopause, the ovaries no longer produce oestrogen, but some oestrogen is made in body fat. This process involves an enzyme (a type of protein) called aromatase. Exemestane belongs to a group of drugs called aromatase inhibitors. Aromatase inhibitors stop the aromatase enzyme from working. This means there's less oestrogen in the body to help breast cancer cells to grow.
answer: Exemestane, also known as Aromasin, is a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause or are receiving ovarian suppression treatment. It works by reducing the amount of estrogen in the body. Some breast cancers, known as estrogen receptor positive (ER+) cancers, use estrogen to grow. Exemestane belongs to a class of drugs called aromatase inhibitors. It stops the aromatase enzyme from working, which is responsible for producing estrogen in the body after menopause. By lowering estrogen levels, exemestane can help prevent ER+ breast cancer cells from growing and spreading.

question: What types of breast cancer can exemestane be used to treat?
section: Breast cancer that has come back or spread
source_excerpt:
Exemestane can also be used to treat people who have: 
• Local recurrence  – breast cancer that has come back in the 
chest/breast area or in the skin near the original site or scar
• Locally advanced breast cancer  – breast cancer that has 
spread to the tissues and lymph nodes (glands) around the 
chest, neck and under the breastbone. Sometimes breast 
cancer is locally advanced when it is first diagnosed. This may 
also happen when breast cancer comes back after treatment 
and may be referred to as regional recurrence
• Secondary (metastatic) breast cancer  – breast cancer that 
has spread to other parts of the body
Exemestane can be given alongside a targeted therapy drug.
answer: Exemestane can be used to treat several types of breast cancer, including local recurrence (when the cancer has come back in the chest/breast area or skin near the original site or scar), locally advanced breast cancer (when the cancer has spread to nearby tissues and lymph nodes), and secondary or metastatic breast cancer (when the cancer has spread to other parts of the body). Exemestane may be given along with a targeted therapy drug to help treat these different stages and presentations of breast cancer.

question: How long will I need to take exemestane for my breast cancer treatment?
section: HOW LONG WILL I HAVE TO TAKE EXEMESTANE?
source_excerpt: People being treated for primary breast cancer will usually take exemestane for five to ten years. Some people start taking exemestane after a number of years of taking another hormone therapy drug called tamoxifen. If you're taking exemestane to treat breast cancer that has come back or spread to another part of the body, you'll usually take it for as long as it's effective and any side effects can be managed.
answer: The length of time you will need to take exemestane depends on your individual situation and the stage of your breast cancer. If you are being treated for primary breast cancer, you will typically take exemestane for 5 to 10 years. Some patients start taking exemestane after taking another hormone therapy drug called tamoxifen for a few years. If your breast cancer has returned or spread to other parts of the body, you will usually take exemestane for as long as it remains effective and the side effects are manageable. Your treatment team will discuss the recommended duration with you based on your specific case.

question: What are some common side effects of taking exemestane?
source_excerpt: Like any drug, exemestane can cause side effects. Everyone reacts differently to drugs and some people have more side effects than others. Having few or no side effects doesn't mean the drug isn't effective. For many people, side effects improve within the first few months of starting the treatment. However, for some people they may cause distress and disrupt everyday life. This booklet does not list all the possible side effects. If you're worried about any side effects, regardless of whether they are listed here, talk to your GP or treatment team. They may be able to offer ways of improving your symptoms. Your specialist may suggest changing to a different aromatase inhibitor such as letrozole or anastrozole, or another hormone treatment, as some women get on better with a different drug.

question: What are some common menopausal symptoms caused by exemestane?
source_excerpt: Hot flushes, night sweats and increased sweating are common side effects of exemestane. A hot flush can range from a mild sensation of warming which just affects the face, to waves of heat throughout the body. Some women also experience a drenching sweat affecting the whole body. Many women get flushes at night, leading to disturbed sleep which can mean being forgetful, feeling irritable and having difficulty concentrating.
answer: Exemestane can cause menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, and increased sweating. Hot flushes can range from a mild sensation of warmth in the face to intense waves of heat throughout the body, sometimes accompanied by drenching sweats. Many women experience hot flushes at night, leading to disturbed sleep, which can result in forgetfulness, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. These menopausal symptoms can be challenging to manage, but there are strategies available to help cope with them.

question: How can I cope with extreme fatigue or tiredness from taking exemestane?
source_excerpt: Cancer-related fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that doesn't go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally. It's a very common side effect of exemestane and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. Occasionally fatigue is a long-term effect. Fatigue can also be caused by conditions such as anaemia (too few red blood cells). It's important to let your GP or treatment team know if you're affected by fatigue to rule out other conditions. Fatigue affects people in different ways and there are a number of ways of coping with and managing it.
answer: Cancer-related fatigue, which is an extreme tiredness and exhaustion that doesn't go away with rest, is a very common side effect of taking exemestane. This fatigue can affect you both physically and emotionally, and may last for weeks or even months after your treatment has finished. In some cases, it can be a long-term effect. It's important to let your GP or treatment team know if you're experiencing fatigue so they can rule out any other underlying conditions like anemia. There are various ways to cope with and manage fatigue - it affects everyone differently. I'd recommend checking out the fatigue information on the Breast Cancer Now website or calling their Helpline for more tips and strategies. Macmillan Cancer Support also has a helpful booklet called 'Coping with Fatigue'.

question: What is the risk of developing osteoporosis while taking exemestane?
source_excerpt: Exemestane reduces the amount of oestrogen in the body. A lack of oestrogen over time can cause osteoporosis. Your treatment team will sometimes check the strength and thickness (density) of your bones with a scan before or shortly after you start taking exemestane. If you have been given bisphosphonates (see below) as part of your treatment you will not need a scan. Your bone density may be checked every two to three years while you're taking exemestane, depending on the results from the initial scan or whether your specialist has any concerns.
answer: Exemestane reduces the amount of estrogen in the body, and a lack of estrogen over time can cause osteoporosis (thinning of the bones). To monitor this, your treatment team will sometimes check the strength and thickness (density) of your bones with a scan before or shortly after you start taking exemestane. If you have already been given bisphosphonates as part of your treatment, you may not need a scan. Your bone density may be checked every 2-3 years while taking exemestane, depending on the initial scan results or if your specialist has any concerns. It's important to be aware of this potential side effect and take steps to keep your bones healthy.
