question: How can I help keep my bones healthy while taking exemestane?
source_excerpt: To help keep your bones healthy you can increase your intake of calcium and vitamin D. Most people do this by taking a supplement. You may also want to eat more foods that are rich in calcium, such as milk, cheese, yoghurt and cereals. For vitamin D, you can increase the amount of oily fish, mushrooms and eggs you eat. Stopping smoking and doing regular weight-bearing exercise can also help keep your bones strong. If your bones are already beginning to show signs of thinning or if you already have osteoporosis, you may be given another drug to increase bone density and strength. This will usually be from a group of drugs called bisphosphonates.
answer: There are several things you can do to help keep your bones strong and healthy while taking exemestane. First, increase your intake of calcium and vitamin D, either through supplements or by eating more foods rich in these nutrients like milk, cheese, yogurt, cereals, oily fish, mushrooms, and eggs. Stopping smoking and doing regular weight-bearing exercise can also help strengthen your bones. If your bones are already showing signs of thinning or you have osteoporosis, your doctor may prescribe medications called bisphosphonates to increase bone density and strength. Don't hesitate to speak with your specialist if you have any concerns about maintaining bone health.

question: What are some common side effects of taking exemestane, and how can they be managed?
source_excerpt:
Nausea and vomiting 
Exemestane may make you feel sick (nausea) or be  
sick (vomiting).
These symptoms usually improve or become easier to  
manage over time. Taking exemestane after food can help 
reduce nausea. 

High cholesterol 
Exemestane may cause the level of cholesterol in the blood to 
rise, although this doesn't usually need treatment. If you have 
a history of high cholesterol you may want to discuss this with 
your specialist or GP. 

Diarrhoea and constipation
If you have diarrhoea, it's important to drink enough fluids.  
Your GP or treatment team can prescribe medication to help 
with diarrhoea. 
It's also important to keep active and eat a high-fibre diet to 
avoid constipation.

Loss of appetite 
If you lose your appetite, you may find eating small frequent 
meals or snacks helps keep up your food intake. It may help to 
take your tablet just after food. 
Indigestion or heartburn – a painful burning feeling in the  
chest after eating – is also common. If you struggle to maintain 
a healthy weight, ask your GP or specialist about being referred 
to a dietitian.

Carpal tunnel syndrome 
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is pressure on a nerve in your 
wrist. This causes pain, tingling and numbness in your arm, 
hand or fingers. Using a wrist splint can help. Sometimes it can 
go away on its own, but it can take months to get better. Speak 
to your GP or specialist if you have any of these symptoms.
answer: Exemestane can cause some side effects like nausea, vomiting, high cholesterol, diarrhea, constipation, and loss of appetite. For nausea, taking exemestane after eating can help reduce it, and the symptoms often improve over time. If you experience diarrhea, it's important to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids, and your doctor can prescribe medication to help. For constipation, staying active and eating a high-fiber diet is recommended. If you lose your appetite, try eating smaller, more frequent meals or snacks, and take your medication after eating. Your doctor may also refer you to a dietitian if you struggle to maintain a healthy weight. If you experience indigestion or heartburn, let your care team know. It's also important to inform your doctor if you develop carpal tunnel syndrome, which can cause pain, tingling, and numbness in the arm, hand, or fingers.

question: What are some potential side effects of taking exemestane for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: You may have some hair loss or thinning while taking exemestane. You may develop a skin rash or itching while taking exemestane. This usually goes away when your treatment finishes. Exemestane can occasionally cause changes to how the liver works. These changes are usually mild and unlikely to cause any symptoms. Once you finish your treatment your liver will usually go back to normal. You can get swollen hands and feet. If you notice this or any other swelling, let your GP know. Vaginal bleeding can happen in the first few weeks after starting exemestane. It most commonly occurs when changing from one hormone therapy drug to another. This may also be due to vaginal dryness. If the bleeding continues for more than a few days, tell your specialist.

Exemestane can occasionally cause mild changes in how your liver functions, but this is typically not a concern and your liver should return to normal after treatment ends. Some patients experience swelling in their hands and feet, so let your doctor know if you notice any swelling. In the first few weeks, you may have some vaginal bleeding, especially if switching from a different hormone therapy. This bleeding is usually minor and temporary, but inform your doctor if it persists for more than a few days.

question: What should I do if I experience symptoms of a blood clot while taking exemestane?
source_excerpt: People with breast cancer have a higher risk of blood clots such as a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Their risk is higher because of the cancer itself and some treatments for breast cancer. If the cancer has spread to other parts of the body (secondary breast cancer), this also increases the risk. People with a DVT are at risk of developing a pulmonary embolism (PE). This is when part of the blood clot breaks away and travels to the lung. Blood clots can be harmful but are treatable so it's important to report symptoms as soon as possible. If you experience any of the following symptoms contact your local A&E department, GP or treatment team straight away: • Pain, redness/discolouration, heat and swelling of the arm or leg • Swelling, redness or tenderness where a central line is inserted to give chemotherapy, for example in the arm, chest area or up into the neck • Shortness of breath • Pain or tightness in the chest • Unexplained cough or coughing up blood
answer: People with breast cancer have an increased risk of developing blood clots like deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE). This risk is higher due to the cancer itself, certain breast cancer treatments, and if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. Blood clots can be serious but are treatable, so it's crucial to report any symptoms right away. If you experience pain, redness, heat, or swelling in your arm or leg, swelling or redness at a chemotherapy injection site, shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, an unexplained cough, or coughing up blood, contact your local emergency department, doctor, or cancer care team immediately. These could be signs of a blood clot, which requires prompt medical attention.

question: How long should I take exemestane for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Your treatment team will tell you when to stop taking exemestane. You won't need to stop taking it gradually. However, not taking the drug for the recommended time may increase the risk of your breast cancer coming back.

question: Can I take other medications while on exemestane for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: If you're taking any other prescribed or over-the-counter medicines, check with your treatment team or pharmacist if you can take these with exemestane. The following medicines should be used cautiously if you take exemestane. Let your doctor know if you are taking medicines such as: Rifampicin – an antibiotic, Carbamazepine or phenytoin – anticonvulsants used to treat epilepsy, St John's wort – a herbal remedy used as a complementary therapy for mild to moderate depression. Do not take other drugs containing oestrogen, such as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), while you're taking exemestane as this may interfere with its effectiveness.

Your healthcare team can provide guidance on safe medication combinations and any necessary precautions.

question: What is letrozole and how does it work?
section: What is letrozole? / How does letrozole work?
source_excerpt: Letrozole is a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through a natural menopause (when periods stop). It can also be used in premenopausal women having ovarian suppression (treatment to stop the ovaries working). Letrozole works by reducing the amount of oestrogen made in the body. Some breast cancers use oestrogen in the body to help them to grow. These are known as oestrogen receptor positive or ER+ breast cancers. Letrozole will only be prescribed if your breast cancer is ER+. Letrozole belongs to a group of drugs called aromatase inhibitors. Aromatase inhibitors stop the aromatase enzyme from working. This means there's less oestrogen in the body to help breast cancer cells to grow.

question: What can be done if experiencing joint or muscle aches from letrozole?
source_excerpt: Aching or pain in the joints and muscles is often mild and temporary, although for some people it's more severe and longer lasting. It can usually be relieved with mild pain relief like paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen. Before using anti-inflammatory pain relief, ask your doctor about the correct dose, how long you should use it for and any possible side effects, especially if you have a stomach ulcer or asthma. Exercise that gently stretches your joints or strengthens your muscles to better support your joints, such as yoga or pilates, may help improve your symptoms. Brisk walking can also be beneficial. A physiotherapist may also be able to suggest exercises to help. If you have secondary breast cancer, check with your specialist before starting any new type of exercise. Some people benefit from switching to a different hormone therapy. For example, it may be possible to switch to another aromatase inhibitor to see if your pain improves, or some people might be offered the drug tamoxifen as an alternative. If the pain is severe, it may be helpful to see a pain management specialist at a pain clinic.

However, check with your doctor first about the correct dosage and duration, especially if you have conditions like stomach ulcers or asthma.  2. Gentle exercises that stretch the joints or strengthen supporting muscles, such as yoga, Pilates, or brisk walking, may help improve the symptoms.  3. A physiotherapist can suggest specific exercises tailored to your needs.  4. In some cases, switching to a different hormone therapy like another aromatase inhibitor or tamoxifen may be an option to see if the joint/muscle pain improves.  5. For severe pain, seeing a pain management specialist at a pain clinic can be helpful.  Don't hesitate to discuss these options with your treatment team to find the best approach for managing any joint or muscle aches you experience.

question: What are some common menopausal symptoms caused by letrozole?

A hot flush can range from a mild sensation of warming which just affects the face, to waves of heat throughout the body. Some women also experience a drenching sweat affecting the whole body. Many women get flushes at night, leading to disturbed sleep which can mean being forgetful, feeling irritable and having difficulty concentrating.

question: How does letrozole affect bone health?
source_excerpt: Letrozole reduces the amount of oestrogen in the body. A lack of oestrogen over time can cause osteoporosis. Your specialist will sometimes check the strength and thickness (density) of your bones with a scan before or shortly after you start taking letrozole. If you have been given bisphosphonates (see below) as part of your treatment you will not need a scan. Your bone density may be checked every two to three years while you're taking letrozole, depending on the results from the initial scan or whether your specialist has any concerns.
answer: Letrozole, a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer, reduces the amount of estrogen in the body. Over time, this lack of estrogen can lead to osteoporosis, which is a condition that causes thinning and weakening of the bones. To monitor this potential side effect, your oncologist will likely order a bone density scan before or shortly after you start taking letrozole. This scan measures the strength and thickness of your bones. Depending on the initial results or any concerns, your bone density may be checked every 2-3 years while you are on letrozole treatment.

question: What can I do to help keep my bones healthy while taking letrozole?
source_excerpt: To help keep your bones healthy you can increase your intake of calcium and vitamin D. Most people do this by taking a supplement. You may also want to eat more foods that are rich in calcium, such as milk, cheese, yoghurt and cereals. For vitamin D, you can increase the amount of oily fish, mushrooms and eggs you eat. Stopping smoking and doing regular weight-bearing exercise can also help keep your bones strong. If your bones are already beginning to show signs of thinning or if you already have osteoporosis, you may be given another drug to increase bone density and strength. This will usually be from a group of drugs called bisphosphonates.

question: What are some common side effects of taking letrozole for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt:
Nausea and vomiting 
Letrozole may make you feel sick (nausea) or be sick (vomiting). 
These symptoms usually improve or become easier to manage 
over time. Taking your letrozole with or after food can help 
reduce nausea. 

Diarrhoea and constipation
If you have diarrhoea, it's important to drink enough fluids.  
Your GP or treatment team can prescribe medication to help 
with diarrhoea. 
It's also important to keep active and eat a high-fibre diet to 
avoid constipation.

Changes to your appetite 
If you lose your appetite, it may help to take your tablet with 
food. You may find eating small frequent meals or snacks helps 
keep up your food intake. 
If your appetite increases it may affect your weight. If you 
struggle to maintain a healthy weight, ask your GP or specialist 
about being referred to a dietitian. 

Changes to hair or facial hair
You may have some hair loss or thinning while taking  
letrozole. A small number of women notice an increase in 
downy facial hair. 

Skin changes 
You may develop a skin rash or dry skin while taking letrozole. 
This usually goes away when your treatment finishes. Your 
pharmaacist, GP or treatment team can tell you what products 
you can use on your skin to help.
answer: Letrozole, a hormone therapy medication used to treat breast cancer, can cause several side effects. Some common ones include nausea and vomiting, which may improve over time. Taking letrozole with food can help reduce nausea. You may also experience diarrhea or constipation. It's important to stay hydrated if you have diarrhea and maintain a high-fiber diet to prevent constipation. Changes in appetite, either loss or increase, can occur. If you struggle to maintain a healthy weight, ask your doctor about seeing a dietitian. Some women experience hair loss, thinning, or an increase in facial hair while on letrozole. Skin changes like rashes or dryness are also possible but typically resolve after treatment ends. Your healthcare team can recommend products to help manage skin issues. With open communication and proper management, many of these side effects can be minimized during your treatment journey.

question: What increases the risk of blood clots for breast cancer patients?

question: Can I get pregnant while taking letrozole for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: Taking letrozole while pregnant may be harmful to a developing baby. It's possible to become pregnant while taking letrozole even if your periods have stopped with ovarian suppression. If you're sexually active with a chance of becoming pregnant, your specialist is likely to advise you to use a non-hormonal method of contraception while taking letrozole. Non-hormonal methods include condoms, Femidoms or a diaphragm. It may also be possible to use a coil (IUD or intrauterine device). However, you would need to discuss this with your treatment team as not all types are suitable for women with breast cancer. If you think you may be pregnant, stop letrozole and tell your specialist as soon as possible.

question: What is Phesgo and what does it treat?
source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
source_excerpt: Pertuzumab and trastuzumab are 2 targeted therapy drugs. Targeted therapy is the name given to a group of drugs that block and stop the growth of cancer. They target and interfere with processes in the cells that help cancer grow. Phesgo can be used to treat HER2-positive: • Primary breast cancer (breast cancer that has not spread beyond the breast of the lymph nodes under the arm) • Secondary breast cancer (breast cancer that has spread to another part of the body, such as the bones, lungs, liver or brain) • Locally advanced breast cancer that cannot be removed by surgery (breast cancer that has spread to the chest wall or skin of the breast, or the lymph nodes around the chest, neck and under the arm or breastbone, but has not spread to other areas of the body)
answer: Phesgo is a combination of two targeted therapy drugs called pertuzumab and trastuzumab. It is used to treat HER2-positive breast cancer, which is a type of breast cancer where the cancer cells have high levels of a protein called HER2. Phesgo can be given for primary breast cancer (cancer that has not spread beyond the breast or nearby lymph nodes), secondary or metastatic breast cancer (cancer that has spread to other parts of the body like bones, lungs, liver or brain), or locally advanced breast cancer that cannot be removed by surgery but has not spread to other areas of the body. These targeted therapies work by interfering with processes in the cancer cells that help them grow and spread.

source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
source_excerpt: Some breast cancer cells have a higher-than-normal level of a protein called HER2 on their surface, which makes them grow more quickly. This is known as HER2-positive breast cancer. All invasive breast cancers (breast cancer that has the potential to spread to other parts of the body) are tested for HER2 levels.
answer: HER2 is a protein found on the surface of some breast cancer cells. When breast cancer cells have higher-than-normal levels of this protein, it causes the cancer cells to grow and divide more rapidly. This type of breast cancer is known as HER2-positive breast cancer. All invasive breast cancers (cancers that have the potential to spread) are tested for HER2 levels to determine if the cancer is HER2-positive or not. Understanding your HER2 status is important because certain treatments like Phesgo are only effective for HER2-positive breast cancers.

question: How is HER2 status tested in breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
source_excerpt: This is done in a hospital laboratory on a sample of breast cancer tissue removed during a biopsy or surgery. There are various tests to measure HER2 levels. A test called IHC (immunohistochemistry) is usually done first. It involves a special staining process performed on a sample of breast cancer tissue. It's reported as a score of 0 to 3+: • 0 or 1+ means the breast cancer is HER2-negative • 2+ is borderline • 3+ means the breast cancer is HER2-positive Breast cancers with a borderline result (2+) should be retested using more specialised techniques. These tests will give a result of HER2-positive, HER2-low or HER2-negative.
answer: HER2 status is tested on a sample of breast cancer tissue removed during a biopsy or surgery. The most common initial test is called immunohistochemistry (IHC), which involves a special staining process on the tissue sample. This test gives a score from 0 to 3+, where 0 or 1+ means HER2-negative, 2+ is borderline, and 3+ means HER2-positive. If the result is borderline (2+), more specialized tests are done to confirm if the cancer is HER2-positive, HER2-low, or HER2-negative.

question: What tests are done before starting Phesgo treatment?
source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
source_excerpt: Before starting your treatment, a member of your treatment team will discuss how and when you'll have Phesgo and how side effects can be managed. You'll have blood tests and your height and weight will be measured. You will also have tests to check your heart function, such as: • An ECG (electrocardiogram), a simple test that checks your heart rhythm • An echocardiogram, an ultrasound scan of the heart This is because there is a chance Phesgo can cause changes to the heart muscle. You will have an echocardiogram every 3 months during your treatment with Phesgo to monitor your heart function.
answer: Before starting Phesgo treatment, your healthcare team will perform several tests to ensure it is safe for you to proceed. You will have blood tests and your height and weight will be measured. Additionally, tests will be done to check your heart function, such as an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check your heart rhythm, and an echocardiogram, which is an ultrasound scan of the heart. These heart function tests are important because Phesgo has a chance of causing changes to the heart muscle. The echocardiogram will be repeated every 3 months during your Phesgo treatment to monitor your heart health.

question: How is Phesgo administered and how often?

question: What are some common side effects of Phesgo treatment?

answer: One of the common side effects of Phesgo treatment, especially when given in combination with chemotherapy, is its impact on your blood cells. If your blood cell counts become too low, your next treatment cycle may be delayed or the dose reduced. Your treatment team may also adjust the dosage to help manage side effects and allow you to continue the treatment for longer.

question: What are the signs of infection I should watch out for during my breast cancer treatment?

question: What are the signs of lung damage I should watch for during Phesgo treatment, and what should I do if I experience them?
source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
source_excerpt: Phesgo can cause interstitial lung disease (ILD). ILD is inflammation in your lungs, which can lead to scarring. Contact your treatment team straight away if you have: • Shortness of breath • A cough, with or without a high temperature • Any new or worsening breathing problems, such as chest tightness or wheezing These symptoms could have a number of causes including side effects of treatment or a lung infection. It's important to let your treatment team know so that they can find out the cause. You may need a chest x-ray or CT scan to check what's causing your symptoms. If Phesgo has caused inflammation to your lungs, you may need to stop treatment temporarily to prevent further damage. You may have steroids to treat the inflammation.
answer: Phesgo can potentially cause a serious side effect called interstitial lung disease (ILD), which is inflammation and scarring in the lungs. If you experience any of the following symptoms, contact your treatment team immediately: shortness of breath, a cough (with or without a fever), or any new or worsening breathing problems such as chest tightness or wheezing. These symptoms could indicate lung inflammation or infection, so it's crucial to report them right away. Your team may order tests like a chest X-ray or CT scan to determine the cause. If Phesgo has caused lung inflammation, you may need to temporarily stop treatment to prevent further damage, and you may be given steroids to reduce the inflammation.

question: What is cytokine release syndrome and what are the symptoms?

source_excerpt: Cytokine release syndrome This is where the drugs stimulate the immune system to make large amounts of a group of proteins called cytokines. Symptoms include: • High temperature • Chills • Headache • Difficulty breathing • Dizziness
answer: Cytokine release syndrome is a rare but potentially serious side effect of Phesgo treatment. While uncommon, this reaction requires prompt medical attention, so it's important to be aware of these symptoms and notify your care team immediately if you experience them during treatment.

question: What are the symptoms of a blood clot that I should watch out for during breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
source_excerpt:
Contact your treatment team or go to your local A&E department straight away if you have any of the following symptoms: 
• Pain in your arm or leg 
• Redness/discolouration of the skin of the arm or leg 
• Heat and swelling of the arm or leg
• Swelling, redness or tenderness where a central line is inserted to give chemotherapy, for example in the arm, chest area or up into the neck 
• Shortness of breath that comes on suddenly
• Pain or tightness in the chest 
• Unexplained cough or coughing up blood
answer: It's important to be aware of the potential symptoms of a blood clot during your breast cancer treatment, as people with breast cancer have a higher risk of developing blood clots like deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE). Contact your treatment team or go to the emergency room immediately if you experience any of the following symptoms: pain, redness, discoloration, heat or swelling in your arm or leg; swelling, redness or tenderness at the site where a central line is inserted for chemotherapy; sudden shortness of breath; chest pain or tightness; or an unexplained cough or coughing up blood. Blood clots can be life-threatening, so it's crucial to seek prompt medical attention if you notice any of these warning signs.

question: What should I do if I experience an allergic reaction during my Phesgo treatment?
source_display_name: Bcn265 Phesgo Pertuzumab And Trastuzumab Web
answer:
Having an allergic reaction to Phesgo is rare. 
If you do have an allergic reaction, it's more likely to happen within the first few minutes of your first or second treatment.
You'll be monitored closely so any reaction can be dealt with immediately.
If you have a severe reaction, treatment will be stopped immediately. 
If you have a less severe reaction, you may need to take medication before future treatments to reduce the risk of further reactions.
Contact your hospital immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms:
• Itchy red or discoloured bumps on your skin (these may be harder to see on black or brown skin) 
• Swelling in your lips, tongue or throat 
• Breathlessness, wheezing, a bad cough or sudden difficulty breathing 
• Tight chest or chest pain

question: What is EC-T chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: EC-T is a combination of 3 chemotherapy drugs. It takes its name from the initials of the 3 drugs: • E – epirubicin • C – cyclophosphamide • T – docetaxel (Taxotere) or paclitaxel (Taxol), which belong to a group of drugs called taxanes Chemotherapy destroys cancer cells by affecting their ability to divide and grow.
answer: EC-T chemotherapy is a combination of three chemotherapy drugs - epirubicin (E), cyclophosphamide (C), and either docetaxel (Taxotere) or paclitaxel (Taxol) which belong to a group called taxanes (T). These drugs work by destroying cancer cells and preventing them from dividing and growing. While effective at treating cancer, chemotherapy can also affect healthy cells in the body, leading to potential side effects. EC-T is a common chemotherapy regimen used to treat breast cancer.

question: What are some common side effects of EC-T chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: EC-T chemotherapy can temporarily affect the number of blood cells in the body. Blood is made up of red cells, white cells and platelets. You'll have regular blood tests. If these show the number of blood cells is too low, your next cycle of treatment may be delayed or the dose of chemotherapy reduced. Not having enough white blood cells can increase your risk of getting an infection.
answer: EC-T chemotherapy can cause various side effects, but everyone reacts differently. Some common side effects include effects on your blood cells and an increased risk of infection. The chemotherapy can temporarily lower the number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in your body. Your treatment team will monitor your blood counts with regular tests and may need to delay your next cycle or reduce the dose if your levels are too low. Not having enough white blood cells puts you at higher risk for infections, so you'll need to watch for signs like fever, feeling unwell, sore throat, cough, or frequent urination. Don't hesitate to contact your healthcare team right away if you notice any potential signs of infection. While side effects can be difficult, they are manageable, and your team is there to support you through the treatment process.

You may begin to lose your hair about 2 weeks after the first treatment, but it can happen earlier. Although hair loss is usually gradual, it can happen quickly, possibly over a couple of days. Hair loss should be temporary and in most cases your hair will begin to grow back in the weeks and months after chemotherapy has finished. There's some evidence that docetaxel treatment may result in longer-term or permanent hair loss. But this is very rare.

question: Is there anything I can do to prevent hair loss during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: You can try scalp cooling to stop you losing some or all of the hair on your head. This involves wearing a cold cap before, during and for 1 to 2 hours after your treatment with chemotherapy drugs. How well the cold cap works depends on the drugs and doses used, and it doesn't work for everyone. Ask your treatment team if scalp cooling is available in your hospital.
answer: Yes, there is an option called scalp cooling that may help prevent or reduce hair loss on your head during chemotherapy. This involves wearing a cold cap before, during, and for 1 to 2 hours after your chemotherapy treatment. The cold cap works by constricting blood vessels in the scalp, which reduces the amount of chemotherapy drugs reaching the hair follicles. However, the effectiveness of scalp cooling depends on the specific drugs and doses used in your chemotherapy regimen, and it doesn't work for everyone. If you're interested in trying scalp cooling, ask your treatment team if this option is available at your hospital.

question: What is fatigue and how can I manage it during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Fatigue is extreme tiredness that does not go away with rest or sleep. It's a very common side effect of EC-T and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. If you think you have fatigue, tell your GP or treatment team. They can assess you and offer advice on how to manage your energy levels.
answer: Fatigue is a common side effect of the EC-T chemotherapy regimen, and it refers to an extreme tiredness or exhaustion that does not go away with rest or sleep. This fatigue can be very debilitating and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. If you think you are experiencing fatigue, it's important to let your GP or treatment team know. They can assess your situation and provide advice on how to manage your energy levels and cope with this side effect. There are strategies and techniques that can help you conserve your energy and make the most of the times when you feel less fatigued. Don't hesitate to reach out for support in managing fatigue during and after your chemotherapy treatment.

question: How long do the symptoms of peripheral neuropathy last?
source_excerpt: For some people the symptoms stay mild and go away soon after treatment stops. However, for most people, the symptoms will gradually improve over the weeks and months after treatment has finished. Symptoms may take longer to improve and, in some cases, may not go away completely.

question: What is extravasation and what should I do if it occurs?
source_excerpt: If chemotherapy drugs leak out of the vein they're being given in (called extravasation), it can damage the surrounding tissue. Tell your treatment team immediately if you have pain, stinging or a burning feeling around the cannula while the drug is being given.
answer: Extravasation is when the chemotherapy drugs leak out of the vein they are being given into the surrounding tissue. This can cause damage to the tissue around the injection site. If you experience pain, stinging, or a burning feeling around the area where the IV is inserted while receiving the chemotherapy drugs, you should tell your treatment team immediately. Alerting them right away is important so they can take steps to minimize tissue damage from the extravasation.

question: What should I expect at the injection site after chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: You might get pain, redness, discolouration or swelling where the small plastic tube (cannula) has been inserted or anywhere along the vein, during or after treatment. After a few weeks you may notice tenderness, darkening and hardening around where the cannula was inserted. This should fade over time.

question: What can cause bladder irritation and pink or red urine during chemotherapy?
section: Bladder irritation and pink or red urine
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy drugs (particularly cyclophosphamide) can irritate the lining of the bladder. It's important to drink plenty of fluids around the time you have your treatment. Try to pee regularly, as soon as you feel the urge. Tell your treatment team if you notice: • Blood in your urine • Irritation, burning or stinging when you pee Epirubicin can cause your urine to become pink or red for a couple of days. This is because of the colour of the drug and is completely normal.
answer: Certain chemotherapy drugs, particularly cyclophosphamide, can irritate the lining of the bladder and cause bladder irritation or pink/red urine. This is a common side effect and not a cause for concern. To help manage this, it's important to drink plenty of fluids around the time of your treatment and pee regularly as soon as you feel the urge. If you notice blood in your urine or experience irritation, burning or stinging when peeing, be sure to let your treatment team know. For epirubicin specifically, it's normal for your urine to turn pink or red for a couple of days after treatment due to the color of the drug.

question: How can I take care of my mouth and prevent sore mouth during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Looking after your mouth, including your teeth and gums, is very important during treatment. You may be given mouthwash to try to reduce soreness and stop mouth ulcers developing. It's a good idea to use a small, soft toothbrush during this time. See your dentist for a check-up before treatment with chemotherapy begins. Avoid dental work during treatment if possible. If you do need to have dental work during treatment, talk with your treatment team about the best time to have this. If you're having difficulty registering with a dentist, let your treatment team know.
answer: Taking care of your mouth, teeth and gums is very important during chemotherapy treatment. You may be given a special mouthwash by your care team to help reduce soreness and prevent mouth ulcers from developing. It's recommended to use a small, soft-bristled toothbrush during this time to be gentle on your mouth. Before starting chemotherapy, it's a good idea to visit your dentist for a check-up. Try to avoid any dental work during treatment if possible, but if you do need it, discuss the best timing with your treatment team. If you're having trouble finding a dentist, let your care team know so they can assist you.

question: Can chemotherapy cause menopausal symptoms?
source_excerpt: EC-T may cause menopausal symptoms if you haven't already been through the menopause. This is because it affects the ovaries, which produce the hormone oestrogen. Your periods may stop or become irregular during chemotherapy. Whether your periods return will depend on many things, including other health conditions, the type of drugs used, the dose given, and your age.
answer: Yes, chemotherapy treatment like EC-T can potentially cause menopausal symptoms if you haven't already gone through menopause. This is because the chemotherapy drugs can affect the ovaries, which produce the hormone estrogen. You may experience irregular or stopped periods during chemotherapy. Whether your periods return after treatment depends on factors like your age, the specific drugs used, the dosage, and any other health conditions you have. If you experience menopausal symptoms, be sure to discuss them with your care team.

question: What are some common menopausal symptoms that can occur during chemotherapy treatment for breast cancer?
source_excerpt:
Other common menopausal symptoms can include: 
• Hot flushes and night sweats 
• Mood changes
• Joint aches and pains
• Vaginal dryness 
• Changes to your sex drive 
You can talk to your breast care nurse or treatment team about 
ways of coping with any of these symptoms. You can also find 
tips in our Menopausal symptoms and breast cancer booklet.
answer: Chemotherapy treatment for breast cancer can sometimes induce menopausal symptoms. Some common menopausal symptoms you may experience include hot flushes, night sweats, mood changes, joint aches and pains, vaginal dryness, and changes to your sex drive. These side effects can be difficult, but your breast care nurse or treatment team can provide guidance on ways to cope with any menopausal symptoms you experience. There are also helpful tips in the 'Menopausal symptoms and breast cancer' booklet from Breast Cancer Now.

question: What can be done to manage painful muscles and joints that may occur after chemotherapy treatment?
source_excerpt:
Your muscles or joints may ache or become painful 2 to 3 days 
after you have treatment, particularly docetaxel or paclitaxel. 
This usually improves after a few days. However, it can be 
very painful and you may need to take mild pain relief such as 
paracetamol or anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen. It's 
a good idea to have some of these available before starting your 
treatment just in case you need them.
answer: It's common to experience muscle aches or joint pain 2 to 3 days after receiving chemotherapy drugs like docetaxel or paclitaxel. While this discomfort usually improves within a few days, it can be quite painful. To help manage this side effect, you may need to take over-the-counter pain medication like paracetamol or anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen. It's a good idea to have some of these pain relievers on hand before starting your chemotherapy treatment, just in case you need them to ease muscle and joint pain.

question: What is fluid retention and how can it be managed during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt:
You may develop a build-up of fluid in the body (oedema), 
particularly when having docetaxel or paclitaxel. It may cause 
swollen ankles and legs and shortness of breath. This can take 
a few weeks to get better.
You'll usually be given steroid drugs to prevent an allergic reaction, 
which will also help reduce the chance of fluid building up.
answer: During chemotherapy treatment, particularly with drugs like docetaxel or paclitaxel, you may experience fluid retention or a build-up of fluid in the body (known as edema). This can cause swelling in the ankles and legs, as well as shortness of breath. The fluid retention can take a few weeks to improve after treatment. To help prevent and manage this side effect, you will typically be given steroid drugs before chemotherapy to reduce the chance of an allergic reaction and fluid build-up.

question: Is weight gain a possible side effect of chemotherapy and how can it be managed?
source_excerpt:
Weight gain
You may put on weight, but you'll usually lose it again once 
treatment finishes. This can vary from person to person and 
may take up to several months. Physical activity and eating a 
healthy diet may help with this. 
For more information on healthy eating, see our booklet Diet 
and breast cancer.

To help manage weight gain, staying physically active and eating a healthy diet during treatment may be beneficial. More information on healthy eating is available in the 'Diet and breast cancer' booklet.

question: What are some less common side effects of chemotherapy that I should be aware of?
source_excerpt:
Heart changes 
Epirubicin can affect your heart and blood pressure. This is usually 
temporary but for a small number of people it may be permanent. 
Before you start chemotherapy, your treatment team may 
arrange a heart (cardiac) function test (see page 4). 
You will also be carefully monitored during your treatment. 
If you have pain or tightness in your chest, feel breathless or 
notice changes to your heartbeat at any time during or after 
treatment, tell your treatment team straight away. 
These symptoms can be caused by other conditions but it's 
important to get them checked. 
Sore eyes and runny nose 
EC-T can cause a runny nose. It can also cause soreness and a 
gritty feeling in your eyes, or your eyes may water. 
If you have sore eyes, you may be given eye drops to relieve 
the soreness. 
Headaches 
EC-T can cause headaches. These are usually mild and can be 
relieved with simple pain relief such as paracetamol. 
If your headache is severe, speak to your treatment team. 
Skin changes 
EC-T can make your skin dry, more sensitive or prone to reactions. 
If you develop a rash tell your treatment team as soon as possible. 
Your skin may be more sensitive to the sun, so use a high 
factor (SPF) sun cream.
answer: Some less common but important side effects to be aware of with chemotherapy treatment include changes to your heart and blood pressure, sore or watery eyes, headaches, skin changes like dryness or rashes, soreness or redness in the palms of your hands and soles of your feet (called hand-foot syndrome), and changes to your nails like discoloration, ridges, brittleness or even nails lifting off. While these effects are less frequent, it's crucial to inform your treatment team right away if you experience any of them so they can provide appropriate care and medication. Don't hesitate to report any unusual symptoms, as catching side effects early allows for better management.

question: What is hand-foot syndrome and how can it be treated during chemotherapy?
source_excerpt:
Sore hands and feet  
You may develop soreness or redness on the palms of your 
hands and soles of your feet. This is called palmar-plantar or 
hand-foot syndrome. 
Redness can be harder to see on black or brown skin. 
Your treatment team or GP can prescribe creams or medication 
to treat hand-foot syndrome.
answer: Hand-foot syndrome, also known as palmar-plantar syndrome, is a side effect where you may develop soreness or redness on the palms of your hands and soles of your feet during chemotherapy treatment. This redness can be harder to notice on darker skin tones. If you experience hand-foot syndrome, your treatment team or GP can prescribe creams or medication to help treat and manage this condition. It's important to report any signs of hand-foot syndrome so you can receive appropriate treatment to alleviate the discomfort and allow you to continue your chemotherapy journey as smoothly as possible.

question: How can chemotherapy affect my nails and what should I do if I notice changes?
source_excerpt:
Nail changes 
Chemotherapy may cause changes to the appearance of your 
nails. This can be a change in the nail colour or texture, such as 
ridges forming. Nails can also become more brittle and cracked.
Occasionally the nail may lift off the nail bed and fall out, but it 
will grow back. 
As you're more at risk of infection while having chemotherapy, tell 
your treatment team about any signs of infection such as redness, 
heat, swelling or pain in or under your fingernails and toenails.
answer: Chemotherapy can cause changes to the appearance and health of your nails. You may notice changes in nail color or texture, such as ridges forming. Your nails may also become more brittle, cracked, or even lift off the nail bed and fall out, though they will grow back eventually. Since you are at higher risk of infection during chemotherapy, it's crucial to inform your treatment team immediately if you notice any signs of infection like redness, heat, swelling or pain in or under your fingernails and toenails. They can provide guidance on properly caring for your nails and preventing infections during this time.

question: What are the symptoms of a blood clot that I should watch for during EC-T chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: People with breast cancer have a higher risk of blood clots. Having EC-T also increases the risk of blood clots such as a DVT (deep vein thrombosis). If you have a DVT, there's a risk part of the blood clot could break away and travel to the lung. This is known as a pulmonary embolism (PE). Blood clots can be life-threatening and should be treated quickly. Contact your treatment team or go to your local A&E department straight away if you have any of the following symptoms: • Pain in your arm or leg • Redness/discolouration of the skin of the arm or leg • Heat and swelling of the arm or leg • Swelling, redness or tenderness where a central line is inserted to give chemotherapy, for example in the arm, chest area or up into the neck • Shortness of breath that comes on suddenly • Pain or tightness in the chest • Unexplained cough or coughing up blood Some symptoms may look different on different skin tones.
answer: People with breast cancer have an increased risk of developing blood clots, and receiving EC-T chemotherapy further raises this risk. Blood clots like deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can be very serious, as part of the clot could potentially break off and travel to the lungs, causing a life-threatening pulmonary embolism. It's crucial to contact your treatment team or go to the emergency room immediately if you experience any of the following symptoms: pain, redness, discoloration, heat or swelling in your arm or leg; swelling, redness or tenderness at the site where chemotherapy is administered; sudden shortness of breath; chest pain or tightness; unexplained cough or coughing up blood. Some symptoms may appear differently on different skin tones. Blood clots require prompt medical attention, so don't hesitate to report any concerning signs to your care team.

question: Can chemotherapy affect my fertility or ability to have children?
source_excerpt: EC-T chemotherapy causes changes in the ovaries, which can affect your ability to become pregnant (fertility). How likely you are to lose this ability (become infertile) also depends on things like whether you have had chemotherapy in the past, other health conditions and your age. If you're aged around 40 and over, your periods are less likely to return after you've finished chemotherapy than if you're under 40. In men, EC-T chemotherapy can affect sperm production which can lead to temporary or permanent infertility.

question: Can I get travel vaccinations while undergoing chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: You should not have any live vaccines while you're having chemotherapy. Live vaccines include: • Mumps • Measles • Rubella (German measles) • Polio • BCG (tuberculosis) • Yellow fever Live vaccines contain a small amount of live virus or bacteria. If you have a weakened immune system, which you may do during chemotherapy, they could be harmful. It's safe to have these vaccinations 6 months after your treatment finishes. Talk to your GP or treatment team before having any vaccinations. If anyone you have close contact with needs to have a live vaccine, speak to your treatment team or GP. They can advise what precautions you may need to take depending on the vaccination.

However, it's safe to get these vaccinations 6 months after your chemotherapy treatment finishes. question: What is considered a healthy diet for someone with breast cancer?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Eating healthily is important for everyone, but if you've been diagnosed with breast cancer, you may become even more aware of what you eat and drink. A balanced diet can have a range of health benefits. The Eatwell Guide shows the different types of foods you should eat and in what proportions. It recommends you: Eat at least 5 portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day Eat plenty of starchy foods like potatoes, bread, rice, yams and pasta. They're a great source of energy and the main source of various important nutrients – choose higher fibre or wholegrain options like brown rice Have some dairy or dairy alternatives – choose lower-fat and lower-sugar options, and check the label to make sure they have added calcium Eat some beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other protein – aim for at least 2 portions of fish every week, 1 of which should be oily, such as salmon or mackerel. Choose lean cuts of meat and mince, and eat less red and processed meat like bacon, ham and sausages You should also try to: • Choose unsaturated oils and spreads, such as olive or sunflower oil, and use them in small amounts • Eat smaller amounts of foods high in fat, salt and sugar, and have them less often • Limit alcohol as much as possible (see page 20) • Drink plenty of fluids – aim for 6 to 8 glasses a day. Carrying a water bottle with you during the day can help you stay hydrated
answer: Eating a balanced diet is important for everyone, but it becomes even more crucial if you've been diagnosed with breast cancer. A healthy diet should include a variety of foods from the four main food groups: fruits and vegetables, starchy foods like potatoes and whole grains, dairy or dairy alternatives, and proteins like beans, pulses, fish, eggs, and lean meats. The Eatwell Guide recommends eating at least 5 portions of fruits and vegetables daily, plenty of fiber-rich starchy foods, some low-fat dairy or fortified alternatives, and lean protein sources including oily fish twice a week. It's also advisable to choose unsaturated oils and spreads in moderation, limit foods high in fat, salt, and sugar, and stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids. While you should aim for a balanced diet, you can still enjoy your favorite treats occasionally.

question: What types of foods should be limited in a healthy diet for breast cancer patients?

The Eatwell Guide advises eating smaller amounts of these foods and having them less often. question: What is the Mediterranean diet and how is it relevant for breast cancer patients?

question: How can breast cancer treatments affect my eating habits and appetite?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Breast cancer treatments can sometimes affect what you want to eat and drink. Your usual routine may be disrupted, which can affect your eating pattern. Feeling worried or stressed can also affect your appetite, causing you to eat more or less than usual.
answer: Breast cancer treatments like chemotherapy can sometimes impact your desire to eat and drink. The side effects and disruption to your normal routine may cause changes in your eating patterns. You may experience a decreased or increased appetite due to feeling worried or stressed. It's important to be aware that your body's reaction to treatments like chemotherapy can vary - some people are able to eat normally throughout, while others experience more significant changes to their eating habits.

question: How can chemotherapy affect my risk of infection and what dietary precautions should I take?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy can cause a drop in white blood cells, which can increase your risk of getting an infection. You'll have regular blood tests throughout your treatment to check your blood count. If you're at an increased risk of infection, you may be given some specific dietary advice to follow. Your chemotherapy team will explain more about this if necessary. Although there aren't any particular foods that will boost your white blood cell count, it's important to follow a healthy diet. Follow good food hygiene when storing, preparing and cooking food. This is particularly important if you're at increased risk of infection. You can find useful information on food safety when your immunity is low by searching for it on the Macmillan Cancer Support website macmillan.org.uk
answer: Chemotherapy can cause a drop in your white blood cell count, which increases your risk of getting an infection during treatment. You will have regular blood tests to monitor your blood count levels. If you are at an increased risk of infection, your chemotherapy team may provide specific dietary advice for you to follow to reduce this risk. While there are no particular foods that can boost your white blood cells, it is still important to follow a healthy, balanced diet. Be sure to practice good food hygiene when storing, preparing and cooking food, as this is especially crucial if your immunity is lowered. You can find useful information on food safety guidelines when your immunity is compromised by searching on the Macmillan Cancer Support website.

question: What can I do if my appetite changes during cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If your appetite is small, or taste changes are affecting your diet, eating little and often can be better than having large meals. It may help to: • Eat 5 or 6 small meals or snacks each day instead of 3 bigger meals • Drink milkshakes, smoothies, juice or soup if you don't feel like eating solid food • Do something active, if you feel able to, as exercise can increase your appetite – you might have more of an appetite if you take a short walk before eating • Avoid drinking lots of liquid before or during meals
answer: It's very common for your appetite to change during cancer treatment. If you find your appetite is smaller or that taste changes are affecting your diet, try eating smaller meals or snacks more frequently throughout the day instead of three large meals. Drinking things like milkshakes, smoothies, juice or soup can also help get nutrients when you don't feel like eating solid foods. Light exercise like taking a short walk before eating may help stimulate your appetite as well. Avoid drinking a lot of liquid right before or during meals as this can make you feel fuller faster.

question: What can I do to manage nausea and vomiting during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You may feel sick or be sick during and after your chemotherapy. Anti-sickness drugs may help – your chemotherapy team can help find one that works for you. Drink plenty of fluids, such as water or herbal teas. Taking frequent sips is better than trying to drink large amounts in one go. Herbal teas such as mint or ginger can help if you're feeling sick. Eating little and often can also help if you're feeling sick. Some people find eating cold food makes them feel less sick because hot food can smell stronger and trigger their nausea.
answer: Nausea and vomiting are common side effects of chemotherapy, but there are things that can help manage them. Your chemotherapy team can provide anti-sickness medications to find one that works well for you. Staying hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids like water or herbal teas can also help - try taking frequent small sips rather than drinking large amounts at once. Ginger or mint herbal teas may help settle nausea. Eating smaller, more frequent meals and choosing cold foods, which tend to have less strong smells that can trigger nausea, may provide some relief as well.

question: What can I do to manage a sore or dry mouth during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy can make your mouth sore or dry, making it uncomfortable to eat. You might find it helpful to: • Clean your teeth or dentures with a soft brush after eating and floss gently • Use an alcohol-free mouthwash (your chemotherapy team may recommend one) • Choose soft or liquid foods such as soups, stews, smoothies and desserts • Soothe your mouth and gums with ice cubes and ice lollies • Drink sugar-free fizzy drinks or fizzy water to freshen your mouth • Use a straw to drink • Avoid crunchy, salty, very spicy, acidic or hot foods • Avoid citrus drinks like lemon, lime, orange and grapefruit juice If you have dentures, clean them regularly and try not to wear them all the time. Smoking and drinking alcohol can make a sore mouth worse.
answer: Chemotherapy can unfortunately cause your mouth to become sore or dry, making it uncomfortable to eat. Here are some tips that may help provide relief:  - Use a soft toothbrush and gently floss after eating to keep your mouth clean without irritating it further. Your chemotherapy team may recommend an alcohol-free mouthwash.  - Choose soft, liquid foods like soups, stews, smoothies, and desserts that won't further irritate your mouth and gums. Avoid crunchy, salty, spicy, acidic, or very hot foods.  - Suck on ice cubes or ice lollies to soothe the soreness. Drink sugar-free fizzy drinks or fizzy water to freshen your mouth.  - Use a straw to drink liquids, which can help bypass mouth sores.  - If you wear dentures, clean them regularly but try not to wear them all the time to give your gums a break.  - Avoid smoking and alcohol, as these can worsen mouth soreness.  Let your treatment team know if your mouth remains very sore, as they may have additional remedies to recommend. Taking care of your mouth can make eating and drinking much more comfortable during this difficult time.

question: How can I manage taste changes during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Your taste may change during chemotherapy, making foods taste bland or different. You may prefer to eat strongly flavoured foods or use herbs and spices when cooking. Try a variety of foods to find the ones you like best. As well as going off your usual foods, you may like foods you previously didn't like. Some types of chemotherapy can give you a metallic taste in your mouth. Using reusable plastic or wooden cutlery, instead of metal, can help reduce the metal taste. Using glass pots and pans when cooking can also help.
answer: Chemotherapy can sometimes cause changes in how foods taste, making them seem bland or have a different flavor than usual. Here are some tips to help manage taste changes:  - Try strongly flavored foods or use herbs and spices liberally when cooking to enhance the taste.  - Experiment with a variety of foods to find new ones you enjoy, as your tastes may change. You may even find you like foods you previously didn't care for.  - If you experience a metallic taste in your mouth from certain chemotherapy drugs, use reusable plastic or wooden utensils and cookware instead of metal, as this can help reduce the metallic taste.  Don't be discouraged if your usual favorite foods don't taste the same for a while. Stay open-minded and keep trying new things to find what appeals to you during this temporary phase. The taste changes should improve once your chemotherapy treatment is completed.

question: What can I do to prevent or manage constipation during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Eating high-fibre foods can help. These include: • High-fibre breakfast cereals, such as bran flakes or shredded wheat • Beans and lentils • Vegetables (fresh or frozen) • Fruit (fresh, frozen, canned and dried) • Brown rice • Wholemeal bread • Wholewheat pasta Drink plenty of fluids (6 to 8 glasses of water a day) and do some regular exercise such as walking if you're able to. If you're still having problems with constipation, ask your treatment team or GP for advice. They can prescribe medication to help if necessary.
answer: Constipation can be a common side effect during chemotherapy due to factors like eating and drinking less, decreased activity, and certain medications. To help prevent or relieve constipation, try incorporating high-fiber foods into your diet such as:  - High-fiber breakfast cereals like bran flakes or shredded wheat - Beans and lentils - Fresh, frozen, or canned vegetables   - Fresh, frozen, canned, or dried fruits - Brown rice - Whole wheat bread - Whole wheat pasta  In addition to increasing your fiber intake, be sure to drink plenty of fluids, aiming for 6-8 glasses of water per day. Regular light exercise like walking can also help stimulate your bowels if you are able.  If constipation persists despite these dietary changes, don't hesitate to ask your treatment team or GP for advice. They may recommend an over-the-counter or prescription medication to provide relief.  Staying hydrated, getting enough fiber, and keeping as active as possible can go a long way in preventing constipation from becoming an additional discomfort during your chemotherapy journey.

question: What should I do if I experience diarrhea during chemotherapy?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: Occasionally, some chemotherapy drugs can cause diarrhoea. Your GP or treatment team can prescribe medication for diarrhoea if necessary. Drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration. Contact your chemotherapy team if you have 4 or more episodes of diarrhoea in 24 hours.
answer: Some chemotherapy drugs can occasionally cause diarrhea as a side effect. If you experience diarrhea during your treatment, here are some recommendations:  - Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration from the fluid loss.  - Contact your chemotherapy team if you have 4 or more episodes of diarrhea within a 24-hour period. They may prescribe medication to help control the diarrhea.  - Your GP can also prescribe anti-diarrheal medication if needed to help get the diarrhea under control.  Diarrhea can be very dehydrating and depleting, so don't hesitate to reach out to your medical team if it becomes severe or persistent. They can provide medications and guidance to manage this side effect and prevent complications from dehydration or electrolyte imbalances.  In the meantime, focus on resting as much as possible and staying hydrated with water, broths, or electrolyte drinks until the diarrhea subsides. Let your care team know if it doesn't improve or you develop other concerning symptoms.

question: What are the potential effects of radiotherapy on diet and eating?

answer: Radiotherapy treatment itself does not typically cause dietary problems. They may recommend taking liquid pain relief like liquid paracetamol before eating to help alleviate discomfort. Additionally, it's still advisable to maintain a balanced diet and stay hydrated by drinking plenty of fluids during radiotherapy.

question: What are some potential side effects of hormone therapy that may affect diet and weight?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you're having hormone therapy, you might find your weight increases. This may be because you're less active due to fatigue or joint pain, or because of appetite changes. Weight gain is also a common menopausal symptom. Hormone therapy drugs such as anastrozole and letrozole can increase the level of bad cholesterol (LDL) in your blood.
answer: If you are undergoing hormone therapy as part of your breast cancer treatment, you may experience some side effects that can impact your diet and weight. One potential side effect is weight gain, which can be caused by factors like decreased activity levels due to fatigue or joint pain, or changes in appetite. Weight gain is also a common symptom of menopause, which hormone therapy can induce. Additionally, certain hormone therapy drugs like anastrozole and letrozole can increase levels of bad cholesterol (LDL) in your blood. It's important to discuss any dietary or weight changes with your healthcare team to manage these side effects effectively.

source_excerpt: If you're having hormone therapy, you might find your weight increases. This may be because you're less active due to fatigue or joint pain, or because of appetite changes. Weight gain is also a common menopausal symptom. Hormone therapy drugs such as anastrozole and letrozole can increase the level of bad cholesterol (LDL) in your blood.
answer: If you're having hormone therapy, you might find your weight increases. This may be because you're less active due to fatigue or joint pain, or because of appetite changes. Weight gain is also a common menopausal symptom. Hormone therapy drugs such as anastrozole and letrozole can increase the level of bad cholesterol (LDL) in your blood.

question: Is it recommended to fast around the time of chemotherapy treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
section: Short-term fasting around the time of chemotherapy
source_excerpt: Some studies suggest short-term fasting around the time of chemotherapy may help reduce side effects. However, more research is needed before any recommendations can be made. If you're thinking about fasting, always talk to your treatment team or GP first.
answer: Some studies suggest that short-term fasting around the time of chemotherapy may help reduce side effects. If you are considering fasting, it's crucial to discuss this with your treatment team or GP first. They can provide personalized guidance based on your specific situation and ensure that fasting does not interfere with the effectiveness of your chemotherapy treatment.

question: What should I do if I have difficulty with shopping and cooking during cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: As you go through treatment and recovery, simple tasks like shopping and cooking can feel exhausting. Try to accept any offers of help, even if you're used to coping on your own. You can also take advantage of online shopping or ask local shops if they have a telephone ordering and delivery service. It's important to have fresh food in your diet, but if you can't shop regularly, frozen and tinned fruit and vegetables are full of nutrients and can be great alternatives. Choose tinned fruit in juice rather than syrup and tinned vegetables that have less salt.
answer: Going through cancer treatment and recovery can be incredibly draining, making simple tasks like grocery shopping and cooking feel exhausting. It's important to accept any offers of help from friends and family, even if you're used to being independent. You can also take advantage of online grocery delivery services or ask local stores if they offer phone ordering and delivery. Having fresh produce is ideal, but frozen and canned fruits and vegetables are nutritious alternatives when you can't shop regularly. Choose canned fruit packed in juice rather than syrup, and opt for low-sodium canned veggies. Don't hesitate to reach out to your care team if you need more suggestions for managing fatigue during this challenging time.

question: How can I manage my cholesterol levels during breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you have too much bad cholesterol it can build up in your artery walls, leading to artery disease or other health conditions. Following a healthy diet and maintaining a healthy body weight can help reduce your levels of bad cholesterol. Your GP can tell you more about how cholesterol levels are measured and what dietary changes you may need to make.
answer: High levels of bad cholesterol (LDL) can build up in your artery walls, increasing the risk of artery disease and other health issues. Following a healthy, balanced diet and maintaining a healthy body weight can help reduce your LDL cholesterol levels during breast cancer treatment. Your doctor can provide guidance on how cholesterol is measured and what specific dietary changes may be beneficial for managing your cholesterol. Making nutritious food choices is an important part of your overall care plan.

question: Do I need to change my diet if I have another medical condition like diabetes or IBS?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you're already following a specific diet because you have a medical condition – such as diabetes, Crohn's disease or irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) – having breast cancer doesn't mean your diet has to change. If you're concerned about how your breast cancer treatment may affect your diet or any existing condition, talk to your breast care nurse or treatment team. They can talk to a dietitian or other medical staff to ensure any existing condition remains under control during your treatment.
answer: If you are already following a specific diet due to a pre-existing medical condition like diabetes, Crohn's disease, or irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), you do not necessarily need to change your diet when undergoing breast cancer treatment. However, it is advisable to discuss your situation with your breast care nurse or oncology team. They can consult with a dietitian or other specialists to ensure your existing condition remains well-managed during cancer treatment. With some guidance, you should be able to continue your recommended diet while receiving appropriate breast cancer care.

question: What should I do if I've gained weight after breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: After treatment for breast cancer, you may have gained or lost weight, or you may want to know if diet can play a role in your recovery and future health. It can be helpful to speak with your breast care nurse, GP or practice nurse. They can assess if your current weight is healthy and determine your body mass index (BMI). They'll also discuss your current diet and lifestyle and can help you put a plan together if changes are required.
answer: It's very common to gain weight during and after breast cancer treatment due to factors like medication side effects, being less active, changes in routine, and hormonal changes from menopause. If you've gained weight, the first step is to speak with your healthcare team like your breast care nurse, GP, or practice nurse. They can assess if your current weight is healthy by calculating your body mass index (BMI). They'll also review your diet and lifestyle to help you develop a plan to make any necessary changes in a safe and sustainable way. The key is to aim for gradual weight loss of around 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 pounds) per week through small adjustments to your eating habits and activity levels.

question: Why might someone gain weight during or after breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You may put on weight during and after treatment due to: • The side effects of some drugs, which can increase appetite • The body retaining fluid • Being less active than usual • Eating more than usual when you're anxious or because your usual routine has changed • The menopause (as a result of your treatment)
answer: There are several potential reasons why someone might gain weight during or after breast cancer treatment:  1. Side effects of certain medications can increase appetite. 2. The body may retain more fluid during treatment. 3. Being less physically active than usual due to treatment and recovery. 4. Eating more than usual, perhaps due to anxiety, stress, or changes in routine. 5. Hormonal changes like menopause caused by the treatment.  It's important to be aware of these factors and work closely with your healthcare team to manage your weight in a healthy way after treatment.

question: How can I safely lose weight after breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you want to lose weight after treatment, aim for a realistic weight loss of about 0.5 to 1kg (1 to 2 pounds) a week. You can do this by making small changes to your usual eating and exercise habits. Try to: • Follow the Eatwell Guide and eat a varied, balanced diet (see page 3) • Avoid keeping too many unhealthy snacks like sweets in the house – try popcorn, rice cakes or fruit instead • Reduce your portion sizes – using a smaller plate can help
answer: If you want to lose weight after breast cancer treatment, it's important to do so safely and gradually. Aim for a realistic weight loss of about 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 pounds) per week. You can achieve this by making small, sustainable changes to your eating habits and activity levels:  - Follow the Eatwell Guide and eat a balanced diet with a variety of foods  - Avoid keeping unhealthy snacks like sweets at home, and opt for healthier options like popcorn, rice cakes, or fruit - Reduce your portion sizes by using a smaller plate - Increase your physical activity levels as you're able  The key is to make lifestyle changes you can stick with long-term. Work closely with your healthcare team to develop a safe and effective weight loss plan tailored to your needs and recovery.

question: What are some tips for maintaining a healthy weight during and after breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: • Be active for 150 minutes a week – you can break this up, for example into 25-minute sessions • Limit the amount of alcohol you drink • Swap sugary drinks for water – you could add some sugar-free squash for extra flavour • Choose healthier options when eating out and remember that takeaways can be high in fat and calories • Avoid skipping meals or extreme dieting • Ask a friend or family member to help support and motivate you – they could join you for healthy meals or workouts
answer: Maintaining a healthy weight is important during and after breast cancer treatment. Here are some tips that can help:  - Be active for at least 150 minutes per week. You can break this up into smaller sessions, like 25 minutes at a time. Regular physical activity can help manage your weight and improve overall health.  - Limit your alcohol intake. Alcohol contains empty calories that can contribute to weight gain.  - Swap sugary drinks for water or add sugar-free squash for flavor. Sugary drinks are high in calories with little nutritional value.  - When eating out or getting takeout, choose healthier options. Many restaurant and takeout meals can be high in fat and calories.  - Avoid skipping meals or extreme dieting, as this can be counterproductive and lead to overeating later.  - Ask friends or family members to support and motivate you on your healthy eating and exercise journey. Having a support system can make it easier to stick to your goals.

question: What resources or support services are available to help with weight management during breast cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: You may find the support from a local weight loss scheme or club helpful. Some pharmacies offer a free weight management service to assess your weight and give you advice and support. Your GP can also recommend and refer you to local support services. They may also refer you to a dietitian. The NHS has a free 12-week weight loss plan. Your GP can tell you about it or you can download the plan and find out more about weight loss on the NHS website nhs.uk There are also NHS digital weight management programmes, such as Oviva and Second Nature, available for people living with obesity and diabetes, high blood pressure or both. You can speak to your GP about joining. If you're not eligible to be referred to these programmes through the NHS, you may have to pay a monthly fee. But your GP should be able to recommend some free alternatives. Obesity UK also has UK-based support groups for people living with obesity. You can find out more at obesityuk.org.uk

question: What dietary changes can help if I've lost weight during cancer treatment?
source_display_name: Bcc98 Diet And Breast Cancer Web
source_excerpt: If you've lost weight during your treatment, some simple changes to your diet can help. To put on weight in a healthy way, you need to eat more calories and more protein. Adding an extra 300 to 500 calories a day is a good aim. You can also try to: • Eat 3 meals and some snacks throughout the day, based on the Eatwell Guide (page 3) – you could also try eating smaller meals more frequently • Have more protein-rich foods like lean cuts of meat, fish, eggs, nuts, seeds and pulses (such as lentils and beans) • Eat healthy fats such as avocados, olive or rapeseed oil, and unsalted peanut butter • Drink high-calorie drinks like milkshakes. Adding milk powder or protein powder to drinks or food may also help • Have snacks that don't need preparation at home, like yoghurt pots • Avoid drinking lots of fluid before a meal because this might make you feel full • Build up your muscles with exercise like strength training or yoga Your GP can prescribe high-protein or high-energy drinks and soups if you need extra help to gain weight, or they may refer you to a dietitian.
answer: If you've lost weight during your cancer treatment, there are some simple dietary changes that can help you regain the lost weight in a healthy way. Firstly, you need to increase your calorie and protein intake. Aim to add an extra 300 to 500 calories per day to your diet. You can do this by eating 3 meals and some snacks throughout the day, based on the Eatwell Guide. Eating smaller meals more frequently can also help. Incorporate more protein-rich foods like lean meats, fish, eggs, nuts, seeds, and pulses (lentils, beans). Include healthy fats like avocados, olive or rapeseed oil, and unsalted peanut butter. Drink high-calorie beverages like milkshakes, and consider adding milk powder or protein powder to drinks or food. Have ready-to-eat snacks like yogurt pots on hand. Avoid drinking too much fluid before meals as it can make you feel full. Additionally, engage in exercises like strength training or yoga to build up your muscles. If you need extra help, your GP can prescribe high-protein or high-energy drinks and soups, or refer you to a dietitian.
