question: What are the symptoms of anemia (low red blood cell count) from breast cancer treatment?
section: Anaemia (low number of red blood cells)
source_excerpt: This treatment can reduce the number of red blood cells in your blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen around the body. If the number of red blood cells is low, this is called anaemia. You may have symptoms such as: •pale skin •lack of energy •feeling breathless •feeling dizzy and light-headed. Tell your doctor or nurse if you have these symptoms. If you are very anaemic, you may need a drip to give you extra red blood cells. This is called a blood transfusion.
answer: Breast cancer treatment can sometimes lead to anemia, which is a low number of red blood cells. Red blood cells carry oxygen throughout the body, so if their levels drop too low, you may experience symptoms like pale skin, lack of energy, feeling breathless, or feeling dizzy and light-headed. If you notice these symptoms, be sure to tell your doctor or nurse, as severe anemia may require a blood transfusion to restore your red blood cell levels. Getting enough red blood cells is important for having the energy and oxygen supply your body needs.

question: What can I do to manage feeling sick during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Your doctor will give you anti-sickness drugs to help prevent or control sickness during your treatment. Take the drugs exactly as your nurse or pharmacist tells you. It is easier to prevent sickness than to treat it after it has started. If you feel sick, take small sips of fluids often and eat small amounts regularly. It is important to drink enough fluids. If you continue to feel sick, or are sick (vomit) more than once in 24 hours, contact the hospital as soon as possible. They will give you advice. Your doctor or nurse may change the anti-sickness drug to one that works better for you.
answer: Feeling sick or nauseous is a common side effect of breast cancer treatment, but there are ways to manage it. Your doctor will prescribe anti-sickness medications to help prevent or control nausea during your treatment. It's important to take these medications exactly as instructed by your nurse or pharmacist. Preventing nausea is easier than treating it once it has started. If you do feel sick, try sipping small amounts of fluids frequently and eating small portions regularly. Stay hydrated by drinking enough fluids. If you continue feeling sick or vomit more than once in 24 hours, contact the hospital right away for advice. Your healthcare team may adjust your anti-nausea medication to find one that works better for you. With the right management strategies, nausea can often be controlled effectively.

question: How can I manage feeling tired during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Feeling tired is a common side effect of this treatment. It is often worse towards the end of treatment and for some weeks after it has finished. Try to pace yourself and plan your day so you have time to rest. Gentle exercise, like short walks, can give you more energy. If you feel sleepy, do not drive or use machinery.
answer: Feeling tired or fatigued is a very common side effect of breast cancer treatment. The fatigue is often worse towards the end of treatment and can persist for some weeks after treatment has finished. To manage this tiredness, try to pace yourself and plan your day with built-in rest periods. Gentle exercise like short walks can actually help give you more energy. If you feel sleepy, avoid driving or operating machinery for safety. Your healthcare team understands how draining the treatments can be and will have advice to help you cope with fatigue. Taking it easy, getting enough rest, and doing light activity as you're able can all help manage cancer-related fatigue during this challenging time.

question: What should I expect in terms of hair loss during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: You usually lose all the hair from your head. You may also lose your eyelashes and eyebrows, as well as other body hair. Hair loss usually starts after your first or second treatment. Scalp cooling is a way of lowering the temperature of your scalp to help reduce hair loss. Your nurse can tell you if this is an option for you. Your nurse can talk to you about ways to cope with hair loss. There are ways to cover up hair loss if you want to. Your scalp may be sensitive. It is important to cover your head to protect your skin when you are out in the sun. Hair loss is usually temporary. Your hair will usually grow back after treatment finishes. Rarely, hair may not grow back. Or it may grow back thinner than before. If you are worried about this, talk to your cancer doctor or nurse.
answer: Hair loss is a common side effect of breast cancer treatment. You will likely lose all the hair on your head, as well as your eyelashes, eyebrows, and other body hair. This hair loss usually starts after your first or second treatment cycle. While it can be distressing, it is important to remember that this hair loss is temporary in most cases. Your healthcare team can discuss options like scalp cooling that may help reduce hair loss for some patients. They can also provide advice on coping with hair loss, such as using wigs, scarves or other head coverings. Be sure to protect your scalp from the sun if it becomes sensitive. After your treatment ends, your hair will usually grow back, though it may initially be thinner than before. Rarely, hair loss can be permanent, so let your doctor know if you have concerns. Hair loss is an unfortunate but manageable side effect.

question: How can I manage a sore mouth or throat during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: This treatment may cause a sore mouth and throat. You may also get mouth ulcers. This can make you more likely to get a mouth or throat infection. Use a soft toothbrush to clean your teeth or dentures in the morning, at night and after meals. If your mouth or throat is sore: •tell your nurse or doctor – they can give you a mouthwash or medicines to help •try to drink plenty of fluids •avoid alcohol, tobacco and foods that irritate your mouth and throat.
answer: Breast cancer treatment can unfortunately cause side effects like a sore mouth, throat or mouth ulcers. This increases your risk of developing a mouth or throat infection, so it's important to take steps to manage it. Use a soft toothbrush to gently clean your teeth or dentures in the morning, at night, and after meals. If your mouth or throat becomes sore, be sure to tell your nurse or doctor right away. They can provide a medicated mouthwash or other medications to help relieve the discomfort. Try to drink plenty of fluids, and avoid anything that could further irritate your mouth and throat like alcohol, tobacco, or spicy/acidic foods. With proper mouth care and the treatments recommended by your care team, a sore mouth and throat can be managed during your breast cancer treatment.

question: What can I do to manage constipation caused by chemotherapy?
source_excerpt: Drinking plenty of fluids, eating more fibre and doing gentle exercise can help with constipation. You may need to take medicine called laxatives to help. Your GP can prescribe these. Or you can buy them at a pharmacy.
answer: Constipation is a common side effect of chemotherapy and anti-sickness medications. To help manage constipation, it's recommended to drink plenty of fluids, eat more fiber-rich foods, and engage in gentle exercise. If constipation persists, your doctor may prescribe laxatives to provide relief. You can also purchase over-the-counter laxatives from a pharmacy. Don't hesitate to discuss any bowel changes with your healthcare team, as they can provide guidance on managing these side effects effectively.

question: What are the potential effects of chemotherapy on my hands and feet?
section: Numb or tingling hands or feet (peripheral neuropathy)
source_excerpt: Some chemotherapy drugs may affect the nerves. This can cause numb, tingling or painful hands or feet. You may find it hard to fasten buttons or do other fiddly tasks. Tell your doctor if you have these symptoms. They sometimes need to lower the dose of the drug. The symptoms usually improve slowly after treatment finishes. But for some people they may never go away. Talk to your doctor if you are worried about this.
answer: Some chemotherapy drugs can affect the nerves, leading to numbness, tingling, or painful sensations in the hands and feet, a condition known as peripheral neuropathy. This can make it challenging to perform tasks that require fine motor skills, such as buttoning clothes or handling small objects. If you experience these symptoms, it's essential to inform your doctor, as they may need to adjust the dosage of your chemotherapy medication. While the symptoms often improve gradually after treatment ends, for some individuals, they may persist. Your healthcare team can provide guidance and support if you have concerns about managing peripheral neuropathy.

question: Do I need to use contraception during chemotherapy treatment?
source_excerpt: Your doctor will advise you not to get pregnant or make someone pregnant while having this treatment. The drugs may harm a developing baby. It is important to use contraception during your treatment and for a while after treatment finishes. Your doctor, nurse or pharmacist can tell you more about this.
answer: Yes, it is crucial to use contraception during chemotherapy treatment and for some time after treatment has finished. Chemotherapy drugs can potentially harm a developing baby, so it's essential to avoid pregnancy or making someone pregnant while undergoing this treatment. Your doctor, nurse, or pharmacist will advise you on the appropriate contraceptive methods and the duration for which you should continue using them after treatment completion. Following their guidance on contraception is vital to ensure the safety of both you and any potential pregnancy.

question: What are the potential effects of chemotherapy on fertility and having children?
source_excerpt: Some chemotherapy drugs can affect your ability to have children (your fertility). If you are worried about how chemotherapy may affect your fertility, talk to your cancer doctor before treatment starts. There are different options that may help to preserve your fertility. These include: •freezing eggs •freezing embryos (fertilised eggs) •storing sperm.
answer: Chemotherapy can potentially affect your ability to have children, known as your fertility. Some chemotherapy drugs may cause temporary or permanent infertility. If you are concerned about how chemotherapy may impact your fertility, it's important to discuss this with your cancer doctor before starting treatment. There are options available that may help preserve your fertility, such as freezing eggs, freezing embryos (fertilized eggs), or storing sperm. Your healthcare team can provide more information and guidance on fertility preservation methods that may be suitable for your situation.

question: Can chemotherapy cause early menopause, and how can I cope with it?
source_excerpt: Chemotherapy can cause an early menopause, which can be difficult to cope with. This risk is higher if you are already close to menopausal age. We have more information about early menopause at macmillan.org.uk/menopausal-symptoms-and-cancer-treatment
answer: Yes, chemotherapy can potentially cause early menopause, which can be a difficult experience to cope with. The risk of experiencing early menopause is higher if you are already close to the typical menopausal age. Early menopause can bring about various physical and emotional challenges. Macmillan Cancer Support provides helpful information and resources specifically on managing menopausal symptoms and the impact of cancer treatment. Your healthcare team can also offer guidance and support to help you cope with the effects of early menopause during and after your chemotherapy treatment.

question: Are there any precautions I should take regarding sexual activity during chemotherapy?

question: What is hormonal therapy and how does it work for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: Hormones help control how cells grow and what they do in the body. The hormone oestrogen can encourage some breast cancers to grow. This may also happen with the hormone progesterone. Hormonal therapy reduces the amount of oestrogen in the body or stops oestrogen attaching to cancer cells. It only works for breast cancer that is oestrogen receptor positive (ER positive) – page 27. Hormonal therapy is also called endocrine therapy.
answer: Hormonal therapy, also known as endocrine therapy, is a type of treatment that targets the hormones that can encourage the growth of certain breast cancers. Specifically, it reduces the amount of estrogen in the body or stops estrogen from attaching to cancer cells. This type of therapy is effective for breast cancers that are estrogen receptor positive (ER positive). Estrogen and progesterone are hormones that can stimulate the growth of some breast cancers. By blocking or reducing these hormones, hormonal therapy aims to slow down or stop the cancer from growing and spreading.

question: Who is typically prescribed tamoxifen as part of their breast cancer treatment?

question: If I'm taking tamoxifen and want to get pregnant, what should I discuss with my doctor?
source_excerpt: If you want to get pregnant, talk to your cancer doctor or nurse about the timing of this. You will need to have a break in your treatment, and you must stop taking tamoxifen for several months before trying to start a pregnancy (conceive). This is because tamoxifen can harm an unborn baby. Your doctor or nurse can give you more information about getting pregnant after breast cancer.
answer: If you are taking tamoxifen and want to get pregnant, it is very important to discuss the timing with your cancer doctor or nurse. You will need to take a break from your tamoxifen treatment, and you must stop taking the medication for several months before trying to conceive. This is because tamoxifen can potentially harm an unborn baby if you get pregnant while taking it.  Your doctor or nurse can provide you with more detailed information and guidance on planning for pregnancy after breast cancer treatment involving tamoxifen. They can advise you on how long before conception you need to discontinue the medication to ensure it is completely out of your system and no longer poses a risk to the baby.

question: If I start taking tamoxifen before menopause, will I need to switch medications later?
source_excerpt: If you are close to menopause when you start tamoxifen, you may change to an aromatase inhibitor after a few years. Your doctors may do blood tests to check your hormone levels first.
answer: Yes, if you start taking tamoxifen before going through menopause, your doctors may have you switch to a different medication called an aromatase inhibitor after a few years. The reason for this is that aromatase inhibitors are generally more effective for postmenopausal women.  Before making the switch, your doctors will likely do blood tests to check your hormone levels and confirm that you have gone through menopause. Switching from tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor at that point can provide more targeted treatment once you are postmenopausal.  So while tamoxifen may be an appropriate initial treatment for premenopausal breast cancer patients, your medication plan may be adjusted over time based on your changing hormone levels and menopausal status. Your care team will monitor you closely to determine the ideal time to transition to an aromatase inhibitor.

question: What are aromatase inhibitors and how do they work in treating breast cancer?
source_excerpt: Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are the main hormonal therapy drugs used if you have been through the menopause. They stop oestrogen being made in the fatty tissue, muscles and in the glands above the kidneys (adrenal glands). Your cancer doctor may prescribe an AI such as anastrozole, letrozole or exemestane. You take AIs daily as a tablet. AIs may sometimes be given if you have not been through the menopause. But they can only be given with drugs to stop the ovaries working, or if the ovaries have been removed.
answer: Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are a type of hormonal therapy drug that is commonly used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause. These drugs work by stopping the production of estrogen in the body's fatty tissues, muscles, and adrenal glands (glands above the kidneys). By reducing estrogen levels, AIs can help slow or stop the growth of hormone-receptor-positive breast cancers, which rely on estrogen to grow. Common examples of AIs include anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane, which are taken daily as a tablet. AIs can sometimes be given to premenopausal women as well, but only in combination with other drugs that stop the ovaries from producing estrogen or if the ovaries have been surgically removed.

question: What are the potential side effects of taking aromatase inhibitors for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: If you take AIs over a long time, they can cause bone thinning. This is called osteoporosis. You may have a scan to check your bone health (density). This is called a DEXA scan. Having your ovaries removed and ovarian suppression can also cause osteoporosis. You may already be having a drug called a bisphosphonate (pages 104 to 106). These are given to help reduce the risk of cancer spreading to the bones. But they are also used to help protect from osteoporosis. If you are at risk of osteoporosis and are not already having bisphosphonates, your cancer doctor may prescribe them to help protect your bones.
answer: One potential side effect of taking aromatase inhibitors (AIs) over a long period of time is bone thinning, also known as osteoporosis. AIs can cause a decrease in bone density, which increases the risk of fractures and other bone-related issues. To monitor this, your doctor may recommend getting a DEXA scan, which is a type of imaging test that measures bone density. Additionally, having your ovaries removed or undergoing ovarian suppression (stopping the ovaries from working) can also contribute to osteoporosis risk while taking AIs. To help protect your bones and reduce the risk of osteoporosis, your doctor may prescribe bisphosphonate drugs, which are medications that help strengthen bones and prevent bone loss.

question: What is ovarian suppression and how does it work for breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Goserelin (Zoladex®) and leuprorelin (Prostap®) are drugs that stop the ovaries making oestrogen. This is called ovarian suppression. It causes a temporary menopause. This means you will not get a period while you are taking them. These types of drugs stop the pituitary gland in the brain from sending messages to the ovaries to produce oestrogen. This causes side effects similar to menopausal symptoms. These include: •hot flushes and sweats •joint pain •low sex drive •mood changes •osteoporosis.
answer: Ovarian suppression is a treatment option for premenopausal women with breast cancer. It involves taking drugs like goserelin (Zoladex®) or leuprorelin (Prostap®) that stop the ovaries from producing estrogen. This causes a temporary menopause and lowers estrogen levels in the body, which reduces the risk of the breast cancer coming back. However, it can also cause side effects similar to menopausal symptoms like hot flashes, joint pain, low sex drive, mood changes, and increased risk of osteoporosis. Your doctor will monitor your bone health and advise you on how to manage these side effects.

question: What is ovarian ablation and how does it differ from ovarian suppression?
source_excerpt: If you have not been through the menopause, your cancer doctor may advise having 1 of these treatments with another hormonal therapy: •ovarian suppression – this stops the ovaries making oestrogen and causes a temporary menopause •removing the ovaries (ablation) – this causes a permanent menopause.

question: What are the hormonal therapy options for breast cancer treatment before menopause?
source_excerpt:
If you have not been through the menopause, your cancer doctor may recommend 1 of the following:
 •tamoxifen
 •goserelin or leuprorelin – with tamoxifen or an AI 
 •surgery to remove the ovaries – on its own or with tamoxifen or an AI.
answer: If you have not gone through menopause yet, your cancer doctor may recommend one of the following hormonal therapy options for treating your breast cancer:  1. Tamoxifen: This is a hormone therapy medication that blocks estrogen from binding to cancer cells, slowing or stopping their growth.  2. Goserelin or leuprorelin, along with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor (AI): These are injections that temporarily stop the ovaries from producing estrogen, essentially putting you into a medical menopause. They are often given with tamoxifen or an AI to further reduce estrogen levels.  3. Surgery to remove the ovaries (ovarian ablation), alone or with tamoxifen or an AI: This is a minor surgical procedure to permanently stop the ovaries from producing estrogen. It induces menopause immediately and may be combined with tamoxifen or an AI.  Your doctor will discuss the best option for your specific situation, considering factors like your age, cancer type, and treatment goals. Don't hesitate to ask questions and voice any concerns you may have about these treatments.

question: What are the hormonal therapy options for breast cancer treatment after menopause?

answer: Ovarian ablation is a surgical procedure to remove the ovaries. It may be recommended as a hormonal therapy option for breast cancer treatment if you have not gone through menopause and do not want to have hormone injection treatments.  The ovarian ablation procedure involves a small operation, typically done using keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery. Here's how it is performed:  1. The surgeon makes a small cut in your abdomen (tummy area). 2. A thin tube called a laparoscope is inserted through the cut. This tube has a tiny light, camera, and surgical instrument attached. 3. The surgeon uses the laparoscope to locate and remove the ovaries through the small abdominal cut.  Ovarian ablation causes immediate menopause since the ovaries, which produce estrogen, are removed. This means your periods will stop right away, and you will no longer be able to get pregnant.  Recovery from this minimally invasive surgery is usually quick, but you may need a short hospital stay. Your doctor will likely recommend taking tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor along with the ovarian ablation to further reduce estrogen levels.

question: What are goserelin and leuprorelin injections used for in breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt:
You have goserelin as a monthly injection under the skin of the tummy (abdomen). You usually have leuprorelin as an injection every 3 months. You usually have 1 of these drugs along with tamoxifen or an AI.

When you finish treatment, the ovaries usually start to produce oestrogen again. This means your periods will come back. But this may not happen if you were close to your natural menopause when you started treatment.
answer: Goserelin and leuprorelin are injectable medications that may be recommended as part of hormonal therapy for breast cancer treatment before menopause. These injections work by temporarily stopping the ovaries from producing estrogen, essentially putting you into a medical menopause.  Specifically:  - Goserelin is given as a monthly injection under the skin of the abdomen (tummy area). - Leuprorelin is typically given as an injection every 3 months.  These medications are usually prescribed along with either tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor (AI). By stopping estrogen production from the ovaries and using additional hormone therapy drugs, the goal is to significantly reduce the levels of estrogen in your body that could potentially fuel breast cancer growth.  After you finish treatment with goserelin or leuprorelin, your ovaries will usually start producing estrogen again, and your periods will likely return. However, if you were close to natural menopause when starting treatment, your periods may not come back.  Your doctor will explain the potential benefits and side effects of these injectable treatments and determine if they are a suitable option for your specific breast cancer case.

question: What are some common side effects of hormonal therapy for breast cancer?

question: What are the potential risks associated with hormonal therapy for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: Some types of hormonal therapy can slightly increase the risk of developing a blood clot. Tamoxifen may also slightly increase the risk of womb changes and womb cancer. Tell your cancer doctor if you have any vaginal discharge or bleeding.
answer: While hormonal therapy is an effective treatment option for breast cancer, it does carry some potential risks. Certain types of hormonal therapy drugs can slightly increase the risk of developing a blood clot, which is a serious condition that requires prompt medical attention. Additionally, the drug tamoxifen may slightly increase the risk of changes in the uterine lining and even uterine cancer. If you experience any vaginal discharge or bleeding during your treatment, it's crucial to inform your cancer doctor immediately, as this could be a sign of an underlying issue.

question: What are targeted therapy drugs and how are they used in breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Targeted therapy drugs interfere with the way cancer cells grow. The targeted therapy drugs used to treat breast cancer are trastuzumab (often called Herceptin®) and pertuzumab (Perjeta®). They help to reduce the risk of HER2 positive breast cancer coming back (page 28). You may have trastuzumab on its own or with pertuzumab. They may be given together as an injection called Phesgo® (page 101). Trastuzumab and pertuzumab may also be given with chemotherapy. You may have them before or after surgery and radiotherapy. There are newer types of targeted therapy drug to treat HER positive breast cancer. You may have these if you have already had trastuzumab and pertuzumab.
answer: Targeted therapy drugs are a type of treatment that interferes with the specific ways cancer cells grow and spread. In the case of breast cancer, the targeted therapy drugs commonly used are trastuzumab (often called Herceptin®) and pertuzumab (Perjeta®). These drugs are particularly effective in reducing the risk of HER2 positive breast cancer recurring or coming back after initial treatment. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab may be given alone or in combination, sometimes as an injection called Phesgo®. They can also be administered along with chemotherapy, either before or after surgery and radiotherapy. If you have already received trastuzumab and pertuzumab, your doctor may recommend newer types of targeted therapy drugs to continue treating your HER2 positive breast cancer.

question: How is trastuzumab administered and for how long?

question: What are the common side effects of trastuzumab?
source_excerpt: The side effects of trastuzumab are usually mild. You may have some side effects while you are having the infusion or injection, or up to 4 hours after. This is more likely to happen with the first dose. These side effects include flu-like symptoms, such as: •a headache •a high temperature (fever) and chills •feeling sick. Any side effects usually get better a few hours after you finish the treatment. Another possible side effect is an allergic reaction, but this is rare. The nurses will check for signs of a reaction. If it happens, they can treat it quickly with drugs. You may get other side effects after treatment. These include: •diarrhoea •headaches •feeling sick.

question: Can trastuzumab affect the heart, and what is done to monitor this?
source_excerpt: Trastuzumab may cause changes in the way the heart works. This can cause problems in some people. Usually, the effect is mild and returns to normal after treatment ends. You may be given heart medicines to help with this side effect. You usually have tests to check your heart before and during treatment. This is usually a scan of the heart called an echocardiogram. It helps to make sure the drug is not causing any damage. Trastuzumab is not usually given to people who have serious heart problems. If there are any changes with your heart, you may be referred to a heart specialist doctor called a cardiologist. They may give you drugs to support your heart.

question: What is pertuzumab and how is it administered?

The nurses will closely monitor you during the infusion and for about an hour afterwards to ensure your safety.

question: What are adjuvant bisphosphonates and when are they used for breast cancer?
source_excerpt: If you have early breast cancer, bisphosphonates can help lower the risk of the cancer coming back. This is called adjuvant treatment. You have bisphosphonates for 3 to 5 years. question: What are some common side effects of bisphosphonates used to treat breast cancer?

Bisphosphonates do not usually cause serious side effects. But rarely

answer: Bisphosphonates are medications sometimes used to treat breast cancer. Some common side effects of these drugs include mild nausea, indigestion, and flu-like symptoms. It's important to take good care of your dental health and have regular checkups to reduce risks. Your doctor will also monitor your kidney function with blood tests. Don't hesitate to report any concerning side effects to your cancer care team.

question: What kind of follow-up care and monitoring can breast cancer patients expect after completing treatment?
section: Follow-up for women with breast cancer
source_excerpt:
After treatment, you will have regular check-ups with your cancer doctor 
or regular contact with your breast care nurse. 
You will have mammograms every year for 5 years on the other breast. 
If you have had breast-conserving surgery, you will have mammograms 
on both breasts. If you have had a double mastectomy, you will not be 
offered mammograms. 
After 5 years, if you are 50 or over, you usually have mammograms 
through the NHS breast screening programmes. Younger women 
usually continue to have yearly mammograms after the first 5 years, 
until they reach 50. 
Instead of regular appointments, your nurse may give you information 
about what to look out for. They will give you contact numbers and 
ask you to contact them or your cancer doctor if there is anything 
you are worried about. You may have your follow-up appointments 
at a nurse-led clinic. This means you will only go to your cancer doctor 
if something needs to be checked further.
It is natural to feel anxious before appointments.
answer: After completing breast cancer treatment, patients will have regular follow-up care and monitoring. This typically involves check-ups with the cancer doctor or breast care nurse on a set schedule. Mammograms will be done yearly for 5 years on the remaining breast(s). After 5 years, women over 50 usually transition to the NHS breast screening program, while younger women may continue yearly mammograms until age 50. Some follow-up may be done at nurse-led clinics, where the nurse provides monitoring and only refers back to the cancer doctor if any issues arise. It's natural to feel anxious before these appointments, but support is available.

question: What should I expect my treated breast to look and feel like after treatment?

question: How long does it typically take to recover from the side effects of breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: It can often take several months to recover from the effects of treatment. You may have treatment side effects that do not improve after a few months. Everyone's recovery journey is different, but be patient and kind to yourself as you navigate this process. If you find that certain side effects are not improving after a few months or if you develop new side effects months or years after treatment, be sure to inform your cancer doctor or breast care nurse right away. They can provide guidance and support to help manage any lingering or new side effects.

question: What is lymphoedema and what causes it after breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Lymphoedema is a swelling of the arm or hand on the side you had treatment. It sometimes happens after surgery or radiotherapy to the lymph nodes in the armpit. It usually develops slowly, months or years after treatment. Lymphoedema is more likely to happen if all or many of your lymph nodes were removed. Having radiotherapy to the armpit as well as surgery increases the risk. If you notice any swelling in your arm, hand or chest, ask your doctor or nurse to check it. The earlier lymphoedema is diagnosed, the easier it is to manage and treat successfully.

question: How can breast cancer treatment affect a person's sex life and fertility?
source_excerpt: Breast cancer and its treatments and side effects may affect your sex life and your feelings about yourself. You may have: •loss of sex drive (low libido) •vaginal dryness – this may be caused by menopausal symptoms (page 117). Difficulties often slowly improve after treatment, but it may take longer. Some people may continue to have difficulties. You may feel insecure and worry about your current or future relationships. If you have a partner, it can help to talk openly with them about your feelings. You may both need some time to adjust. Let your doctor or nurse know if any difficulties with your sex life do not improve. They may be able to reassure you or offer further help and support. If you feel uncomfortable talking to your doctor or nurse, you can call us on 0808 808 00 00. We have more information in our booklet Cancer and your sex life (page 134). Some people may find it helpful to talk to a sex therapist. You can contact a therapist through the College of Sexual and Relationship Therapists (page 144).

It's common to feel insecure or worried about current or future relationships. Open communication with your partner can help as you both adjust to the changes. If sexual difficulties don't improve, let your doctor or nurse know so they can provide reassurance, support, or further help. Speaking to a sex therapist may also be beneficial for some.

question: What is a sentinel lymph node biopsy and how does it relate to the risk of lymphoedema?
source_excerpt: You may have had only 1 or 2 lymph nodes removed. This is called a sentinel lymph node biopsy (pages 48 to 50). The risk of lymphoedema is low after this. If you are not sure what type of lymph node surgery you had, your breast care nurse can tell you.
answer: A sentinel lymph node biopsy is a procedure where only 1 or 2 lymph nodes are removed from the armpit area during breast cancer surgery. If you're unsure what type of lymph node surgery you had, your breast care nurse can clarify this for you. Knowing whether you had a sentinel node biopsy or more extensive lymph node removal can help understand your personal risk level for lymphoedema.

question: How can breast cancer treatments affect fertility?
source_excerpt: Some breast cancer treatments may affect your fertility. Your periods may stop during treatment. If you are younger, they may start again after treatment has ended. But it may take several months for them to start again. If you are close to your natural menopause, chemotherapy can cause an early menopause.
answer: Breast cancer treatments like chemotherapy can potentially affect your fertility. During treatment, your periods may stop temporarily. If you are younger, they may start again after treatment ends, but it can take several months. However, if you are close to natural menopause, chemotherapy may cause an early menopause. It's important to discuss your fertility concerns with your cancer doctor before starting treatment. In some cases, it may be possible to remove and freeze your eggs or fertilized embryos beforehand to preserve your fertility. Becoming infertile can be very difficult emotionally, whether you already have children or not. Don't hesitate to seek counseling support to help cope with these feelings.

question: What options are available to preserve fertility before breast cancer treatment?

question: What advice is given regarding contraception during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Your doctor will advise you not to get pregnant while having treatment and for some time afterwards. The drugs can affect your eggs. This may harm a developing baby. It is important to use effective contraception. You can talk about this with your doctor or nurse. Your cancer doctor or nurse will advise you not to use contraception that contains hormones. This includes the pill or implants that release hormones. Your GP can give you advice about methods of contraception. These may include: •coils (intra-uterine devices) that do not contain hormones •barrier methods such as condoms •diaphragms or caps.
answer: During breast cancer treatment and for some time afterwards, it is important to use effective contraception. The cancer drugs can affect your eggs and potentially harm a developing baby. Your doctor or nurse will advise you not to use contraceptive methods that contain hormones, such as the pill or hormone-releasing implants. Instead, they may recommend non-hormonal options like copper coils (IUDs), barrier methods like condoms, diaphragms, or caps. It's best to discuss your contraceptive choices with your cancer care team or GP to find the most suitable option for your situation.

question: Is the Mirena coil a suitable contraceptive option for breast cancer patients?
source_excerpt: Mirena® coil The Mirena® coil works by releasing a small amount of a hormonal medicine into the womb. The medicine is called levonorgestrel. It is an artificial type of progesterone. Doctors are unsure how much of it reaches other parts of the body after it has been released into the womb. Studies have tried to find out if the Mirena coil could cause cancers that depend on hormones to grow. The results have been mixed. But there is currently no strong evidence to show that the Mirena coil encourages these types of cancer to grow. Because it contains progesterone, it is not usually recommended for people who have had cancers that depend on hormones to grow. This includes breast cancer. If you are concerned, you can talk to your GP or specialist about what contraception is best for you.
answer: The Mirena coil releases a small amount of the hormone levonorgestrel, which is a type of progesterone, into the womb. While studies have had mixed results on whether it could encourage hormone-dependent cancers to grow, there is currently no strong evidence that the Mirena coil promotes the growth of these cancers, including breast cancer. However, because it contains progesterone, the Mirena coil is generally not recommended for people who have had hormone-dependent cancers like breast cancer. If you have concerns, it's best to discuss contraceptive options with your GP or cancer specialist to determine what method is most suitable for your individual situation.

question: What advice is given about getting pregnant after breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: Having a family can be an important part of life after cancer. Your doctor may advise you to wait for 2 years before trying to get pregnant. This is because breast cancer is most likely to come back during this time. But it also gives you time to recover from treatment. Studies show that getting pregnant after breast cancer does not increase the risk of it coming back. If you are taking hormonal therapy and are thinking of getting pregnant, it is important to talk to your cancer doctor first (pages 88 to 96). If you are taking tamoxifen, you must not get pregnant. This is because it may harm a developing baby. Talk to your cancer doctor before you stop taking any medicines. We have more information about getting pregnant in our booklet Managing the late effects of breast cancer treatment (page 134).

question: How can breast cancer treatments affect menopause and what are the risks?
source_excerpt: Some treatments can cause an early or temporary menopause. Hormonal therapy can cause side effects that are the same as menopausal symptoms. Doctors do not recommend hormone replacement therapy (HRT). This is because it contains oestrogen. This could encourage breast cancer cells to grow. Early menopause can increase the risk of bone thinning (osteoporosis). We have more information about looking after your bones, including tips on keeping them healthy, in our booklet Bone health and cancer treatment (page 134).
answer: Some breast cancer treatments can cause early or temporary menopause. Hormonal therapy medications used to treat breast cancer can also cause side effects that mimic menopausal symptoms. Doctors do not recommend taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for menopausal symptoms in breast cancer patients, as HRT contains estrogen which could potentially encourage any remaining breast cancer cells to grow. Going through early menopause can increase the risk of developing osteoporosis or bone thinning. The booklet 'Bone health and cancer treatment' provides more information on keeping bones healthy during and after breast cancer, including tips to reduce osteoporosis risk.

question: What lifestyle changes can I make after breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: After breast cancer treatment, you may choose to make some positive lifestyle changes. You may have already had a healthy lifestyle before breast cancer. But you may be more focused on making the most of your health.
answer: After going through breast cancer treatment, it's a great time to focus on making positive lifestyle changes to support your overall well-being and recovery. Maintaining a healthy weight through a balanced diet with plenty of fruits and vegetables, limiting saturated fats and sugars, and being physically active can help reduce the risk of the cancer returning as well as other health conditions like heart disease and diabetes. Regular exercise not only helps manage your weight but can also reduce stress, fatigue, and keep your bones and heart strong. Making these lifestyle adjustments can empower you to take control of your health during this new chapter.

question: Why is it important to maintain a healthy weight after breast cancer treatment?
section: Eat well and keep to a healthy weight
source_excerpt: Keeping to a healthy weight reduces the risk of some other cancers, heart problems and other conditions such as diabetes. There is some evidence that keeping to a healthy weight after menopause may help reduce the risk of breast cancer coming back.
answer: Maintaining a healthy weight after breast cancer treatment is important for several reasons. First, treatments like chemotherapy and hormone therapy can sometimes lead to weight gain, so getting back to a healthy weight range is advisable once you're feeling better. Keeping your weight in a healthy range reduces the risk of other cancers, heart problems, diabetes, and other conditions. There is also some evidence that maintaining a healthy weight after menopause may help lower the risk of breast cancer recurrence. Your doctor can advise if your current weight is within the recommended range for your height.

Making these dietary adjustments can help you reach and sustain a healthy weight, which provides numerous benefits for overall health and may even reduce the risk of cancer recurrence.

question: What can I do to keep my bones healthy during breast cancer treatment?
source_excerpt:
To keep your bones healthy:
 •keep physically active 
 •eat a healthy diet with enough calcium and vitamin D 
 •avoid smoking.
answer: It's important to take steps to keep your bones healthy during breast cancer treatment, especially if you are receiving treatments that can reduce estrogen levels like aromatase inhibitors or cause early menopause. Here are some tips:  1. Stay physically active with regular exercise as tolerated. Weight-bearing activities like walking can help strengthen bones.  2. Eat a healthy diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, which are essential for bone health. Good sources include dairy products, leafy greens, and fatty fish.  3. Avoid smoking, as it increases the risk of osteoporosis (bone thinning).  By following these lifestyle measures, you can help minimize bone loss and maintain strong, healthy bones throughout your treatment journey. If you have concerns, discuss them with your care team.

question: How can I protect my heart health during breast cancer treatment?

answer: Some breast cancer treatments can potentially increase the risk of heart problems later on, so it's important to take steps to protect your heart health. Here are some recommendations:  1. Eat a nutritious, heart-healthy diet focused on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins.  3. Don't smoke, as smoking is a major risk factor for heart disease.  4. Follow sensible alcohol drinking guidelines and avoid excessive alcohol consumption.  By adopting a heart-healthy lifestyle with exercise, good nutrition, avoiding smoking and limiting alcohol, you can help minimize any potential cardiac risks associated with your breast cancer treatment. Your care team can provide more personalized guidance.

question: Why is it important for breast cancer patients to quit smoking?
source_excerpt: If you smoke, stopping is one of the healthiest decisions you can make. Smoking increases your risk of osteoporosis and is a major risk factor for smoking-related cancers and heart disease.
answer: Quitting smoking is one of the healthiest decisions a breast cancer patient can make. There are several important reasons why stopping smoking is highly recommended:  1. Smoking increases the risk of osteoporosis (bone thinning), which can be a concern with certain breast cancer treatments that lower estrogen levels.  2. Smoking is a major risk factor for many other cancers, as well as heart disease. As a cancer survivor, reducing cancer risk is crucial.  3. Smoking can impair the effectiveness of cancer treatments and negatively impact recovery and outcomes.  4. Smoking cessation improves overall health and well-being during and after cancer treatment.  By quitting smoking, breast cancer patients can protect their bones, reduce future cancer risk, optimize their treatment efficacy, and improve their overall health. Smoking cessation support resources are available to help make this positive lifestyle change.

question: What are the recommended alcohol drinking guidelines for breast cancer patients?
source_excerpt:
Current NHS guidelines suggest that you should:
 •not regularly drink more than 14 units of alcohol in 1 week
 •spread the alcohol units you drink in 1 week over 3 or more days
 •try to have several alcohol-free days every week.
answer: According to current NHS guidelines, breast cancer patients should follow these sensible alcohol drinking recommendations:  - Do not regularly drink more than 14 units of alcohol in a single week.  - Spread out the alcohol units you do drink over 3 or more days in the week. - Try to have several alcohol-free days every week.  Limiting alcohol intake is advisable for breast cancer patients for a few reasons. Alcohol can increase the risk of certain cancers and negatively impact heart health. It can also potentially interact with some cancer treatments.  By sticking to these guidelines and moderating alcohol consumption, breast cancer patients can make healthier choices to support their overall treatment and recovery. However, it's best to discuss your specific situation with your care team.

question: How can breast cancer patients manage stress during their treatment journey?
section: Try to reduce stress in your life
source_excerpt:
Try to reduce stress in your life 
Being diagnosed with breast cancer can be stressful. One way 
of coping with stress is to make time to relax. This could include:
 •going for a walk
 •having a meal with family or friends
 •listening to music or watching a film
 •trying activities such as yoga, or relaxation techniques 
to control breathing
 •being more physically active and looking after your well-being
 •talking to someone about how you feel.
answer: Being diagnosed with and treated for breast cancer can understandably cause a lot of stress and anxiety. It's important to find healthy ways to cope with this stress during your treatment journey. Here are some suggestions:  - Make time for relaxing activities like going for a walk, listening to music, or watching a favorite movie. Anything that helps calm your mind.  - Try stress-relieving practices like yoga, meditation, or breathing exercises to promote relaxation.  - Stay physically active through exercise as you are able. Physical activity is a great stress-reducer.  - Focus on your overall well-being through good nutrition, adequate sleep, and self-care activities you enjoy.  - Talk to loved ones about how you are feeling. Sharing your thoughts can help release stress.  - Consider joining a support group to connect with others going through similar experiences.  The key is finding stress management techniques that work for you. Managing stress in a healthy way can help you feel better physically and emotionally as you navigate this challenging time.

question: What information is available about talking to children when an adult has cancer?

Sometimes their fears can be worse than the reality. How much you tell children will depend on their age and how mature they are. It may be best to start by giving only small amounts of information and gradually tell them more to build up a picture. We have more information in our booklet Talking to children and teenagers when an adult has cancer.

It may be best to start by providing small amounts of information gradually to build up a full picture. Macmillan has a dedicated booklet called 'Talking to children and teenagers when an adult has cancer' that provides guidance on this sensitive topic.

question: How can I manage work during and after cancer treatment?
source_excerpt: You may not know how cancer will affect your work, now or in the future. It is a good idea to talk to your manager or human resources (HR) department soon after you are diagnosed. This will help them to support you better. Some people stop working during cancer treatment and for a while after, until they feel ready to go back. Others carry on working, sometimes with reduced hours or other changes to their job. Your cancer doctor, GP or specialist nurse can help you decide whether you should stop working, and when and if you should go back to work. Our booklets Work and cancer, Working while caring for someone with cancer and Self-employment and cancer have more information that may be helpful. You can also find out more about your employment rights in our booklet Your rights at work when you are affected by cancer (page 134).
answer: Dealing with cancer treatment can significantly impact your ability to work, both during treatment and in the recovery period afterwards. It's advisable to have an open discussion with your manager or HR department soon after your diagnosis. This will allow them to better support you through this challenging time. Some people choose to take a temporary leave from work during treatment and recovery, while others continue working with reduced hours or modified job responsibilities. Your cancer doctor, GP, or specialist nurse can provide guidance on whether you should stop working temporarily, and when it may be appropriate to return to work. Macmillan offers several helpful resources on navigating work and cancer, including booklets on employment rights, working while caregiving, and self-employment during cancer treatment.

question: What are some ways I can help support people with cancer?
source_excerpt: 5 ways you can help someone with cancer 1. Share your cancer experience Support people living with cancer by telling your story, online, in the media or face to face. 2. Campaign for change We need your help to make sure everyone gets the right support. Take an action, big or small, for better cancer care. 3. Help someone in your community A lift to an appointment. answer: There are several meaningful ways you can help support those affected by cancer. One option is to share your own cancer experience, whether online, in the media, or in person, to provide encouragement and solidarity. You could also get involved in campaigning for positive changes to improve cancer care and ensure everyone receives the right support. Offering practical assistance in your local community, like providing transportation to appointments or helping with shopping, can make a big difference. Additionally, you can raise funds through participating in events or creating your own fundraiser. Even small monetary donations can contribute to the cause. The key is finding a way to lend a hand that resonates with you.

question: What kind of support does Macmillan Cancer Support provide?
source_excerpt: At Macmillan we know cancer can disrupt your whole life. We'll do whatever it takes to help everyone living with cancer in the UK get the support they need right now, and transform cancer care for the future.
answer: Macmillan Cancer Support is a charitable organization dedicated to helping individuals living with cancer in the UK. They offer comprehensive support services, including information, emotional support, and practical assistance. Macmillan recognizes that cancer can disrupt every aspect of a person's life, and they are committed to doing whatever it takes to help those affected by cancer get the support they need right now. Additionally, Macmillan aims to transform cancer care for the future, ensuring better support and resources for cancer patients and their loved ones.
